Cardiac arrest Aetiology: Three-quarters of out of hospital cardiac arrests are due to ventricular fibrillation in patients with pre- existing heart disease, although across a general population this is only true of 20% of cardiac arrests Only a small proportion can be attributed to pulseless electrical activity (PEA); the rest are due to asystole PEA may have a potentially reversible cause: hypovolaemia

stem: A 68-year-old woman recently diagnosed with multiple myeloma presents to her GP with progressively increasing breathlessness, reduced exercise tolerance and ankle swelling. On examination, there is bilateral pitting leg oedema to her thighs, ascites and raised JVP. The apical impulse is impalpable. An ECG shows diffusely diminished voltage. Chest X-ray is normal and the echocardiogram shows small, thick ventricles and dilated atria with a thickened interatrial septum. The ventricular myocardium has a granular sparkling texture on echo, and minimal fluid in the pericardial space is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis leading to symptoms of cardiac failure?
explanation:
Restrictive cardiomyopathy
The key feature in this scenario is that the patient has multiple myeloma which is known to produce excessive immunoglobulin light chains, which can cause a secondary cardiac amyloid; this is a type of restrictive cardiomyopathy. Restrictive cardiomyopathy Aetiology: Restrictive cardiomyopathy can develop secondary to amyloidosis associated with an immunocyte dyscrasia. Examination and investigation findings:

stem: A 17-year-old boy is reviewed in the clinic with increasing shortness of breath. He and his family have not consulted medical services for many years. On examination, he looks mildly cyanosed at rest and has a respiratory rate of 21/min. His blood pressure is 122/51 mmHg, and he has a pulse of 105 bpm. He has a continuous machinery murmur, loudest in the left upper chest, which is accentuated partially in systole. Colour- flow Doppler echocardiography identifies flow directly between the aortic arch and pulmonary artery. There are signs of pulmonary hypertension. Given the probable diagnosis, what is the likely nature of his pulse on clinical examination?
explanation:
Collapsing
This patient's symptoms suggest that he is suffering from significant pulmonary hypertension. Preferential blood flow through the low-resistance pulmonary circulation via a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is leading to a collapsing peripheral pulse. He is likely to be at an increased risk of pulmonary haemorrhage, periods of severe hypoxia, and respiratory tract infection. Once pulmonary hypertension is established, it is thought that surgical repair will be ineffective. If intraoperative occlusion does not reduce pulmonary pressures and increase aortic diastolic pressure in particular, then the PDA should not be closed.

Jerky
Jerky is incorrect. A Jerky (‘bisferiens’) pulse refers to a collapse of the pulse followed by a secondary rise. A jerky pulse may be present in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who is known to have a cardiac murmur becomes pregnant. It is noted that the intensity of her murmur diminishes during her pregnancy. Which cardiac abnormality is she likely to have?
explanation:
Aortic regurgitation
The fall in diastolic blood pressure during pregnancy leads to a reduction in the murmur of aortic regurgitation. Murmurs follow pressure gradients – if the blood pressure is lower, then the difference between the aortic pressure and LV pressure is less, making the murmur quieter. Haemodynamic changes in pregnancy: During pregnancy, cardiac output and blood volume increase from the second month up to the 30th week to 30–50% above the normal levels The average increase in blood volume during pregnancy amounts to 1600 ml, and there is also an increased metabolic workload The increase in cardiac output is mediated via increase in both stroke volume and to a lesser extent heart rate, along with a dramatic fall in total peripheral vascular resistance. Examination findings: Warm extremities

stem: A 71-year-old woman with a history of one previous myocardial infarction presents to the Emergency Department. She has sudden onset shortness of breath and palpitations, which happened after her dinner a couple of hours earlier. A previous ECG from clinic a month earlier shows sinus rhythm, the clinic notes indicate that there were no abnormal findings on examination that day. The patient is currently taking ramipril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily and aspirin 75 mg. On examination her blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg, her pulse is 140 bpm irregular and she has evidence of left ventricular failure. Clinical results are given in the table below: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 140 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.7 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 190 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ECG Fast atrial fibrillation, lateral ST depression Which one of the following is the most appropriate medication to control her atrial fibrillation?
explanation:
Amiodarone
Amiodarone will both slow the ventricular rate and increase the chances of successful cardioversion – either alone or in conjunction with electricity. This is a reasonable goal as we have both clinical and ECG evidence that this atrial fibrillation (AF) is of recent onset. This patient is in AF which is likley to have occurred within the last 24 hours. Given the fast rate of the patient's AF, it can be concluded with reasonable certainty this is the patient’s definite time of AF onset. If a patient is not known to have pre-existing AF or paroxysmal AF (PAF) then it is reasonable to persue a rhythm control approach in this situation, particularly as she is showing some signs of heart failure )as fast AF can cause transient LV dysfunction which will become permanent if left untreated). Digoxin is not the best choice with regards to rhythm control and is much more effective at rate control. Also it takes too long to work and would be of little help in this situation. Flecanide is a good drug for rate control, however the patient does have a history of ischaemic heart disease and is also showing signs of rate related ischaemia (ST depression on ECG), this may be due to some further underlying ischaemic heart disease. In that case it would be best avoided due to the associated increased mortality. Sotalol and verapamil would also be less effective due to their negatively inotropic effects and as such are used far less frequently in clinical practice. This therefore leaves amiodarone which can be given IV to both promote sinus rhythm and slow her heart rate down. If sinus rhythm wasn’t restored with this alone, cardiovertion of the patient should be within 24 hours. If there was any indication this could be PAF a trans-oesphageal echo should be carried out before cardioverting to ensure there was no thrombus within the left atrial appendage. Also commence anticoagulation in these patients, as this patient's CHADSVASC score would be 3.

Digoxin
Digoxin is incorrect. Although digoxin would be effective at slowing the ventricular rate, it seems that this epiosode of AF is of recent onset, making cardioversion a better goal.

Flecainide
Flecainide is incorrect. Flecainide, although effective at cardioverting AF, is contraindicated in patients with a history of ischaemic heart disease, as the CAST post- infarct trial demonstrated increased mortality in patients treated with flecainide.

Sotalol
Sotalol is incorrect. Sotalol is negatively inotropic and likely to worsen left ventricular failure.

Verapamil
Verapamil is incorrect. Verapamil is negatively inotropic and likely to worsen left ventricular failure.

stem: A 67-year-old man is referred to the clinic with intermittent diarrhoea over the past 3 months, vague abdominal pains and a new onset mitral murmur which was discovered by his GP. He is usually fit and well and until recently continued to hold down a job in his solicitor’s practice. On further questioning you discover that he has suffered from night sweats for the past 3-4 weeks. His BP is 135/72 mmHg, pulse is 90/min and regular. There is a mitral regurgitation murmur and mild bilateral ankle swelling. You notice splinter haemorrhages on examination of his hands. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 104 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 192 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 84 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 159 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Barium enema (referred by GP) Splenic flexure colonic lesion What is the likely causative organism to be found on blood culture?
explanation:
Streptococcus bovis
The clinical scenario is consistent with endocarditis, in the presence of a colonic lesion suspicious of an underlying carcinoma, S. bovis must be considered as a probable cause. Streptococcus bovis infection is associated with underlying colonic carcinoma or infection of the biliary tree. Where it is found on blood culture in a diagnosis of endocarditis, then imaging of the large bowel is essential. Where no colonic lesion is found, pathology of the biliary tree is the next consideration. Both benzyl penicillin and ceftriaxone are considerations for antibiotic therapy.

Streptococcus pyogenes
Streptococcus pyogenes is incorrect. Streptococci are the most common cause of community acquired native valve endocarditis (40%) and the second most common organism overall to cause endocarditis (17%). The most common species is Streptococcus viridans and not streptococcus pyogenes. Streptococcus bovis and other non- group A streptococci are also found sometimes. Streptococcus pyogenes mainly causes pharyngitis and is associated with rheumatic fever, rheumatic heart disease and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and not infective endocarditis.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus is the overall most common cause of infective endocarditis (31%). It is also the most common cause of health-care associated native valve endocarditis (53%); however, in this case the presence of colonic carcinoma makes streptococcus bovis more likely than staphylococcus aureus.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is incorrect. Pseudomonas aeuroginosa and mycobacterium tuberculosis are rare causes of infective endocarditis. Pseudomonas aeruginosa usually causes right sided endocarditis in injection drug users and addicts; this is an unlikely possibility here as the patient is not an injection drug user.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Mycobacterium tuberculosis is incorrect. Tubercular endocarditis caused by mycobacterium tuberculosis is rare and usually seen in patients with disseminated tubercular infection. There are no pulmonary symptoms here to suggest tuberculosis. Although the presence of night sweats and a high ESR could indicate tuberculosis, both of these are non-specific and can be seen in multiple conditions including cancers. The absence of pulomonary tuberculosis makes this very unlikely to be tuberculous endocarditis.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents with 15 minutes of central crushing chest pain. The electrocardiogram (ECG) shows 0.5 mm ST elevation in leads V1 and V2. His blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg and his heart rate is 110bpm. He has bibasal crepitations and an elevated jugular venous pressure. You are in a district general hospital that does not have an acute cardiac catheterisation laboratory. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Aspirin + heparin and repeat ECG in 15 min
No treatment and repeat ECG in 15 min
explanation:
Aspirin + heparin and repeat ECG in 15 min
The criteria for STEMI is new (or increased) and persistent ST-segment elevation in at least two contiguous leads of ≥1 mm in all leads, other than leads V2-V3 where the following cut points apply: ≥ 2.5 mm in men <40 years old ≥ 2 mm in men >40 years old ≥ 1.5 mm in women regardless of age. Therefore, thrombolysis is not indicated here. However, in the context of a good history of cardiac pain and borderline ECG, an acute coronary event should be strongly suspected and aspirin and heparin given prophylactically, with a repeat ECG in 15 min. Therefore, Option B is the correct answer.

stem: A 73-year-old man is admitted via the Emergency Department some 4 weeks after routine pacemaker insertion. He has been suffering increasing lumbar spine pain and over the past 48 h has developed diarrhoea and fevers. Past history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension and ischaemic heart disease is noted. On examination, his temperature is 37.9°C, pulse is 70 bpm and regular and BP is 122/82 mmHg. His abdomen is soft, although he is mildly tender in the left iliac fossa. Palpation of the lumbar spine reveals significant tenderness over L4. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 122 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 181 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Glucose 8.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* Plain X-ray lumbar spine Minor loss in height of L4 and L5 Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Infective discitis
The clue here is the pacemaker insertion a few weeks earlier, which raises the possibility of staphylococcal infection. This, coupled with the gradual increase in back pain and the point tenderness over L4, suggests discitis. In the early stages plain X-ray may be normal or just show minor loss in height of the vertebral body. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the investigation of choice, with over 90% sensitivity to detect changes consistent with discitis after 2 weeks of symptoms. A minimum of 6 weeks’ antibiotic therapy is usually required, with some patients requiring surgical debridement if symptoms fail to resolve.

Clostridium difficile
Clostridium difficile is incorrect. C. difficile would not lead to the back pain seen here.

Diverticulitis
Diverticulitis is incorrect. Diverticulitis would not lead to the back pain seen here.

Osteoporosis lumbar spine
Osteoporosis lumbar spine is incorrect. Osteoporosis would not explain the fevers or raised CRP.

Prolapsed lumbar disc
Prolapsed lumbar disc is incorrect. A prolapsed lumbar disc would not explain the fevers or raised C-reactive protein (CRP).

stem: A 45-year-old man was diagnosed with new onset atrial fibrillation after visiting his GP complaining of palpitations. An ECG confirmed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 85 bpm, and an ECHO did not reveal any significant structural heart disease. On advice of the hospital he was given low-molecular-weight heparin and stabilised on warfarin, with an INR of 2.5. You arrange for him to be cardioverted a few weeks later, and the procedure is successful. According to current guidelines, how long is it recommended to continue his warfarin therapy?
explanation:
For 4 weeks
UK guidelines recommend warfarinisation for at least 3 weeks pre-cardioversion and for 4 weeks post- cardioversion. The aim is for a target international normalised ratio (INR) of 2.5, although this can be allowed to drift up to 3 a few days before the procedure to minimise any risks of cancellation due to inadequate anticoagulation. The period of 4 weeks post-procedure is recommended because there is a high relapse rate in the first few weeks.

stem: A young man comes to the Emergency Department complaining of feeling unwell and palpitations. Supraventricular tachycardia is confirmed on ECG and he responds to carotid sinus massage. Subsequently, the ECG shows a PR interval of 0.09 s, widened QRS complex in all leads with a slurred upstroke, dominant R wave in V1 and left axis deviation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome
Diagnosis and treatment: Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome is classically associated with a short PR interval (< 0.12 s). Slurring of the QRS complex is owing to an extra wave called a delta wave. As the AV node and bypass tract have different conduction speeds and refractory periods, a re-entry circuit can develop, causing paroxysms of tachycardia. Carotid sinus massage or intravenous adenosine will often terminate an episode of this form of tachycardia.

Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation is incorrect. The presence of P waves (as a PR interval is provided) rules out atrial fibrillation.

stem: You review a 68-year-old woman who presents with a sudden episode of collapse while taking communion in church. This has been her third syncopal episode. Past medical history of note includes recently diagnosed severe hypertension, for which her GP has commenced enalapril therapy. She has been a smoker of 20 cigarettes per day for 40 years. On examination her blood pressure is 160/130 mmHg, she has left ventricular hypertrophy on clinical examination and a loud ejection systolic murmur. Auscultation of the chest reveals bibasilar crackles consistent with mild heart failure. Which one of the following is the investigation of choice to aid diagnosis in this patient?
explanation:
Echocardiogram (ECHO)
This patient is suffering from symptomatic aortic stenosis (AS), as evidenced by the history of syncope, hypertension, left ventricular hypertrophy and harsh ejection systolic murmur. Of the investigations listed, echocardiogram is the most likely to provide the diagnosis, by enabling the confirmation of the preesnce of AS, allowing assessment of the extent of calcification of the valve as well as idenification of other valvular/cardiac/aortic pathology. Doppler echocardiography is preffered for assessing the severity of AS, wheras trans-oesophageal echo may be required for further more detailed information.

stem: A 21-year-old woman has a history of palpitations and light-headedness. The electrocardiogram (ECG) shows a short PR interval and inferior Q waves. Her symptoms improve with atenolol 25 mg/day, but she has had two short episodes of similar symptoms in the previous 24 hours. What is the long-term management of choice?
explanation:
Radiofrequency ablation
The management of WPW and LGL syndromes is similar: radiofrequency ablation is recommended for these patients and can be curative. Recurrent palpitations with a short PR interval suggest the presence of an accessory pathway (atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT)). Wolff–Parkinson–White (WPW) is the most well known, but for the diagnosis of WPW there should be delta wave (slurred upstroke) and a broadening of the QRS. In this case, there is only a short PR interval – this suggests Lown–Ganong–Levine (LGL) instead. In this syndrome there is an accessory pathway close that connects the atria directly to the bundle of His – so the AV node is bypassed. There are rapid palpitations with supraventricular tachycardias transmitted to the ventricles at a high rate. It is likely her palpitations and light-headedness come from short periods of supraventricular tachycardia.

Increase the dose of atenolol
Increase the dose of atenolol is incorrect. Atenolol may be useful to manage ventricular rate during periods of tachycardia, but again is a suboptimal choice for this patient in the long term.

stem: A 54-year-old man is 48 h post-myocardial infarction. You are asked to review him as he has new pulmonary oedema and falling urine output. On examination he has a pansystolic murmur, loudest at the apex. Which one of the following complications of his myocardial infarction is most likely to have occurred?
explanation:
Acute mitral regurgitation
Mechanical complications of treated myocardial infarction are now thankfully rare (acute MR, VSD and ventricular rupture). Early reperfusion should prevent most, but late presenting infarctions, or those that cannot be adequately reperfused (e.g. high clot burden with challenging coronary anatomy) will still have full thickness infarction with subsequent risk of complications. Acute mitral regurgitation is the most likely condition in this patient. There is a clear, loud, pansystolic murmur with pulmonary oedema. As cardiac output falls from the acute regurgitation (most of the cardiac output is now returning to the LA) there would be a fall in urine output. Acute mitral regurgitation Acute mitral regurgitation associated with myocardial infarction may occur due to ruptured chordae tendineae. This is more likely in infarctions affecting the lateral wall (eg circumflex vessel). Other causes of acute mitral regurgitation include: papillary muscle dysfunction from acute ischaemia infective endocarditis

stem: A 70-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with a swollen left leg 4 weeks after undergoing an elective total hip replacement. An above-knee DVT is diagnosed by ultrasound. She is in sinus rhythm at 60 bpm and her blood pressure is 160/80 mmHg. She is commenced on the appropriate dose of low molecular weight heparin and warfarin loading. The following day she becomes acutely short of breath. Examination reveals a resting tachycardia (110 bpm) with blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. Her jugular venous pressure is elevated at 7 cm above the sternal notch. Arterial blood gas measurement reveals her to be hypoxaemic with a p a(O2) of 7 kPa. Echocardiography reveals the right ventricle to be severely impaired. What would be the first-line therapy after administering high-flow oxygen?
explanation:
Thrombolysis with reteplase
This patient has clinical features of a massive pulmonary embolus and the event is consistent with recent surgery and confirmed DVT. Massive PE causes significant obstruction of the pulmonary arteries causing haemodynamic compromise – namely shock or systemic hypotension (systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg or a drop of > 40 mmHg for > 15 min) Those patients with these features should be considered for thrombolysis – as it is not only life-saving but will reduce the long-term complications of pulmonary hypertension. The presence of significant RV impairment (the right ventricle is unable to pump against the clot) is often a deciding factor to proceed to thrombolysis. Treatment

stem: A 55-year-old man has infective endocarditis. He has refused dental work for several years and presented with night sweats and lethargy to his general practitioner. Subsequent blood cultures demonstrated bacteraemia due to infection by Streptococcus viridans. On examination he is pyrexial (37.8 °C), his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, and pulse is 95 bpm. Finger examination reveals splinter haemorrhages. Auscultation reveals a murmur consistent with mitral regurgitation. His chest is clear. The table below contains investigation results: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 107 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 13.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 211 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 139 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate 0–10 mm in the 1 st 72 mm/h (ESR) hour PR interval 180 ms, otherwise no significant ECG on admission changes mitral regurgitation with evidence of Echocardiogram vegetations Which one of the following would be considered an urgent indication for surgical intervention after 12 days of antibiotic therapy?
options: Systolic murmur after 10 days of antibiotics
explanation:
Increasing PR interval
An Increase in the PR interval suggests extension of endocarditic infection into the myocardium. This also raises the possibility of abscess formation, particularly given the duration of antibiotic treatment so far. As such, urgent surgical referral is indicated. Rupture into the pericardium is an indication for same-day surgical intervention. You may wish to refer to: Delahaye et al., Heart 2004; 90: 618–620. Other indications for urgent surgical intervention include: mitral regurgitation or aortic regurgitation with heart failure septal perforation valvular obstruction. Particularly large vegetations (> 15 mm) are also an indication for surgical assessment (though not necessarily for urgent intervention).

Systolic murmur after 10 days of antibiotics
Systolic murmur after 10 days of antibiotics is incorrect. Systolic murmur being present after antibiotic therapy may indicate vegetation or valve damage. However, urgent surgery may not be indicated.

Persistent fever 48hrs after starting treatment
This is incorrect. Fever is a common presentation in endocarditis and generally has no bearing on the severity of the condition. The European Society of Cardiology guidelines are reference by NICE and suggest considering early surgery in patients with persistent bacteraemia or fever after seven days of appropriate treatment (assuming other sources of persistent infection excluded). This is, however, less of a clear indication than an increasing PR interval.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer is admitted with acute dyspnoea. Her respiratory rate on admission is 42 breaths per minute and her oxygen saturations are 87% on room air. A pulmonary embolism is suspected and she is transferred to the High Dependency Unit after being treated with oxygen and enoxaparin. She is given a 500 ml bolus of fluid. Which one of the following would be the strongest indication for thrombolysis post fluid bolus?
explanation:
Systolic blood pressure 80 mmHg
The clinical scenario is of a woman with a massive pulmonary embolism, and persistent hypotension despite fluid bolus suggests significantly reduced ventricular filling pressure and is an indication for thrombolysis. Where the patient is in a cardiothoracic surgical centre, embolectomy could also be considered.

O 2 saturation 93% on 10 litres O 2
O2 saturation 93% on 10 liters O2 is incorrect. This indicates hypoxia due to ventilation perfusion mismatch in case of PE. Hypoxia is commonly seen in patients with PE and is managed with oxygen. It is not an indication for thrombolysis.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with a history of well controlled asthma presents with shortness of breath for some days. She is also treated with ramipril 10 mg daily. On examination her blood pressure is 135/85 mmHg, and her pulse is 100 bpm (atrial fibrillation). She is not in cardiac failure. Examination of the respiratory system reveals wheeze consistent with asthma. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 132 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 240 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 125 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Cardiomegaly consistent with long-standing Chest X-Ray hypertensive heart disease ECHO Increased left atrial size, ejection fraction 30% Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her atrial fibrillation?
explanation:
Digoxin
This patient has been in atrial fibrillation (AF) for an unknown period of time, and her pressing need at this point is rate control. Options include: Diltiazem Verapamil Atenolol Digoxin. Digoxin is effective for rate control under these circumstances and has a tolerable side-effect profile in this particular patient. Digoxin should be used with caution in patients with severe respiratory disease; however, as this patient's asthma is usually well controlled, this would still be the most appropriate answer here.

Amiodarone
Amiodarone is incorrect. This patient is unlikely to attain sinus rhythm. The optimal intervention therefore is rate control and given the low ejection fraction, digoxin is the preferred option.

Atenolol
Atenolol is incorrect. Atenolol may lead to worsening of the patient’s asthma and should not be used.

Diltiazem
Diltiazem is incorrect. Diltiazem is negatively inotropic and may precipitate cardiac failure (presence of cardiomegaly on chest X-ray).

Dysopyramide
Dysopyramide is incorrect. Dysopyramide is a class 1a anti-arrhythmic agent used for ventricular (not atrial) tachyarrhythmias.

stem: A patient presents with congestive heart failure. Which drug may be effective in reducing mortality outside the acute situation?
explanation:
Enalapril
A number of studies have conclusively demonstrated that reduction in left ventricular afterload prolongs survival rates in congestive heart failure: this is best achieved by vasodilators such as angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, e.g. enalapril, and angiotension II receptor antagonists (ARBs), e.g. candesartan. These drugs block the formation or action of angiotensin II and thus reduce blood pressure and afterload; over time this leads to an improvement in left ventricular dimensions and function. There is strong evidence to show these drugs are associated with a mortality benefit.

Furosemide
Furosemide is incorrect. Standard drugs like diuretics, while a mainstay of the treatment of exacerbations of heart failure, have not been shown to improve survival rates. In fact, loop diuretic use is associated with worse outcomes and it is recommended they are stopped when the patient is fully stabilised and euvolaemic.

stem: A 67-year-old man with chronic heart failure is reviewed in the cardiology clinic. He has a history of ischaemic heart disease as a cause of his chronic heart failure. He is currently taking a number of medications and would like a review of his drug therapy. Which one of the following treatments has no proven mortality benefit?
explanation:
Digoxin
Digoxin reduces the risk of death due to heart failure but overall cardiovascular mortality is similar to that on placebo, probably reflecting a small increase in the risk of arrhythmic death with digoxin therapy.

Enalapril
Enalapril is incorrect. Enalapril was shown in the CONSENSUS trial to provide a survival benefit in patients with heart failure. In this double-blind study, 253 patients were randomised to receive either placebo (n=126) or enalapril (n=127). After a follow-up averaging 188 days, patients who were taking enalapril had a longer survival.

stem: A 36-year-old woman who is 8 weeks’ pregnant presents with a swollen left leg. Doppler studies confirm a deep vein thrombosis. What would be the management in this case?
options: Start low molecular weight subcutaneous heparin throughout pregnancy
Oral anticoagulation with warfarin daily throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period
Aspirin 300 mg daily throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period
Elastic band compress of her left leg, bedrest and foot elevation
explanation:
Start low molecular weight subcutaneous heparin throughout pregnancy
This option mitigates the risk of developmental abnormalities from warfarin during organogenesis.

Commence intravenous heparin
Commence intravenous heparin is incorrect. Continuous IV heparin for the remaining 32 weeks would be impracticable and there is a higher risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) with unfractionated heparin (1–3%) as compared to a LMWH (0.1%).

Aspirin 300 mg daily throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period
Aspirin 300 mg daily throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period is incorrect. High-dose aspirin is contraindicated in pregnancy as it can cause premature ductal closure.

stem: A 72-year-old man was discharged following successful prosthetic aortic valve replacement. Apart from a small Venflon abscess, which healed with appropriate dressings and cannula removal, his progress had been unremarkable. Now, some 6 weeks later, he is brought to the Emergency Department by his wife, suffering from malaise, fever and night sweats. On examination you can hear a normal S1 with an ejection systolic murmur and a metallic sounding S2. Blood testing reveals mild anaemia and raised CRP. Transoesophageal echocardiography shows some dehiscence of the aortic valve replacement. He is previously been found to be MRSA positive. Which one of the following regimens is the most appropriate initial choice of antibiotic therapy?
options: Intravenous vancomycin, gentamicin and oral rifampicin
explanation:
Intravenous vancomycin, gentamicin and oral rifampicin
This patient presents with signs of infection in the early phase after aortic valve replacement. They should be treated as infective endocarditis of the prosthetic valve until proven otherwise. Both cardiologists and cardiothoracic surgeons should be alerted immediately and antibiotics started promptly, once at least three sets of blood cultures have been taken. The choice of antibiotics to treat endocarditis should be guided by local policy, but in the case of possible prosthetic valve endocarditis, intravenous vancomycin, gentamicin and oral rifampicin is the most appropriate regime, this is because early prosthetic valve endocarditis is usually caused by a Staphylococcus and this option includes vancomycin to provide optimal cover. Rifampicin is indicated to

stem: In which one of the following scenarios have statins not been shown to be of benefit?
options: Post MI with elevated cholesterol to decrease risk of cardiovascular events
Post MI with normal cholesterol to decrease risk of cardiovascular death
Post MI with normal cholesterol to decrease risk of non-fatal MI
Primary prevention in a diabetic male aged 60 with a cholesterol 6.2 mmol/l
explanation:
Primary prevention with cholesterol 3.9 mmol/l
Statins and cholesterol Statins are drugs that competitively inhibit 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase, which is involved in cholesterol synthesis, especially in the liver. The main role of statins is to reduce low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and overall cholesterol levels. They are better than ion exchange resins at reducing LDL. They are less good than fibrates at reducing triglycerides or increasing high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol. Statin trials There have been several important trials with statins. 4S demonstrated that for post myocardial infarction (MI) in patients with elevated cholesterol there was a 33% reduction in cardiovascular events with a cholesterol reduction of 25%. CARE demonstrated a 24% decrease in cardiovascular death and non-fatal MI in patients with both high and average cholesterol levels post MI.

stem: A 36-year-old woman is referred to the rheumatology clinic by her GP. She has a history of Raynaud’s phenomenon over the past 2-3 years, intermittent joint pains, and night sweats. She has recently completed 6 months of therapy for a pulmonary embolus and had a benign tumour removed from her left breast some 5 years ago. On examination, her BP is 123/80, a pulse of 80 and regular. You can hear a murmur consistent with tricuspid stenosis. Her BMI is 21. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Right atrial myxoma
The chronic symptomatology spreading back over 2-3 years, coupled with signs of right sided heart disease including tricuspid stenosis and pulmonary emboli, raises the possibility of a right atrial myxoma. The benign tumour removed from the left breast may have been a myxoma, (they are also known to exist in the skin and in neurological tissue.) Features which may confuse with vasculitis, including night sweats and anorexia are also relatively common in patients with myxoma.

Right sided bacterial endocarditis
Right sided bacterial endocarditis is incorrect. The prolonged history of 2-3 years makes right sided bacterial endocarditis much less likely as the cause of her symptoms.

stem: A 70-year-old obese man is admitted with a 6-hour history of chest pain. An electrocardiogram reveals an inferior wall myocardial infarction. Measurement of which one of the following would be most sensitive and specific for confirmation of myocardial damage?
explanation:
Cardiac-specific troponin T
Troponin T and troponin I are regulatory proteins released into the circulation upon damage to cardiac muscle. High-sensitivity assays have been developed and are now recommended by the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. These allow detection of lower levels of troponin compared with older assays, and so can be used to detect increases in troponin levels earlier. With older assays, troponin was repeated 10–12 hours after symptom onset. High-sensitivity assays allow earlier (< 4 hours) exclusion of myocardial infarction (MI), leading to a shorter inpatient stay for those found not to have increased levels of troponin, as well as earlier treatment for those diagnosed with MI.

Aspartate aminotransferase
Aspartate aminotransferase is a non-specific enzyme that is used rarely nowadays for MI diagnosis.

stem: A 52-year-old man is admitted to the intensive therapy unit with left ventricular failure post-myocardial infarction. Despite prompt activity including angioplasty within a few minutes of the onset of chest pain, his systolic BP on admission to the unit was only 80 mmHg, with a pulse of 105 bpm. Auscultation of the chest revealed crackles up to the mid zones on both sides consistent with cardiac failure. The team decide to insert an intra-aortic balloon pump timed to coincide with the dicrotic notch. Which one of the following does the dicrotic notch refer to?
explanation:
Aortic valve closure
The cardiac cycle refers to a complete heartbeat from its generation to the beginning of the next beat, and so includes the diastole (relaxation phase), the systole (contraction phase), and the intervening pause. The graph of aortic pressure throughout the cardiac cycle displays a small dip (the "incisure" or "dicrotic notch"), which coincides with the aortic valve closure. The dip in the graph is immediately followed by a brief rise (the "dicrotic wave") then gradual decline. Just as the ventricles enter into diastole, the brief reversal of flow from the aorta back toward the left ventricle causes the aortic valves to shut. This results in the slight increase in aortic pressure caused by the elastic recoil of the semilunar valves and aorta. The aortic valve closure also coincides with the aortic component of the second heart sound (A2) and is followed by the phase of isovolemic ventricular relaxation. Mechanism of intra-aortic balloon pump and timing with dicrotic notch - Intra-aortic balloon pumps deflate during systole, which then increases forward blood flow because of the reduction in afterload. The pump then re-inflates during diastole, increasing the blood flow to coronary arteries.

stem: You are asked to review a 71-year-old man on the cardiology ward. He underwent stenting of coronary artery 3 days previously. He has a history of type-2 diabetes mellitus and ischaemic heart disease. Currently, he is asymptomatic. On examination, his blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, heart rate is 60 bpm, and he has no abnormality on examination of the chest or heart. He has been treated post-procedure with aspirin and clopidogrel. Which one of the following correctly describes the mechanism of action of clopidogrel?
explanation:
P2Y12 inhibitor
P2Y12 is an adenosine diphosphate chemoreceptor on platelet surfaces that is inhibited irreversibly by clopidogrel.

Potassium channel activator
Potassium channel activator is incorrect. Nicorandil is a potassium-channel activator. It induces dilatation of coronary arteries in patients with ischaemic heart disease, so is used commonly to treat angina. Other potassium-channel activators include diazoxide, minoxidil and retigabine.

stem: A 60-year-old man suffered an anterior myocardial infarction. He is a current smoker, hypertensive (although treated with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor with good control: blood pressure of 145/100 mmHg) and has hypercholesterolaemia (last cholesterol level was 5.9 mmol/l despite simvastatin 40 mg, once daily). Which one of the following non-pharmacological interventions will be most helpful in reducing his risk of a future ischaemic event?
explanation:
Stopping smoking
All of these interventions are effective at reducing the risk of future ischaemic events, but stopping smoking is the single most effective, non-pharmacological intervention. Several studies have shown that smoking cessation is as effective as having a coronary artery bypass graft. Smoking cessation is vital for reducing the risk of worsening coronary artery disease.

Alcohol reduction
Alcohol reduction is incorrect. There is no mention of excessive consumption of alcohol in this case. Excessive consumption of alcohol can result in worsening cardiovascular health, but it is not linked directly to cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk.

stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review. He underwent a repair of tetralogy of Fallot in the first year of life. Which of the following is the most likely defect to be found in tetralogy of Fallot?
explanation:
Large ventricular septal defect (VSD)
A VSD is a key feature of tetralogy of Fallot alongside an overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy. Clinical features associated with tetralogy include low birthweight, poor feeding and failure to gain weight. There is often breathlessness after exertion (prolonged crying). Most cases of tetralogy in the United Kingdom are diagnosed antenatally, present with low oxygen saturations or are diagnosed following assessment for a heart murmur. Repair is recommended in infancy.

Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid insufficiency is a feature in some patients with Ebstein’s anomaly, pulmonary stenosis is the valvular disorder associated with tetrology of Fallot. Specific abnormalities of Ebstein's anomaly include: adherence of the septal and posterior leaflets of the tricuspid valve to the underlying myocardium downward (apical) displacement of the functional annulus of the tricuspid valve

stem: You are reviewing 72 h Holter monitors from patients referred to the Falls Clinic. This man has suffered three syncopal episodes over the past three months. He has a past medical history of ischaemic heart disease. On physical examination, his blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg and his heart rate is 50 bpm. Which of the following findings on the recording is an indication for permanent pacemaker insertion?
options: Sinus pause whilst asleep of 2.7 s
Short period of atrial fibrillation (ventricular rate 62/min)
Right bundle branch block and ventricular rate 50/min whilst asleep
explanation:
Trifascicular block
Selected potential indications for permanent pacing are listed below: persistent symptomatic bradycardia trifascicular block mobitz type 2 AV block sinus pause > 3 s. Pacing also has a role in the management of selected patients with tachyarrythmias, and in the management of patients with symptomatic heart failure on maximal medical therapy that fulfil NICE guidance for cardiac resynchronisation therapy.

stem: A 42-year-old man, known to be hypertensive, ran out of his medication 2 days ago. He presented to the Emergency Department feeling short of breath and dizzy. His blood pressure on admission was 230/140 mmHg. Fundoscopy showed blurred disc margins. His chest revealed bibasal crepitations. With therapy, what blood pressure should you aim for in the next 1 hour in such cases?
options: Decrease in mean arterial pressure (MAP) by 40–50%
explanation:
Decrease in MAP by 15–25%
This patient presents with a hypertensive emergency; a blood pressure > 180/120 mmHg with progressive target organ damage. The aim is to reduce the BP in a controlled manner with close monitoring targeting a 25% drop in the MAP in the first instance. Greater reductions than this in the first hour risk organ hypoperfusion due to a dysfunction in tissue autoregulation. Hypertensive emergency: The patient has a hypertensive emergency with markedly elevated blood pressure and evidence of target organ damage; this situation requires immediate attention to prevent disability or death Here, the aim is to reduce the blood pressure promptly but partially, to prevent end-organ damage without compromising tissue perfusion The initial target is to lower the mean arterial pressure (MAP) by no more than 25%, or reduce the diastolic blood pressure by one-third

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with pleuritic chest pain and haemoptysis. Her blood pressure is stable at 130/80 mmHg. A CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) shows evidence of bilateral basal pulmonary emboli. There is no evidence of RV dysfunction, clinically and on echocardiography. In addition to oxygen, which one of the following is the appropriate management for this patient?
explanation:
Rivaroxaban and analgesia
This patient has potentially had up to two small to moderate pulmonary embolisms (PEs), probably associated with pulmonary infarction. The management in this case would be rivaroxaban or apixaban and simple analgesics to control her chest pain. Dose initially should be 15 mg twice daily for 21 days and then maintenance 20 mg once daily, to be taken with food, for duration of treatment. If there were signs of a large/massive PE (hypotension, right ventricular dysfunction), the ideal management would include thrombolytic therapy or mechanical intervention (e.g. catheter insertion into the pulmonary vessels to physically break down the clot).

Heparin plus thrombolytic therapy
Heparin plus thrombolytic therapy is incorrect. Thrombolytic therapy would be indicated if there were signs of a large PE. However, this patient has a stable blood pressure and no right ventricular dysfunction, which indicates that the pulmonary embolisms are small to moderate.

stem: A patient has broad-complex tachycardia. The presence of which following feature increases the likelihood that the rhythm is a ventricular tachycardia as opposed to a supra-ventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction?
options: Absence of capture or fusion beats
The QRS complex shows an rsR pattern
An R to S interval < 100ms in all pre-cordial leads
P wave preceding wide QRS complex
Absence of an RS complex in all pre-cordial leads
explanation:
Absence of an RS complex in all pre-cordial leads
The absence of an RS complex, i.e., all the leads are concordant, increases the likelihood that the rhythm is ventricular tachycardia. All the other options increase the likelihood that the rhythm is a supraventricular tachycardiac with aberrant conduction. Diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia: Supraventricular tachycardia with bundle-branch block may resemble ventricular tachycardia on the ECG Eighty percent of all broad complex tachycardias are secondary to ventricular tachycardia and the proportion is even higher in patients with structural heart disease. Be very wary of diagnosing an SVT with aberrancy in a patient with a history of ischaemic heart disease. In all cases of doubt, the rhythm should be treated as a ventricular tachycardia. If the patient is unstable, eg. Blood pressure is low, emergent electrical cardioversion should be performed.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with atypical chest pains. He has a strong family history of ischaemic heart disease. Electrocardiogram (ECG) exercise testing shows J-point depression of 1 mm with a heart rate of 150 bpm. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat ECG exercise testing on anti-anginal medication
explanation:
Reassure and discharge
J-point depression is a physiological response to an increase in heart rate; ST segments should therefore be measured 80 ms post-J. J-point depression produces upward-sloping ST depression, which has little predictive value for coronary artery disease. Horizontal and downward-sloping segments are more predictive than upward-sloping ones. In a young man with atypical chest pain, this exercise test would be reassuring and there would be no indication for further investigation or treatment.

Coronary angiography
Coronary angiography is incorrect. Coronary angiography would be useful only if true coronary artery disease with stenosis is suspected.

stem: A 78-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with three episodes of syncope in the previous 24 hours. There is no history of chest pain. She is taking furosemide (80 mg, once daily) and ramipril (10 mg, once daily) for hypertension. She is conscious with a blood pressure of 100/40 mmHg. Potassium is 5.3 mmol/l. The electrocardiogram (ECG) shows complete heart block with a rate of 40 bpm. QRS duration is 150 ms with a right bundle branch block. What is the optimum definitive management?
explanation:
Temporary transvenous pacing
This woman has complete heart block with an unstable escape rhythm. The latter is exemplified by three syncopal episodes. Her QRS duration is prolonged (normal up to 120 ms), and this is generally more unstable than an escape rhythm of normal duration (i.e. < 120 ms) because this originates from around the bundle of His. Her blood pressure is low, particularly in light of her background of hypertension. Cardiac output will be influenced by the heart rate. In the elderly, cerebral vascular dysregulation may compound this effect, thereby contributing to cerebral hypoperfusion. Ideally she should receive a transvenous temporary pacemaker. If further acute problems occur while waiting for a transvenous temporary pacemaker (e.g. awaiting transfer to a room with fluoroscopy) then external pacing can be instituted in the short term with appropriate sedation.

stem: A 31-year-old man has been referred following a ‘blackout’. This had occurred the previous morning. He recalls waking from sleep, standing up, feeling light-headed and nauseated, falling back on to the bed and losing consciousness. He then woke up on the floor. He had not bitten his tongue but his head was badly bruised. His wife woke up when she heard him falling to the ground and describes him as being pale and sweaty before giving a loud moan followed by ‘spasms’ of his arms and legs lasting about 20 seconds, he was propped up against the side of the bed when the spasms occurred. He was rousable after a minute. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Vasovagal syncope
The prodrome of nausea/light-headedness and association with postural change are highly suggestive of vasovagal syncope, as is the rapid recovery. The witness’s description of the patient being pale and sweaty before moaning and jerking suggests that this is ‘convulsive syncope’ and not an epileptic seizure. Jerking is common in syncope, and should not be assumed to suggest epilepsy. In this case the jerking may have occurred because the patient was propped up against the bed and not lying flat. An ECG should be performed in all patients with a loss of consciousness to detect underlying abnormalities that can predispose to arrhythmias (such at the long QT syndrome), but there is little in this history to positively suggest a cardiac arrhythmia. Cardiogenic syncope often occurs suddenly without the prodromal symptoms of presyncope or may occur during exercise.

stem: An elderly, normotensive man with poor left ventricular function presents to the Emergency Department with dizziness and palpitations. An ECG shows a broad-complex tachycardia. Which of the following drugs would be the best choice of treatment?
explanation:
Amiodarone
This patient, a normotensive man with poor left ventricular function and a broad-complex tachycardia, has ventricular tachycardia (VT). Amiodarone may be used to cardiovert VT to sinus rhythm and to prevent ventricular fibrillation. Amiodarone may be administered by repeated IV bolus doses, or continuous IV infusion.

Flecainide
Flecainide is incorrect. Flecainide may cause ventricular fibrillation in patients with ventricular tachycardia, particularly in patients with underlying heart failure and ischaemic heart disease.

Sotalol
Sotalol is incorrect. In the presence of poor left ventricular function, lidocaine and β-blockers should not be used.

stem: Which one of the following antiarrhythmics has the highest risk of producing torsades de pointes (TdP)?
explanation:
Sotalol
Among these agents sotalol (a class III agent – predominantly K+ channel blocker), has the highest risk of producing torsades, which is a polymorphic, pause-dependent ventricular tachycardia causing syncope and sudden cardiac death. Patients started on sotalol should have an ECG 2–3 days after initiation – look for prolongation of the QT interval.

Flecainide
Flecainide is incorrect. Flecainide is a class Ic agent and may be associated with QT prolongation as part of QRS widening due to its effect as a sodium channel blocker. Its association with TdP is most commonly observed in patients with pre-existing structural heart disease has an almost zero risk of producing TdP.

Lidocaine
Lidocaine is incorrect. Lidocaine is a class Ib agent and has an almost zero risk of producing TdP.

stem: A 28-year-old West African man is admitted with probable Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. After initially improving on a co-trimoxazole-based regimen he deteriorates on the morning of his 6th day as an inpatient. On examination, his BP is 90/60 mmHg, pulse is 95/min and thready and he has a skin rash consistent with erythema multiforme. JVP is markedly elevated and his heart sounds are diminished. There are bilateral crackles on auscultation of the chest. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Allergic myocarditis
Allergic myocarditis is reported as a rare adverse event in association with co-trimoxazole therapy. Allergic myocarditis can occur at any time from several days to months after administration of the causative agent. This diagnosis fits with the presentation here, with signs of heart failure and possible myocardial rupture leading to a significant pericardial effusion. Indeed, Beck’s triad of hypotension, diminished heart sounds and elevated JVP is present. He requires urgent echocardiography to assess the need for intervention (i.e. a pericardial drain), and co-trimoxazole therapy should be discontinued immediately.

Myocardial infarction
Myocardial infarction is incorrect. Myocardial infarction may present with central chest pain radiating to the left arm and jaw. There may be associated nausea, vomiting and sweating. The symptoms are Chat acute. It withisAInot Tutor associated with co-trimoxazole therapy.

stem: A 72-year-old man is referred to the Cardiology Clinic by his GP, complaining of chronically increased shortness of breath and decreased exercise tolerance over the past 3–4 weeks. He has a history of ischaemic heart disease including a previous inferior myocardial infarction (MI), and takes a number of medications including aspirin, atorvastatin, amlodipine, lisinopril and furosemide. He may have been in atrial fibrillation (AF) for some time and the GP has already commenced warfarin therapy. On examination his BP is 155/85 mmHg, with pulse is 105/min (atrial fibrillation). He is not in cardiac failure. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.1×10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 200×10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 108 µmol/l 50–120µmol/l ECG Atrial fibrillation, old inferior Q waves Chest X-Ray Cardiomegaly, prominent pulmonary vasculature His amlodipine is discontinued. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Bisoprolol
Bisoprolol is preferred, as it has proven outcome benefits without the liabilities associated with amiodarone (photosensitivity and thyroid disease), and will slow the ventricular rate. Echocardiography, to assess the likelihood of success of cardioversion (related to atrial size), is the next most appropriate step. The amlodipine would usually be discontinued.

Amiodarone
Amiodarone is incorrect. Amiodarone is less preferred due to side effects such as photosensitivity and thyroid disease. It will slow the ventricular rate.

Digoxin
Digoxin is incorrect. Whilst digoxin and verapamil slow the ventricular rate, they are not associated with an outcome benefit.

Flecainide
Flecainide is incorrect. In this situation flecainide is contra-indicated due to the history of ischaemic heart disease.

stem: A 21-year-old medical student is admitted to the Emergency Department by paramedic ambulance. He collapsed whilst out running with his friends. On arrival in the Emergency Department he is found to be in ventricular tachycardia (VT) with a rate of 225/min and a BP of 80/50 mmHg. He undergoes emergency cardioversion and a 12-lead ECG recorded afterwards reveals significant QT prolongation. On further questioning it transpires that his uncle and father died suddenly in their 40s whilst exercising. You suspect autosomal dominant long-QT syndrome, and genotyping reveals LQT1 genotype. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention to prevent recurrence?
explanation:
Atenolol
Beta blockade may be enough to prevent further episodes of VT as a result of long QT. It is always best to try to use medication first, prior to more definitive treatment with patients with LQT1 or LQT2, such as an implantable cardioverter defibrillator. Note that atenolol in the acute setting of hypotension would not be indicated. However, this question is about secondary prevention. The assumption here is that the patient will not be hypotensive after the acute event.

Amiodarone
Amiodarone is incorrect. Conventional anti-arrhythmics such as amiodarone are generally avoided in this situation because of risk of further lengthening the QT interval.

stem: A 65-year-old man is admitted with a broad complex tachycardia. He has a heart rate of 140 bpm and his blood pressure is 90/50 mmHg. Which one of the following features would suggest a diagnosis of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) with aberrancy and help to exclude ventricular tachycardia (VT)?
options: Past history of ischaemic heart disease
Right bundle-branch block morphology with left axis deviation on the ECG
Temporary alleviation by carotid sinus massage
Variable intensity of the first heart sound
explanation:
Temporary alleviation by carotid sinus massage
VT does not involve the AV node and therefore is not be affected by adenosine or carotid sinus massage, which temporarily blocks the AV node. Therefore, if carotid sinus massage is performed and there is slowing of heart rate, this would suggest a diagnosis of SVT with aberrancy and help exclude VT.

Capture beats on the electrocardiogram (ECG)
Capture beats on the electrocardiogram (ECG) is incorrect. VT may be distinguished from SVT by ECG features that indicate atrioventricular (AV) dissociation (i.e. the atria and ventricles are no longer linked in rate and rhythm). The three characteristic features of AV dissociation are irregular notching of the QRS complex, capture beats and fusion beats. Capture beats alone do not suggest SVT with aberrancy, therefore is incorrect.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents complaining of periodic attacks of wheezing, flushing, and loose motions. He has no significant history. On examination, he has prominent precordial pulsations. Urinalysis show increased urinary excretion of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Carcinoid heart disease
The clue is a cluster of symptoms suggestive of systemic disease with a predominant heart complication (because it is a cardiology question and we are told that the patient has prominent precordial pulsations suggesting right heart disease). Carcinoid heart disease occurs if there is accumulation of fibrous tissue in the heart, especially to the under surface of the tricuspid valve. Carcinoid heart disease can hold the tricuspid valve in a semi-closed position, so tricuspid stenosis and regurgitation can occur. Pulmonary regurgitation/stenosis occurs if carcinoid heart disease affects the pulmonary valve. Right-sided heart valves are implicated because, in most cases, the primary carcinoid tumour is in the bowel and with liver metastases. The latter release serotonin and kallikrein that travel through liver sinusoids and empty into the central vein of each lobule. The central veins coalesce into hepatic veins, which leave the liver and drain into the inferior vena cava and right side of the heart.

stem: A 30-year-old man with known hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) presents to casualty with an episode of witnessed syncope: a passer-by provided initial resuscitation. On admission he is unwell with pulse rate of 160 bpm, blood pressure 70/40 mmHg and decreased conscious level. ECG confirms ventricular tachycardia. Sinus rhythm is restored with a DC shock. What would be the most appropriate strategy for the long term?
explanation:
Automatic implantable cardioverter defibrillator
Patients who have survived a sudden cardiac arrest, regardless of the type of underlying structural heart disease, are suitable for an AICD. This reduces sudden death and total mortality compared with therapy using anti-arrhythmic drugs. HOCM is the most common cause of cardiac arrest in those under 40 years of age. Overall, ≈1% of HOCM patients with HOCM die each year. AICDs have been shown to be effective in those with HOCM at terminating ventricular arrhythmias.

Dual-chamber pacemaker
Dual-chamber pacemaker is incorrect. A pacemaker is not beneficial in the context of cardiac arrest. The implanted device requires a defibrillator function to provide DC cardioversion in the event of cardiac arrest.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Pacemaker Clinic with symptomatic biventricular failure despite maximised doses of ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. He is also treated with furosemide, aspirin and atorvastatin. On examination, his BP is 110/50 mmHg and his pulse is 65 bpm and regular. He has bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of his chest and bilateral pitting lower limb oedema. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.6 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 302 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 131 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Chest X-Ray Cardiomegaly, evidence of mild LVF ECG Left bundle branch block You decide that he is suitable for a pacemaker device. Which of the following is the most appropriate option?
explanation:
Biventricular pacemaker
The clinical scenario is of a 62-years old man who presents to the pacemaker clinic with symptomatic biventricular failure. He is being treated with aspirin, furosemide, atorvastatin and is on the maximum dose of ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists. This indicates that he is on optimal and maximum medical management and is still symptomatic with biventricular failure; hence he needs further interventional therapy to help with his management. On examination, his pulse and B.P are normal (P = 65 bpm; B.P = 110/50 mmHg). On auscultation of his chest, he has bilateral basal crackles and bilateral pitting oedema in the lower limbs. This indicates that the patient is in heart failure. Blood investigations are normal; K = 5.0 mmol/L (normal range = 3.5 - 5.5 mmol/L) and creatinine = 131 μmol/l (normal range = 70 - 150 μmol/l) are also normal. CXR shows cardiomegaly, mild LVF and ECG shows LBBB pattern (left bundle branch block pattern). Bundle branch blocks can commonly lead to ventricular dyssynchrony (both the ventricles beating separate from each other and not together). Ventricular dyssynchrony leads to impaired ventricular function and subsequent heart failure. All these indicate that this patient has heart failure (biventricular failure) secondary to left bundle branch block (LBBB). The heart can function properly and pump out blood efficiently only when both the ventricular are working in synchrony. Ventricular dyssynchrony can occur commonly in patients with bundle branch blocks and impair ventricular pump function. Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) involves simultaneous pacing of both ventricles (biventricular or BiV pacing) or of one ventricle in patients with bundle branch block to reduce dyssynchrony. This is done with the use of a biventricular pacemaker. Leads are placed in the right atrium, right ventricle and left ventricle. Resynchronization can: 1. Improve pump performance 2. Reduce functional mitral regurgitation 3. Reverse the deleterious process of ventricular remodelling in patients with heart failure. Since this patient has evidence of symptomatic cardiac (biventricular) failure despite maximal medical therapy, NICE guidance supports the use of biventricular pacemakers in this population to improve cardiac synchrony and cardiac function.

Dual chamber pacemaker
Dual chamber pacemaker is incorrect. Dual chamber pacemakers are those where the 2 leads are placed in the right atrium and right ventricle. They are recommended to treat symptomatic bradycardia in people with sick sinus syndrome, atrioventricular block, or both and are not used for biventricular failure; hence Option B is

Dual site atrial pacemaker
Dual site atrial pacemaker is incorrect. Dual site atrial pacemakers are those where the leads are placed in the atria. This is used to maintain atrial synchrony rather than ventricular synchrony; hence it has been proposed as a preventative therapy for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation as well as managing patients with AF and symptomatic bradycardia. It is not used for patients with ventricular dyssynchrony or biventricular failure; hence Option C is incorrect.

stem: A 37-year-old man is admitted by ambulance to the Emergency Department from the local municipal pool after collapsing following a morning swim. This is the second time that he has been admitted to the hospital in the past three months, having lost consciousness on the first admission. On this occasion, according to the paramedics, he was found to be incontinent of urine. On examination, his BP is 152/90 mmHg and his pulse is 80 bpm. There is a systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. An ECG reveals LVH and left axis deviation. Routine bloods are entirely normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
Echocardiogram
The clinical scenario is of a young man (37 years old) with a history of collapse following a morning swim. This is the second episode in 3 months. On this occasion, he was incontinent of urine (would could be indicitive of a syncopal episode). Observations were normal and chest auscultation revealed a systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. ECG reveals LVH and left axis deviation and routine bloods are normal. The history of recurrent collapse following physical exertion, syncopal episode, systolic murmur and ECG changes all point towards a likely diagnosis of Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM). HOCM is an autosomal dominant condition and most mutations have a high degree of penetrance, hence first- degree family members of an affected individual should be screened for the disease. Family screening should include history, physical examination, ECG and ECHO. Routine genetic testing is not recommended for screening of first-degree relatives.

stem: A 40-year-old woman is admitted with a stroke after a prolonged pyrexial illness. Her GP was unclear as to the potential cause of her fevers and had prescribed a course of oral Co-amoxiclav in the expectation it would cover both respiratory and urinary pathogens. On examination she is in sinus rhythm, has splenomegaly and a pansystolic murmur at the apex. Blood cultures confirm an infective endocarditis. Which one of the following is the most common causative organism?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is now recognised as the commonest cause of endocarditis overall (both acute and subacute), associated with around 31% of cases in recent series. It may be acquired through skin infections, abscesses, vascular access sites or intravenous drug misuse.

Staphylococcus epidermidis
Staphylococcus epidermidis is incorrect. Staphylococcus epidermidis are skin commensals that are the most commonly found pathogen associated with early (< 90 days of surgery) prosthetic valve endocarditis. Typically, these bacteria enter the blood stream from the skin via central lines post-operatively. There is no suggestion of recent surgery and therefore this is not the correct answer.

stem: A 60-year-old gentleman is under observation in the Coronary Critical Care Unit for observation following stenting for inferior myocardial infarction. You are talking to him when he loses consciousness and develops ventricular fibrillation (VF) on the monitor. He has pads present on his chest. Which of the following is the therapy of choice?
explanation:
Defibrillate
Early defibrillation is crucial with respect to maximising the chances of recovery from VF, and given the environment, a defibrillator will be close at hand. In this specific scenario where a bedside defibrillator is available, the usual resuscitation protocol of supporting the airway, commencing chest compressions and calling the cardiac arrest team would all waste valuable time.

Precordial thump
Precordial thump is incorrect. A precordial thump is next best with respect to delivering kinetic energy to the heart; as such, if a defibrillator was unavailable for any reason then this would be the next best option, although these are no longer recommended as routine practice in ALS guidelines.

stem: An 18-year-old woman comes to the clinic with increased shortness of breath and palpitations. A murmur consistent with patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is noted on auscultation. What would you expect to be the character of the pulse in PDA?
explanation:
Collapsing
In PDA a widened pulse pressure is noted; this is of course also seen in patients with severe aortic regurgitation.

Jerky
Jerky is incorrect. A jerky pulse may be seen in patients with HOCM.

Pulsus alternans
Pulsus alternans is incorrect. Pulsus alternans is seen in patients with left ventricular failure. Pulsus paradoxus is seen in constrictive pericarditis, cardiac tamponade and severe asthma.

stem: A 34-year-old professional footballer is evaluated for symptoms of ‘dizziness’ during exercise. Physical examination reveals a laterally displaced apical impulse. On auscultation, there is a 2/6 mid-systolic murmur in the aortic area that increases on sudden standing. The ECG shows LVH and Q waves in the V2–V5 leads. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
In this case, we should consider the causes of a mid-systolic murmur in the aortic area in a young patient. This is the correct answer because the features are all consistent with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Patients classically have a systolic murmur that becomes worse on standing and becomes quieter on squatting. Patients typically complain of dizziness on exertion and have displaced and forceful apex. ECGs in HCM typically have LVH. Other ECG changes can give the appearances of ischaemia despite normal coronary arteries; deep T-wave inversion or anterior Q waves are common. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy Adverse effects: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the single most common cause of sudden death in young athletes Syncope and sudden death are associated with severe exertion and competitive sports, which should be avoided in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. stem: A patient with left ventricular failure undergoes echocardiography. Which one of the following is the correct formula for calculating the ejection fraction (EF)?
explanation:
EF = [end-diastolic volume (EDV) – end-systolic volume (ESV)] ÷ EDV
EF is calculated using the following equation: EF = [EDV – ESV] ÷ EDV. It is the difference in volume between when the ventricle is full of blood (end diastole) as opposed to when it is the most empty of blood (end systole), expressed as a percentage. Normal patients usually have an ejection fraction between 50–65%. The other equations given here do not describe this difference between the ventricle post-filling and post-ejection.

EF = [EDV – ESV)] ÷ heart rate (HR)
This equation takes the correct answer and divides it by heart rate, giving an answer that would be far too low. The ejection fraction is calculated by looking at a single cardiac cycle and does not therefore need dividing by heart rate.

EF = [ESV – EDV] ÷ EDV
By reversing systole and diastole, it tries to assess ejection during the filling phase – clearly, this is wrong.

stem: A 49-year-old man is noted to have shortening of the QT interval on the ECG. Which drug is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Digoxin
The cardiac glycosides (digoxin and ouabain) shorten the QT interval. Therefore, digoxin is the correct answer. Class Ia (e.g. disopyramide), class Ic (e.g. flecainide) and class III drugs (e.g. amiodarone and sotalol) all prolong the QT interval (hence are all incorrect answers). Beta blockers have a neutral effect on the QT interval but are effective at stabilising the QT in long QT syndromes (they are used as a treatment for long QT). More common questions look for causes of a long QT. Causes of a prolonged QTc (> 440 ms) are: hypokalaemia hypomagnesaemia hypocalcaemia hypothermia myocardial ischaemia post-cardiac arrest raised intracranial pressure

stem: A 50-year-old male is brought to the Emergency Department with acute-onset central chest pain that started 1½ hours ago. His ECG taken on arrival showed ST elevations of 4 mm in leads II, III, aV F and V 4–V 6 with hyperacute T waves. His pulse was 60 bpm and his BP was 146/60. The SaO2 was 92%. He was given O 2 by mask and two large intravenous cannulas were inserted. Which one of the following blood tests would be most useful to wait for prior to commencing definitive treatment?
explanation:
None
This question requires recognition that there are clear signs of acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction and there should be no delay to await blood tests. He has typical chest pain with significant ST-elevation in multiple leads. He should be treated immediately with reperfusion by primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) if possible. Acute myocardial infarction Diagnosis criteria: The WHO criteria for the diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction (MI) requires the presence of at least two of three elements history of ischaemic-type chest discomfort evolutionary ECG changes rise and fall in serum cardiac markers

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to the Emergency department after returning from a trip to Australia. She has a swollen left lower limb which is painful. There is a 3/5 power weakness and poor co-ordination affecting the right arm, and she has a right facial weakness. There is no significant past medical history of note. On examination her BP is 178/82 mmHg, heart rate is 80 bpm and regular. Respiratory and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal volume Haemoglobin 131 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 209 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 10 mm/1 st hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Left leg venous ultrasound large area of thrombus Over the next few hours her neurological symptoms thankfully resolve. Which of the following investigations is most likely to reveal the source of her neurological event?
explanation:
Trans-oesophageal echocardiogram
The clinical scenario is of a young women (23 years old) with an acutely swollen left leg after returning from a trip to Australia. Her left leg venous ultrasound shows large area of thrombus. The diagnosis is deep vein thrombosis (DVT). She also complains of poor coordination and weakness of her right arm and right side of her face (3/5 power and poor coordination in her right arm and right facial palsy). Her pulse is normal (P=80/min, regular) and blood pressure is high (B.P = 178/82 mmHg). She has no past medical history and her respiratory and abdominal examination is normal. Her symptoms resolve over the next few hours; hence the diagnosis is transient ischaemic attack (TIA) affecting the right arm and right side of the face (most likely an embolus affecting the left sided of the brain). Since this patient has had an arterial event (embolus causing TIA) secondary to a venous thrombus (DVT), she must have a paradoxical embolus. Her neurological event is related to passage of clot from her left leg DVT via a patent foramen ovale (PFO) into the arterial circulation causing TIA. Out of the options given only a trans- oesophageal echocardiogram can be used to assess the cardiac defect. A colour flow Doppler can estimate the flow and pressure through the PFO. Usually a bubble-ECHO is done to determine the presence of a patent foramen ovale but it is not given in the options. A paradoxical embolism (also called a crossed embolism) refers to an embolus that is carried from the venous side of circulation to the arterial side, or vice versa. It is a kind of stroke or other form of arterial thrombosis (e.g. TIA) caused by embolism of a thrombus, air, tumor, fat, or amniotic fluid of venous origin, which travels to the arterial side through a lateral opening in the heart, such as a patent foramen ovale. The opening is typically an atrial septal defect, but can also be a ventricular septal defect. Paradoxical embolisms represent 2% of arterial emboli.

Abdominal ultrasound scan
Abdominal ultrasound scan is incorrect. Abdominal ultrasound may be used here for assessing the proximal extension of the leg clot and for any intraabdominal pathology that might predispose to venous stasis and development of a DVT; however, it would have no utility in determining the cause of her neurological event.

Carotid ultrasound scan
Carotid ultrasound scan is incorrect. Carotid ultrasound scan is used to determine the cause of the embolus in patients with TIA suspected to have a carotid plaque giving off emboli. All patients with TIA should have a carotid doppler and ECHO to determine the cause of the embolus; however in this case the most likely cause of the emboli is a paradoxical embolus from left leg DVT and not a carotid plaque. She is also very young and has no risk factors for TIA (carotid plaques are usually present in elderly patients with comorbidities, age related atherosclerotic plaques and narrowing of arteries); hence carotid ultrasound scan will not be useful in this case to determine the cause of her neurological event.

stem: A 43-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with acute-onset central chest pain that has not resolved despite regular analgesia. His past medical history includes hypertension, for which he takes amlodipine, ramipril and indapamide every morning. On examination, he is pale, sweaty and looks extremely unwell. He has a blood pressure of 155/75 mmHg in his right arm and 120/65 mmHg in his left and his heart rate is 99 bpm and regular. There is equal air entry bilaterally on auscultation, with an audible diastolic murmur. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 140 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 4.3 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Troponin 20 ng/l < 14 ng/l D-dimer 6000 ng/l < 400 ng/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 10 mg/l < 5 mg/l Electrocardiogram: ST-segment depression in leads II, III and aVF. Which of the following is the next most appropriate investigation to confirm the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Computed tomography aortography
