definitive management for such cases, especially in those who are haemodynamically unstable.  Chronic cases of AR with mild or no symptoms are monitored every six months to 1–2 years to assess cardiac size via echocardiography.  Angiotensin-converting-enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) or calcium channel blockers may be

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI used in patients with chronic AR to reduce afterload by treating hypertension.  Severe symptomatic cases or those with significant cardiomegaly as a complication of AR are offered valve replacement surgery.  Prognosis  Cases that prompt emergency surgery have a much higher risk of mortality  usually, this is because such acute cases are often associated with infective endocarditis or dissecting aneurysm.  Chronic cases have a much better prognosis.  Predictors of prognosis include left ventricular size, systolic function and ejection fraction.  Surgical intervention at an early stage before complication onset results in a much better prognosis.  Other  Complications associated with AR include:  congestive heart failure  pulmonary oedema  ischaemic cardiomyopathy  arrhythmias  sudden death. Aortic Stenosis The aortic valve is a tricuspid valve that sits between the left ventricle and the aorta.  Overview Key Facts  The aortic valve is a tricuspid valve that sits between the left ventricle and the aorta.  In aortic stenosis, this valve does not open as efficiently as it should. Epidemiology Approximately 2% of people over 65 have a degree of aortic stenosis. Aetiology  Aortic stenosis  age-related calcification (most common)

DR. JAM  congenital bicuspid valve  acute rheumatic fever  Fabry disease  lupus  Paget's disease  uraemia. Pathophysiology  Aortic stenosis describes a physical dysfunction of the valve and does not describe any particular underlying cause:  congenital causes including bicuspid valve  rheumatic aortic stenosis  senile degenerative aortic stenosis.  In aortic stenosis, there is an increased pressure gradient across the valve.  The left ventricle will compensate to a point by becoming hypertrophied and increasing the force of contraction.  As the degree of stenosis progresses, the pressures in the left ventricle may exceed coronary artery perfusing pressure, causing angina.  In addition, the stenotic valve restricts the ability of the left ventricle to increase output in response to exercise or stress. ECG showing features of left ventricular hypertrophy:  Clinical Presentation  Initially asymptomatic, may be detected as an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids over the aortic area:  dyspnoea  angina  syncope  pulmonary oedema.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Mid/late systolic murmur:  innocent murmur  aortic stenosis or sclerosis  coarctation of the aorta  pulmonary stenosis  hypertrophic cardiomyopathy  papillary muscle dysfunction  atrial septal defect (due to high pulmonary flow)  mitral valve prolapse.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Definitive diagnosis is via echocardiography (ECHO).  An ECHO will be able to classify the degree of severity of stenosis by calculating the pressure gradient across the aortic valve.  Management  In asymptomatic patients, a ‘watchful waiting’ strategy may be employed as they tend not to have poor outcomes.  There is a severe increase in mortality associated with aortic stenosis in which patients develop symptoms.  In patients with symptoms, replacement of the valve should therefore be undertaken. Aortic valve replacement:  Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVI).  TAVI is an alternative to surgical aortic valve replacement.  The prosthesis is mounted on a stent and fed into the heart via the femoral artery.  It sits over the native valve. It has less immediate complications than a traditional aortic valve replacement as it removes the need for a sternotomy. Atrial Fibrillation Cardiac arrhythmias are a group of conditions characterised by  Overview Key Facts  Cardiac arrhythmias are a group of conditions characterised by abnormal conduction of the electrical activity in the heart.

DR. JAM  This may result in abnormal mechanical function of the heart.  Arrhythmias can be classed by:  rate – tachycardias (heart rate (HR) >100) or bradycardias (HR <60))  the origin of the aberrant conduction – atrial, junctional (AV node) or ventricular  the duration of the QRS complex on electrocardiogram (ECG) – narrow or wide complex arrhythmias.  The most common arrhythmia is atrial fibrillation (AF) with a prevalence of 2.5% in the United Kingdom (UK).  AF is supraventricular tachycardia (atrial arrhythmia) associated with irregular, disorganised electrical atrial activity, ineffective contraction of the atria, chaotic firing of the atrioventricular node and resultant irregular contraction of the ventricles.  Episodes may be classed as:  paroxysmal:  recurrent episodes last longer than 30 seconds but less than seven days  self-terminating.  persistent:  episodes lasting longer than seven days or  less than seven days but requiring pharmacological/electrical cardioversion.  permanent:  fails to terminate using cardioversion or  is terminated but relapses within 24 hours or  long-standing AF (usually over one year), in which cardioversion is not indicated or has not been attempted.  There is a slight predominance in men (3 : 2) over the age of 50.  Prevalence increases with age, with over half of all people aged between 85 and 94 years having the condition.  There are numerous causes, which can be divided into cardiac and non-cardiac.  Management depends on the following:  acuteness of onset  haemodynamic stability  the underlying cause  presence or absence of heart failure.  Management aims to treat symptoms as well as reduce the risk of complications and may involve admission and cardioversion, rate or rhythm control and anticoagulation, as well as treating underlying causes.  Stroke and thromboembolism are the main complications of AF.  The condition is generally associated with reduced life expectancy in older patients. Epidemiology  The most common arrhythmia is atrial fibrillation (AF) with a prevalence of 2.5% in the UK.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  There is a slight predominance in men (3 : 2) over the age of 50 years.  Framingham data indicates a prevalence of 76 per 1000 men and 63 per 1000 women aged 85–94 years. Aetiology  Cardiac conditions:  congestive heart failure  rheumatic valvular disease  atrial or ventricular dilatation or hypertrophy  pre-excitation syndromes (such as Wolff–Parkinson– White syndrome)  sick sinus syndrome  congenital heart disease  inflammatory or infiltrative disease (such as pericarditis, amyloidosis or myocarditis).  Non-cardiac conditions, such as:  acute infection  autonomic neuronal dysfunction (such as vagally induced AF)  electrolyte depletion (such as hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia)  cancer  pulmonary embolism  thyrotoxicosis  diabetes mellitus.  Dietary and lifestyle factors, such as:  caffeine  alcohol  obesity  smoking  medications (eg thyroxine or bronchodilators). Pathophysiology  The source of AF is often from myocardial tissue in the entrance to the four pulmonary veins or at the point they attach to the left atrium, causing rapidly firing foci.  The autonomic nervous system may also play a role in some cases.  This causes propagating wavelets, which may lead to re-entrant circuits in abnormal atrial myocardium.  The atrioventricular node receives more electrical impulses than it can conduct.  This leads to an irregular ventricular rhythm.  The ventricular rate of untreated AF often averages between 160 and 180 beats per minute.  The rate is often slower in older patients.

DR. JAM  Clinical Presentation  Patient presentation depends on the rate of tachycardia and the presence of haemodynamic instability.  Note the condition may be found incidentally in many patients during an examination of the pulse:  shortness of breath  palpitations  tachycardia/bradycardia  syncope  dizziness  chest pain.  Examination of the pulse will reveal an irregular rate.  Irregular jugular pulsations will also be present.  Patients may also present with sequelae of emboli, eg stroke.  Episodes of AF may be classed as:  paroxysmal:  recurrent episodes last longer than 30 seconds but less than seven days  self-terminating.  persistent:  episodes lasting longer than seven days or  less than seven days but requiring pharmacological/electrical cardioversion.  permanent:  fail to terminate using cardioversion or  terminate but relapse within 24 hours or  long-standing AF (usually over one year), in which cardioversion is not indicated or has not been attempted.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  atrial flutter  atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia (AVRT)  atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia (AVnRT)  sinus arrhythmia  ventricular tachycardia  torsades de pointes  ventricular fibrillation.  Diagnosis/Investigation Bloods  Full blood count (anaemia).  Electrolytes and renal function (eg potassium/calcium/magnesium).

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Thyroid function tests (AF can occur with hyperthyroidism). Electrocardiogram (ECG)  ECG is diagnostic (unless the patient has paroxysmal AF and is in between episodes):  loss of P wave on ECG is characteristic with irregular ventricular rhythm  a 24-hour Holter ECG or event recorder ECG may be required to confirm episodes of paroxysmal AF. ECG showing AF: Other tests  Chest X-ray may reveal structural cardiac causes, or demonstrate cardiac failure.  Transthoracic and possibly oesophageal echocardiograms may be indicated to:  assess for structural cardiac anomalies  record baseline cardiac function levels  look for mural thrombi which may have been precipitated by the condition  further assess if cardioversion is being considered.  Patients who present with signs of stroke require CT/MRI scans.  Management  Management aims to reduce symptoms and prevent complications such as thromboembolism and stroke.  Management depends on the following:  acuteness of onset  haemodynamic stability  the underlying cause (identify and treat these in all cases)  the presence of cardiac failure. Patients with AF for less than 48 hours and who are haemodynamically unstable

DR. JAM  Signs of haemodynamic instability include:  systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg  heart rate over 150 beats per minute  breathlessness, loss of consciousness, chest pain, palpitations, syncope.  These patients require urgent admission and assessment using the ABCDE approach.  Oxygen may be indicated if the patient is hypoxic.  Patients with signs of life-threatening haemodynamic instability require urgent direct current cardioversion, without waiting for anticoagulant cover.  Patients without life-threatening haemodynamic instability can be offered rate or rhythm control (if the onset of arrhythmia is less than 48 hours).  Reversible causes should be identified and treated in all cases.  Vagal manoeuvres may also be considered initially to terminate supraventricular tachycardia (SVT):  Valsalva manoeuvre  carotid sinus massage  immersion of face in ice water.  Pharmacological or electrical cardioversion can be considered based on clinical circumstances.  Pharmacological cardioversion can be achieved with amiodarone, or flecainide (if no structural heart disease).  If urgent rate control is required, a beta-blocker (not sotalol) or verapamil may be used intravenously (IV).  Also consider anticoagulation of these patients.  IV furosemide may be required in patients with acute cardiac failure. Patients with symptoms for over 48 hours or duration of onset is uncertain  Rate control is the preferred mode of management:  beta-blockers (except sotalol) or diltiazem/verapamil are first-line for rate control (2021 NICE updates)  digoxin may be used if the patient is sedentary or if other rate-limiting drug options unsuitable due to comorbidities or the person's preferences (2021 NICE update).  If symptoms are not controlled with monotherapy, a combination of two drugs may be used.  Rhythm control should be considered if rate control is ineffective.  If AF has been present for more than 48 hours and cardioversion is required, electrical cardioversion is preferred:  it should not be attempted until the patient has been fully anticoagulated for at least three weeks.  Rhythm control with drug therapy is with a standard betablocker unless contraindicated.  Dronaderone and amiodarone (consider as 1st line for patients with heart failure or left ventricular impairment) may be considered as second-line options

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Patients with infrequent episodes of paroxysmal AF or where symptoms are triggered by known precipitants may wish to have no treatment or a ‘pill in the pocket’ (PRN treatment) approach.  In patients who have ongoing symptoms despite rate and rhythm control, or if drug treatment is unsuitable, consider radiofrequency point-by-point ablation.  If radiofrequency point-by-point ablation is assessed as being unsuitable, consider cryoballoon ablation or laser balloon ablation. Long-term considerations Use the CHA2DS2-VASc stroke risk score to assess stroke risk in patients with:  symptomatic or asymptomatic paroxysmal, persistent or permanent atrial fibrillation  atrial flutter  a continuing risk of arrhythmia recurrence after cardioversion back to sinus rhythm or catheter ablation.  Offer anticoagulation (with direct acting oral anticoagulants) to those with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or above and consider anticoagulation in men with a score of 1 or above, taking bleeding risk and patient preferences into account.  Assess the risk of bleeding, ideally using the ORBIT bleeding risk score (2021 recommendation by NICE).  Anticoagulant agents that can be used depending on individual clinical circumstances and patient preference, but can include:  apixaban  dabigatran etexilate  rivaroxaban  edoxaban  Vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) can be used if direct acting anticoagulants are contraindicated, not tolerated, or not suitable.  Patients should also be given lifestyle advice such as:  reducing alcohol intake  smoking cessation  caffeine intake reduction  weight loss (if overweight).  The patient should be advised to contact the DVLA to inform them of their diagnosis.  Prognosis  Stroke and thromboembolism are the main complications of AF.  The atria do not contract correctly and so there is blood stasis, leading to clot formation.  Virchow’s triad of venous thromboembolism (VTE):  hypercoagulable state  endothelial damage  blood stasis.  A large meta-analysis carried out in 2016 found that AF was associated with:

DR. JAM  a 46% increase in all-cause mortality  a 61% higher risk of ischaemic heart disease  a 64% higher risk of chronic kidney disease  an 88% higher risk of sudden cardiac death  a 96% higher risk of a major cardiovascular event  a two-fold increase in cardiovascular mortality  a 2.3-fold increased risk of stroke  a five-fold increased risk of congestive heart failure. Atrial Flutter Atrial flutter is a supraventricular tachycardia caused by a re-entrant circuit in the atria which often co-exists with atrial fibrillation.  Overview Key Facts  Atrial flutter is a supraventricular tachycardia caused by a reentrant circuit in the atria which often co-exists with atrial fibrillation.  Type I atrial flutter (common or typical atrial flutter) occurs when the re-entrant circuit originates from the cavotricuspid isthmus in the right atrium.  Type II atrial flutter (atypical atrial flutter) occurs when the reentrant circuit originates from somewhere other than the cavotricuspid isthmus in the right atrium.  Clinical features include palpitations, shortness of breath, chest pain and syncope.  Atrial flutter appears on an electrocardiogram (ECG) as ‘sawtooth-like flutter waves’ with a rate of 200–300 bpm.  Treatment is similar to atrial fibrillation (rate versus rhythm control); however, catheter radiofrequency ablation can be performed as a definitive treatment.  Like atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter increases the risk of thromboembolism, and anticoagulation is required in patients with a significant stroke risk (calculated using CHA2DS2VASc). Epidemiology  Atrial flutter is the second most common arrhythmia after atrial fibrillation.  It commonly presents with atrial fibrillation; patients may alternate between atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter:  fifty per cent with atrial flutter are predicted to have atrial fibrillation within the next eight years.  More common in men (80% of cases). Aetiology  Atrial flutter is caused by a re-entrant circuit in the atria.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Risk factors:  underlying coronary heart disease, cardiomyopathy, valvular disorders, congenital heart disease  hypertension  hyperthyroidism  chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)  obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA)  obesity  alcohol abuse. Pathophysiology  Atrial flutter is due to a re-entrant circuit in the atria:  premature impulse in the atria that repeats itself in loops  propagated in continuous loops due to difference in refractory time periods. Type I Atrial Flutter (common or typical atrial flutter)  The re-entrant circuit originates from the cavotricuspid isthmus in the right atrium.  Usually slower than type II (240–340 bpm).  Subdivided based on the direction of the re-entrant circuit:  counter-clockwise atrial flutter: flutter waves inverted in leads II, III, avF  clockwise atrial flutter: flutter waves upright in leads II, III, avF. Type II Atrial Flutter (atypical atrial flutter)  The re-entrant circuit originates from somewhere other than the cavotricuspid isthmus in the right atrium.  Faster than type I (340–350 bpm).  Usually only occurs in people who have had previous ablation or previous heart surgery:  eg left atrial flutter after incomplete left atrial ablation.  Clinical Presentation  Patients with atrial flutter may be asymptomatic.  Symptoms may include:  palpitations  shortness of breath  chest pain  pre-syncope or syncope  reduced exercise tolerance.  In some patients, atrial flutter may not be picked up until they develop complications (eg acute stroke).

DR. JAM  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  atrial fibrillation  sinus tachycardia  Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Atrial flutter is diagnosed on a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and described as ‘saw-tooth-like flutter waves’ with a rate of 200–300 bpm. It is a regular tachycardia as compared with atrial fibrillation which is an irregular tachycardia. Atrial Flutter:  A specific Lewis Lead ECG may be useful if atrial flutter is not clearly demonstrated on the 12-lead ECG. The Lewis Lead would be interpreted as lead one on the ECG and may show atrial flutter waves more obviously:  move right arm electrode to manubrium next to the sternum  move left arm electrode to right fifth intercostal space next to the sternum  move left leg electrode to right lower costal margin.  An echocardiogram should be performed to look for structural abnormalities and assess cardiac function.  Other investigations should include investigations for underlying causes of atrial flutter (eg thyroid function tests).

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Management Non-pharmacological  Stroke risk assessment: CHA2DS2-VASc score.  Cardioversion: emergency synchronised cardioversion should be performed for unstable patients. Pharmacological  Treat underlying conditions (eg hyperthyroidism)  Consider anticoagulation depending on stroke risk assessment:  apixaban  dabigatran  rivaroxaban  warfarin (vitamin K antagonist).  Antiplatelet:  do not offer aspirin alone for stroke prevention.  Rate control:  monotherapy:  beta-blocker (avoid sotalol)  rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker  if monotherapy does not control symptoms, consider a combination of two of the following:  beta-blocker  diltiazem  digoxin.  Rhythm control:  pharmacological and/or electrical cardioversion if rate control unsuccessful. Surgical  Catheter radiofrequency ablation (fist line, > 90% success rate):  ablates the cavotricuspid isthmus to eliminate the reentrant circuit. Advanced Life Support Resuscitation Guidelines:

DR. JAM *Conscious patients require sedation or general anaesthesia for cardioversion.  Prognosis  Prognosis is good if treated with catheter ablation which is successful in 90–95% of patients; patients may still develop atrial fibrillation after being treated with catheter ablation.  Complications:  like atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter increases the risk of thromboembolism  adequate anticoagulation is required in patients with significant stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc score > 1 in men, > 2 in women).

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Atrial Myxoma Atrial myxomas are a rare type of tumour which arise from the atrial muscle of the heart.  Overview Key Facts  Atrial myxomas are a rare type of tumour which arise from the atrial muscle of the heart.  Myxomas are usually benign, with 75% occurring in the left atrium.  It is the most common type of cardiac tumour.  There is a higher predominance in female patients (2 : 1).  Symptoms are often nonspecific; therefore, diagnosis can be a challenge.  Diagnosis is confirmed via echocardiography.  Surgical resection is the definitive treatment.

DR. JAM Epidemiology  The incidence of atrial myxomas does not exceed 1 case per 1 000 000/year, but are the most common form of cardiac tumour in adults, accounting for 50–85% of all cases. Aetiology  90% are sporadic while 10% are inherited as part of a syndrome, eg Carney syndrome.  Primary cardiac tumours are rare.  Risk factors include:  a family history of myxoma  female sex  Carney syndrome.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations of atrial myxoma include:  fever  weight loss  transient mitral stenosis  early diastolic ‘plop’  finger clubbing and Raynaud’s  pulmonary hypertension  intracardiac obstruction and systemic embolism  shortness of breath and dyspnoea  syncope  cough  joint pain  haemoptysis.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for atrial myxoma include myocarditis and cardiomyopathy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnoses and investigations for atrial myxoma are as follows:  bloods may show raised white cell count (WCC) and low platelets with either haemolytic anaemic or polycythaemia  immunoglobulins and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) will be raised in 60% of those with myxoma  chest X-ray may show a slightly enlarged heart  diagnosis will be through transoesophageal or 2D echocardiogram for atrial myxomas with masses most commonly occurring on the interarterial septum  magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) scan can be used to evaluate the tumour further.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Management Pharmacological:  Drug therapy is reserved for complications such as arrhythmia or heart failure. Surgical:  Atrial myxomas grow rapidly with a risk of embolisation and sudden death, so they should be resected surgically without delay.  Follow-up valvular replacement may be needed.  Cardiac transplant is a final resort for very large myxomas.  Prognosis  Although the condition is histologically benign, there is risk of embolisation leading to significant morbidity and death.  Heart failure, mechanical obstruction of valves, arrhythmia, heart failure and sudden death are all possible complications.  Surgery is usually curative and long-term prognosis is good.  There is a risk of recurrence following resection (up to 5%); especially in younger patients. Therefore monitoring with echocardiogram is recommended. Atrial Septal Defect Atrial septal defects are the most common congenital defects found in adulthood.  Overview Key Facts  Atrial septal defects (ASDs) are the most common congenital defects found in adulthood.  The interatrial septum may be defective or absent, allowing mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.  The outcome is increased pulmonary blood flow and overload of the right ventricle during diastole.  There is left-to-right shunting at the atrial level.  This can worsen with age, leading to Eisenmenger syndrome.  The main treatment is surgery; prognosis is good post-surgery.

DR. JAM Epidemiology ASD accounts for 5-10% of standalone congenital heart defects. It is the third most common congenital heart defect. Aetiology  Most cases have no identifiable cause.  Holt–Oram syndrome (triphalangeal thumb with ASD):  A rare syndrome, which is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetration. It is associated with absence (or reduction anomalies) of the upper arm.  Lutembacher syndrome:  A rare combination of an ASD with mitral stenosis (the latter is probably rheumatic in origin). Pathophysiology There are three main subtypes:  Secundum (70%):  Features central fossa ovalis defects often associated with mitral valve prolapse (10–20% of cases).  Primum (15%):  Sited above the AV valves,often associated with varying degrees of mitral regurgitation (MR) and tricuspid regurgitation (TR) and occasionally a ventricular septal defect (VSD), thus usually picked up earlier in childhood. Associated with Down, Klinefelter and Noonan syndromes.  Sinus venosus (15%):  Defect in the upper septum, often associated with anomalous pulmonary venous drainage directly into the right atrium. Atrial septal defect:

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  The size of shunting and reduction in oxygenation will depend upon the size of the defect.  In smaller ASD, the left atrial pressure may still be higher than right atrial pressure.  With a larger defect, the mean atrial pressures may be equal.  ASD causes a left to right shunt.  This occurs late in ventricular systole and earlier in diastole.  The outcome is increased pulmonary blood flow and overload of the right ventricle during diastole.  ASD can worsen with age, leading to Eisenmenger syndrome, in which chronic left to right shunt causes irreversible pulmonary vascular injury leading to increased pulmonary vascular resistance.  Right to left shunting occurs, causing hypoxia.  Clinical Presentation  Fixed splitting of the second heart sound is the hallmark of an uncorrected ASD. There may be a left parasternal heave and a pulmonary ejection systolic murmur (ESM) due to increased blood flow.  Usually asymptomatic in infants and children, rarely can cause poor weight gain.  Can also cause:  shortness of breath (SOB)  palpitations  fatigue  reduced exercise tolerance  arrhythmias above the age of 40  Eisenmenger syndrome.  Differential Diagnosis  • Pulmonary stenosis  Diagnosis/Investigation Right atrial and right ventricular dilatation may be seen on any imaging technique, as may pulmonary artery conus enlargement. Other characteristic features include:  Chest radiograph  Electrocardiogram (ECG)  tall P waves (R atrial enlargement)  secundum (incomplete RBBB, right axis deviation)  primum (RBBB, left axis deviation, 1st degree heart block)  right ventricular hypertrophy  atrial flutter  atrial fibrillation.  Echocardiogram

DR. JAM  paradoxical septal motion  septal defect  right-to-left flow of contrast during venous injection with Valsalva’s manoeuvre.  Catheterisation  pulmonary hypertension.  Raised right ventricular pressures and step-up in oxygen saturation between various parts of the right circulation (eg superior vena cava (SVC) to high right atrium).  Management  There is no specific medical therapy for ASDs; they are managed by either closure (percutaneous or surgical) or clinical and echocardiographic follow-up.  Indications for closure:  symptoms (dyspnoea)  chamber dilatation  elevated right heart pressures  significant left-to-right shunt  systemic embolism (typically stroke). Non-pharmacological  n/a Pharmacological  Diuretics can be given if heart failure develops. Surgical  Surgical closure is recommended with pulmonary : systolic flow ratios > 1.5 : 1.  Closure of secundum defects may be performed via cardiac catheterisation.  Prognosis  Isolated defects that are repaired in children have an excellent prognosis.  Rarely, they may present as stroke in young people, due to paradoxical embolus that originates in the venous system and reaches the cerebral circulation via right-to-left shunting.  Other Patent foramen ovale (PFO)

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  A PFO is a channel within the interatrial septum, typically covered by a ?ap that opens to allow right-to-left communication when right-sided pressures elevate.  During fetal development, the interatrial septum allows communication through the foramen ovale.  Upon birth, the reduction in resistance in lungs lowers rightsided pressure, and the septum primum shuts, sealing the foraman ovale.  In a quarter of adults, this closure is incomplete, allowing venous embolic material to cross into the arterial circulation.  There may be a history of headaches, migraine or paradoxical embolism.  Stroke may occur in young patients.  PFOs are visualised on echocardiography using bubble contrast, by injecting agitated saline into a peripheral vein, which is then seen under echocardiography travelling from the right to the left atrium during Valsalva’s manoeuvre. Common congenital circulations: In the table below Eisenmenger syndrome  Refers to any untreated congenital cardiac defect with intracardiac communication that leads to:  severe irreversible pulmonary hypertension  reversal of left-to-right shunts  cyanosis.  Long-standing left-to-right shunts (eg in large VSDs, patent ductus arteriosus (PDAs) or ASDs) cause remodeling of the pulmonary microvasculature, with obstruction and pulmonary blood ?ow and raised pressures.  This causes shunts to reverse, sending deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation, which is evident as cyanosis.  Signs of development include:  clubbing and central cyanosis  decrease of original pansystolic (left-to-right) murmur  decreasing intensity of tricuspid/pulmonary ?ow murmurs  single S2 with louder intensity, palpable P2; right ventricular heave  appearance of Graham Steell murmur due to pulmonary regurgitation  pansystolic murmur and V waves due to TR.  Causes  VSD (Eisenmenger’s complex)  ASD  PDA  Complications of Eisenmenger syndrome

DR. JAM Bicuspid Aortic Valves The aortic valve is typically trileaflet, but can be congenitally bicuspid in 0.5–1% of the population, with strong male predominance.  Overview Key Facts  The aortic valve is typically trileaflet, but can be congenitally bicuspid in 0.5–1% of the population, with strong male predominance.  This abnormal valve development can lead to accelerated degeneration with aortic stenosis presenting many years sooner than typical (40–50s versus 60–70s).  In cases of bicuspid aortic valves, aortic regurgitation can also occur.  Many patients with bicuspid valves will never develop symptoms.  If symptoms develop, they relate to the development of aortic stenosis, aortic insufficiency.  Bicuspid aortic valve can on occasion be recognised as part of a syndrome incorporating aortic valve disorders and aortic wall abnormalities, including aortic dilation, dissection or rupture.  Other congenital heart disorders, infective endocarditis, thrombus formation, elevated cholesterol and c-reactive protein may all be associated with the condition.  Hypertension is a risk factor for calcific aortic stenosis in both bicuspid and tricuspid valves.  Treatment with surgical valve replacement is the definitive management for severe symptomatic aortic stenosis. Epidemiology  Bicuspid aortic valves is one of the most common types of congenital heart disease affecting roughly 1% of the population  There is a 2-3:1 male:female ratio. Aetiology  Bicuspid aortic valves can occur sporadically or as a result of autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance.  It can occur as an isolated lesion or as part of more complex congenital defects or with aortopathy syndromes.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pathophysiology  The anatomical variations of the bicuspid AV includes unequal cusp size (due to fusion of two other cusps) a raphe and smooth cusp margins.  A raphe or fibrous ridge is the size of fusion of the two conjoined cusp and is often identifiable on 3D echocardiography.  The right and left coronary leaflets are the most commonly fused (up to 85% approx.)  Calcification of the bicuspid aortic valve occurs more rapidly than with tricuspid valves and increases with age.  Blood flow turbulence during the cardiac cycle may play a role in the premature degeneration of the valve.  Clinical Presentation  Commonly picked up following an incidental finding of an ejection systolic murmur with or without an ejection click.  Less frequently it is diagnosed following admission with heart failure, a new diagnosis of bacterial endocarditis or following an aortic (type A) dissection.  Patient with bicuspid aortic may remain asymptomatic for a long period of time, until severe aortic stenosis develops when typical progressive symptoms include:  exertional dyspnoea  reduction in exercise tolerance  angina  pre-syncope  syncope.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Trans-thoracic echocardiogram (TTE) is the mainstay of bicuspid valve diagnosis with a detection sensitivity up to 92% and specificity of 96%.  Parasternal short axis views are often the most helpful in reaching a diagnosis.  Serial TTE including CW doppler assessment of the aortic valve are required to monitor the progression of aortic stenosis.  A degree of aortic regurgitation (AR) is common with bicuspid aortic valves but moderate to severe AR purely as a result of a bicuspid valve is rare.  Patients with bicuspid valves must undergo cross-sectional imaging of the entire ascending aorta by either cardiac MRI or CT if it is not visualised on TTE to assess for coarctation of the aorta, (bicuspid aortic valves occur in up to 50% of cases of coarctation).  Management  Surgical valve replacement is indicated in patients who develop aortic stenosis; when the diagnostic criteria of severe aortic stenosis are met in addition to symptoms, a mean paravalvular gradient of >40mmHg, AVA <1.0cm2.

DR. JAM  Prognosis  The vast majority of patients will suffer no adverse sequalae.  Around 30% of patient with a bicuspid AV will develop complications. Bradyarrhythmia Bradyarrhythmias are bradycardic arrhythmias with the definition of a heart rate < 60 bpm (however some sources define bradycardia as a heart rate < 50 bpm).  Overview Key Facts  Bradyarrhythmias are bradycardic arrhythmias with the definition of a heart rate < 60 bpm (however some sources define bradycardia as a heart rate < 50 bpm).  They can be physiological or pathological bradyarrhythmias which are divided into:  non-cardiac causes  cardiac causes  drug-induced.  Sinus bradycardias are common in young fit people; pathological causes are more common in older patients.  Clinical features may include pre-syncope or syncope, lethargy, shortness of breath and chest pain.  Intravenous (IV) atropine is given if adverse features are present (eg shock).  Temporary pacing (transcutaneous or transvenous) is used if atropine does not resolve bradyarrhythmia.  Permanent pacing is required for patients with second-degree (Mobitz) type II and third-degree heart block. Epidemiology  Sinus bradycardias are common in young fit people.  Pathological causes of bradyarrhythmias such as AV block are more commonly found in older people.  The incidence is hard to determine as many people have physiological bradycardia. Aetiology Physiological causes:  sinus bradycardia in athletes or young fit people  during sleep.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Cardiac causes:  AV block:  first degree: prolonged PR interval of > 200 ms  second degree:  type I (Wenckebach): prolongation of PR interval until a P wave drops off and does not conduct  type II:  constant PR interval with occasional P wave dropped  2:1/3:1/irregular pattern.  third-degree: no connection between P wave and QRS (atria and ventricles).  sick sinus syndrome: sinus node dysfunction. Non-cardiac causes:  hypothermia  hypothyroidism  hyperkalaemia  vasovagal syncope. Drug-induced causes:  digoxin  beta-blocker  diltiazem  amiodarone. Pathophysiology  Pathophysiology is dependent on the cause of the bradyarrhythmias:  AV blocks are due to a delay in the conduction from the atria to ventricles either due to the Bundle of His-Purkinje system or a problem with the AV node.  Clinical Presentation  Patients will have a slow peripheral pulse rate or slow heart rate on the cardiac monitor.  Symptoms may include:  pre-syncope or syncope  lethargy  shortness of breath  chest pain.  Patients may present with features of shock and hypotension due to reduced cardiac output.

DR. JAM  Diagnosis/Investigation  A 12-lead ECG is required to identify the exact bradyarrhythmia.  Episodic bradyarrhythmia may only be detected using ambulatory ECG monitoring or a Holter monitor. Rhythm Strip Showing Third-Degree Heart Block  Management Non-pharmacological  ABCDE approach as per Resuscitation Council UK guidelines:  airway:  maintain patent airway.  breathing:  give oxygen if low oxygen saturation  attach pulse oximetry.  circulation:  attach cardiac monitor.  identify any reversible and underlying cause  12-lead ECG  attach defibrillator pads.  Percussion pacing is an interim measure:  only in extreme life-threatening bradycardia as a temporary measure:  repeated rhythmic thumps  side of closed fist at left lower sternum edge  rate 50–70 bpm  attempt to stimulate the heart.  Transcutaneous pacing temporarily if atropine does not resolve bradyarrhythmias:  give appropriate sedation and anaesthesia.  Transvenous pacing wire when possible if atropine does not resolve bradyarrhythmias.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Observe if no adverse features:  if risk of asystole – treat as if adverse features present:  recent asystole  Mobitz type II  ventricular pause > 3 seconds  complete heart block with broad QRS. Pharmacological  IV atropine if adverse features are identified:  0.5 mg given up to 3 mg  repeated every 3–5 minutes  do not give in cardiac transplant patients.  If pacing is not possible, second-line drug treatment:  isoprenaline 5 µg/min IV  adrenaline 2–10 µg/min IV  alternative drugs:  aminophylline 100–200 mg slow IV infusion  dopamine 2.5–10 µg/kg/min  glucagon (if the cause is beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker)  glycopyrrolate (instead of atropine).  Review drug chart and stop any causative medications. Surgical  Pacemaker if needed (eg second-degree (Mobitz) type II and third-degree heart block).  Prognosis  If the pathological cause is known and can be treated (such as a pacemaker), the prognosis is good. If the patient presents in cardiac arrest, then the prognosis is poor. Brugada Syndrome Brugada syndrome is a rare genetic syndrome that increases the risk of sudden cardiac death.  Overview Key Facts  Brugada syndrome is a rare genetic syndrome that increases the risk of sudden cardiac death.  The most common mutation is the SCN5A sodium channelopathy, though there are many unidentified genetic mutations.

DR. JAM  The Brugada sign on an electrocardiogram (ECG) is ST elevation in V1-3 (> 2 mm) with negative T wave and right bundle branch block (RBBB).  Brugada syndrome is diagnosed with type I ECG characteristics and clinical criteria.  The only definitive treatment is an implantable cardiac defibrillator.  If undiagnosed and untreated, the mortality rate is approximately 10% per year. Epidemiology  The range of frequency is from 1 to 30 per 10 000 people.  It is more common in people of South-East Asian descent and in men.  It is responsible for up to 8% of sudden cardiac deaths.  Symptoms usually develop in adulthood. Aetiology Brugada is a genetic syndrome:  mutation:  autosomal dominant inheritance  or a new mutation.  most common gene mutation (20%):  SCN5A – sodium channel:  reduced flow of sodium ions.  majority – unable to identify the specific genetic mutation. Pathophysiology  The exact pathophysiological mechanism is unclear; however, there are two main theories.  Sodium contributes to the action potential of myocardial cells:  causes upstroke of action potential (phase 0)  leads to early repolarisation by potassium going out (phase 1).  Sodium channel is affected causing a slower flow of sodium ions:  slower sodium ion flow leads to the electrical activity being slowed down or blocked during phase 0 and phase 1 (depolarisation and early repolarisation).  First theory:  decrease in sodium release causes voltage gradient in the early repolarisation that is demonstrated by the ST elevations on ECG.  Second theory:  slow conduction and delays in activation in the right ventricle due to sodium channelopathy leads to the ECG findings.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation  The spectrum of clinical presentation is from asymptomatic (70% of patients) to sudden cardiac arrest.  Patients may present with cardiac syncope due to ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation.  The abnormal cardiac rhythm on ECG is commonly present at rest when the vagus nerve is activated. It can also be triggered by pyrexia, electrolyte disturbances and medication.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  acute pericarditis  ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)  pulmonary embolism  Romano–Ward syndrome  cardiomyopathy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Brugada syndrome is usually identified on a 12-lead ECG, although ECG findings may be transient.  The Brugada sign is ST elevation in V1-V3 with RBBB.  Ajmaline, flecainide or procainamide may be injected through the vein and help identify abnormal rhythms caused by Brugada syndrome.  Genetic testing may also be performed to aid in the diagnosis. Further imaging (echocardiography and/or magnetic resonance imaging) may also be considered to identify other causes of arrhythmias.  Brugada syndrome is diagnosed by:  type I Brugada ECG pattern  with at least one of the following clinical criteria:  documented ventricular fibrillation (VF) or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT)  family history of sudden cardiac death age < 45 years  family history of coved-characteristic ECG  VT that can be induced by electrical stimulation  syncope  nocturnal agonal respiration. Brugada Syndrome

DR. JAM  There are three types of Brugada syndrome. Types II and III are not diagnostic of Brugada syndrome but may prompt further investigation.  Type I:  Brugada sign:  coved ST elevation > 2 mm in at least one of V1-V3 leads associated with negative T wave.  Type II:  saddleback-shape ST-elevation > 2 mm.  Type III:  either type 1 or type 2 characteristics but < 2 mm ST elevation.  Management Non-pharmacological  Avoid triggers:  fever: treat promptly with antipyretics  binge alcohol consumption  dehydration  medications  strenuous activity. Pharmacological  Anti-arrhythmic drug:  quinidine:  commonly used in conjunction with implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) for people with recurrent episodes of arrhythmias  can also be used alone if ICD is not suitable for patient  isoprenaline:  used in an emergency as IV infusion in patients with recurrent life-threatening arrhythmias.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Surgical  ICD is the mainstay of management.  Catheter ablation: only in patients who have needed shocks delivered from their ICD.  Prognosis  If undiagnosed and untreated, the mortality rate is approximately 10% per year. Genetic counselling may be offered to patients with Brugada syndrome. Cardiac Arrest Cardiac arrest is a sudden state of circulatory failure.  Overview Key Facts  Cardiac arrest is a sudden state of circulatory failure.  This occurs when there is a loss of cardiac systolic function.  There are around 60 000 cases of suspected cardiac arrest in the United Kingdom (UK) annually.  Fewer than 1 in 10 people survive an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, whereas closer to 20% are able to return home following an in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA).  Immediate initiation of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) can double or quadruple survival from out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.  Defibrillation within 3–5 minutes of collapse can produce survival rates up to 50–70% in out-of-hospital arrests.  Cardiac arrest should be suspected if a person is unresponsive and not breathing normally.  Many cardiorespiratory arrests that occur in hospital are preventable (up to 80%).  Patients who are at immediate risk of arresting are described as being in ‘peri-arrest.  These patients need assessing and managing using the ABCDE pathway to try and stabilise them before arrest happens.  Good-quality chest compressions with as little interruption as possible are key to improving the chance of survival postcardiac arrest (in any heart rhythm).  This algorithm requires practitioners to identify the underlying heart rhythm in order to administer the correct interventions.  The four main underlying heart rhythms in a cardiac arrest are: Shockable Non-shockable Pulseless VT Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) Ventricular fibrillation Asystole  Practitioners can use:

DR. JAM  automated external defibrillator (AED) which will identify the underlying heart rhythm and administer shocks appropriately  manual defibrillator (practitioners must identify heart rhythms and administer shocks manually).  Adrenaline (1 : 10 000) and amiodarone are included in the advanced life support (ALS) algorithm and should be given as directed.  The common reversible causes of cardiac arrest can be summarised by four Hs and four Ts:  H – hypoxia  H – hypovolaemia  H – hypothermia  H – hypo/hyperkalaemia (or other metabolic disturbances, eg magnesium or calcium)  T – thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary – myocardial infarction (MI)/pulmonary embolism (PE))  T – tension pneumothorax  T – tamponade (cardiac)  T – toxins.  If the patient recovers spontaneous circulation, they must receive immediate post-cardiac arrest treatment and a full ABCDE assessment.  It is also important to consider when resuscitation may not appropriate:  if a mentally competent patient has consistently stated or recorded the fact that they do not want to be resuscitated  if the patient has signed an advance directive forbidding resuscitation  if resuscitation is not in a patient's interest or resuscitation is very unlikely to be successful  when in doubt, resuscitate. Epidemiology  There are around 60 000 cases of suspected cardiac arrest every year, but fewer than 1 in 10 people survive an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.  The mean age of patients suffering in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is approximately 66 years old.  Men > women.  Around 80% of IHCA have a non-shockable underlying heart rhythm (PEA or asystole).  The most common cause of IHCA is cardiac events (50–60%) followed by respiratory insufficiency (15–40%). Aetiology  Deterioration and cardiorespiratory arrest can be caused by problems with a patient's:  A – airway  B – breathing or  C – circulation.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pathophysiology  Airway obstruction  Can be complete or partial.  Partial airway obstruction is usually accompanied by additional sounds such as snoring, choking, rattling or stridor.  Partial obstruction may progress into complete obstruction if not resolved.  Partial obstruction may result in:  cerebral or pulmonary oedema  exhaustion  secondary apnoea  hypoxic brain injury  cardiac arrest.  Complete airway obstruction is usually silent and can rapidly cause cardiac arrest.  A classic sign of complete airway obstruction is ‘see-saw breathing’ – the chest and abdomen move oppositely (chest is drawn in and the abdomen expands on inspiration and chest expands and abdomen is drawn in on expiration).  Causes of airway obstruction can include:  central nervous system (CNS) depression (eg loss of primitive reflexes such as gag reflex, loss of muscle tone, tongue causing obstruction) resulting from any one of: head injury, intracerebral disease, hypercapnia, hypoglycaemia and drugs (especially alcohol, opioids and anaesthetic agents)  blood  vomit  foreign body (eg food, tooth)  direct trauma to face or throat, resulting in soft-tissue swelling  epiglottitis  pharyngeal swelling (eg infection, oedema)  laryngospasm (can occur during instrumentation or intubation)  bronchospasm (eg acute severe asthma, anaphylaxis)  bronchial secretions  blockage of a tracheostomy or laryngectomy.  Breathing difficulties  Can be acute or chronic.  Conscious patients who have breathing difficulty may complain of being short of breath and be distressed.  Early signs include tachypnoea (respiratory rate (RR) > 15 breaths/minute), irritability, confusion, lethargy (from hypercapnia and hypoxia) and pulse oximetry < 94% (or < 88% in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with long-standing CO2 retention).

DR. JAM  Late signs include cyanosis (especially centrally), arterial blood gas (ABG) results showing raised PaCO2 and decreased pH.  Patients with chronic respiratory inadequacy with acute complications, eg chest infection, muscle weakness or rib fractures, may experience exhaustion.  CNS depression can result in diminished or abolished respiratory drive.  Muscle weakness and/or nerve damage can result in breathing inadequacy, eg spinal cord injury (C3-C5), myasthenia gravis, Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) and multiple sclerosis (MS).  Restrictive chest wall abnormalities may prevent adequate breathing, eg kyphoscoliosis, and fractured ribs/sternum causing pain.  Severe lung disease may impair gas exchange, eg infection, acute exacerbation of COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, lung contusion, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), pulmonary oedema and pneumothorax/haemothorax.  Circulatory problems  May be caused by primary heart disease or by heart abnormalities as a result of secondary problems.  Signs and symptoms include:  chest pain  dyspnoea  syncope  tachycardia  bradycardia  tachypnoea  hypotension  poor peripheral perfusion (eg cool peripheries and prolonged capillary refill time)  altered mental state  oliguria.  Primary heart problems include:  most commonly take the form of arrhythmia secondary to acute coronary syndromes (ACS), split into:  ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)  non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI)  unstable angina.  valvular disease  cardiomyopathy (hypertrophic or dilated)  inherited (eg Brugada syndrome, congenital heart disease).  Secondary heart problems include:  cardiac arrest following airway obstruction/breathing difficulties  hypovolaemia  severe anaemia  hypothermia

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  severe septic shock.  Reversible causes (four Hs and four Ts)  Hypoxia – oxygen saturations may help. Patients may be confused, drowsy, irritable.  Hypothermia – easily determined using a thermometer.  Hypovolaemia – evidence of severe bleeding, hypotension, tachycardia, poor peripheral perfusion, oliguria.  Hypo/hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, acidosis, etc – investigate with blood tests:  ABG/venous blood gas (VBG)  blood glucose  full biochemical profile – may take time to obtain results.  Thrombosis – coronary most common cause (eg ACS – history, ECG, blood troponins) or massive pulmonary embolus (PE) – history (look for risk factors), examination (DVT), CTPA/Ddimer (usually not useful acutely).  Tension pneumothorax – clinical diagnosis: reduced air entry, reduced chest expansion, hyper-resonance on percussion, tracheal deviation away from a pneumothorax (late sign).  Tamponade – difficult to diagnose clinically, signs include distended neck veins, hypotension (neither can be assessed during cardiac arrest), history of penetrating chest injuries.  Toxins – history/collateral history, drug charts may be useful, pinpoint pupils may be evident; seek advice from local toxicology department.  Clinical Presentation  Depending on the cause, patients may exhibit one or more of these signs and symptoms:  fall/collapse  drowsiness/unresponsiveness  confusion or irritability  active distress (eg if airway obstructed/unable to breathe adequately)  partial airway obstruction – additional breath sounds (eg snoring, stridor, rattling, choking)  complete airway obstruction – silent breathing, see-saw breathing  tachypnoea/dyspnoea  use of accessory muscles of respiration  cyanosis  tachycardia  chest pain  hypotension  prolonged capillary refill time.

DR. JAM  Differential Diagnosis  The events leading up to a cardiac arrest in hospital may be witnessed or unwitnessed – it often occurs in the form of a fall or collapse.  Differential diagnoses for a patient who has collapsed (and is yet to be assessed) include:  syncope – can occur for a number of reasons:  vasovagal  cardiac  postural hypotension  most common reason for loss of consciousness.  epilepsy – loss of consciousness can occur following an epileptic episode  hypoperfusion – reduced oxygen delivery to the brain can cause loss of consciousness (eg in the event of inadequate ventilation/cardiac arrest, hypovolaemia, anaphylaxis, sepsis, etc)  intoxication – multiple substances which suppress the CNS may cause loss of consciousness (eg alcohol, opioids, drug overdoses such as paracetamol)  central nervous system disruption – eg from head injury or stroke/transient ischaemic attack  metabolic disturbance – eg hypoglycaemia/hyperglycaemia (diabetic complications very common cause), hyponatraemia, hypercapnia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  A useful indicator for identifying patients who are deteriorating/peri-arrest is the National Early Warning Score (NEWS):  this evaluates patient observations and generates a score that correlates with how unwell the patient is.  It uses:  respiration rate  oxygen saturations  blood pressure  pulse  consciousness  temperature.  With the above, it generates a total score out of 20 (a score of 0 is the best, 20 is the worst).  If a patient is found to have an increasing NEWS score, observations should be repeated more frequently than usual and they should be escalated appropriately to prevent further deterioration.  If the patient does lose consciousness/arrest then they should be rapidly assessed:  shout for help immediately  assess the patient for signs of life  ask ‘are you alright?’ – if they can talk, then A, B and C are relatively intact

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  if there is no response, perform the head tilt and chin lift airway manoeuvre (use jaw thrust if there is a risk of Cspine injury) and assess for breathing for a maximum of 10 seconds using ‘Look, Listen and Feel’ (look for chest movements, listen for breath sounds and feel for breath against your cheek).  Depending on your findings, follow the appropriate algorithm to manage them.  Management  Management differs depending on the cause and severity of the patient illness.  If the patient is sick or has collapsed, first assess for signs of life and breathing (for a maximum of 10 seconds using the ‘Look, Listen and Feel’ approach).  If the patient is breathing – assess them immediately using ABCDE and identify the causative pathology and manage this:  if the patient is severely unwell or in peri-arrest, consider calling the resuscitation team.  If the patient is not breathing – call the resuscitation team immediately (and follow the ALS algorithm).  If the patient is not breathing it is important to consider if resuscitation is appropriate.  It is also important to consider when resuscitation may not be appropriate such as:  if a mentally competent patient has consistently stated or recorded the fact that they do not want to be resuscitated  if the patient has signed an advance directive forbidding resuscitation  if resuscitation is not in a patient's interest or resuscitation is very unlikely to be successful  if there is any doubt, then proceed to resuscitation measures.  Patient is breathing  AIRWAY – if the airway is compromised:  clear the mouth of foreign bodies or secretions using suction or Magill forceps  head tilt/chin lift or jaw thrust manoeuvre  establish an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal (contraindicated in basal skull fracture) airway and ventilate with bag-and-mask ventilation with 15 litres of oxygen  if required, seek senior advice to secure a definite airway (eg endotracheal tube) or ventilation  C-spine: either manual immobilisation or triple-point immobilisation (blocks, straps and a C-spine collar) if suspected injury (high-level trauma, unconscious following trauma etc); if in-hospital arrest, C-spine is unlikely to be newly damaged.

DR. JAM BREATHING – if breathing is insufficient  Provide supplementary oxygen (if not already done so in A).  Look for/treat the six main life-threatening chest injuries:  airway obstruction (completed in A)  tension pneumothorax  open pneumothorax  massive haemothorax  flail chest  cardiac tamponade.  Gain an ABG sample to assess acid-base status. CIRCULATION – assess the patient’s haemodynamic status  Identify any sites of haemorrhage (internally or externally).  Establish intravenous (IV) access (usually 2 × 14–16 G cannulas in the antecubital fossae).  Take blood samples for cross-matching and other investigations.  Give an IV bolus of fluid if the patient is shocked.  If the patient is haemodynamically unstable and losing blood, they may need to undergo treatment to stop the bleeding, eg surgery. DISABILITY – assess patients’ neurological status  Using either Alert Verbal Painful Unresponsiveness (AVPU) or Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), pupils and blood glucose measurements:  if blood glucose is abnormal, then take measures to correct this. EXPOSURE/ENVIRONMENT  Expose the patient fully to look for any other findings, eg bleeding, rashes, bruising, etc:  it is important to assess (and manage) the patient’s temperature, eg using warming blankets in a hypothermic patient  examine other appropriate systems (eg abdominal, urinary).  Patient is NOT breathing  If the patient is unconscious and not breathing, then they are in cardiac arrest and require treatment under the ALS algorithm:

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  it is important to CALL FOR HELP immediately – resuscitation/crash team required ASAP  begin chest compressions (uninterrupted until defibrillator pads can be applied and monitor the heart rhythm):  good chest compressions should be administered to the centre of the patient’s chest at a rate of approximately 120 compressions per minute at a depth of 5–6 cm.  once the pads are in place, stop chest compressions to analyse the heart rhythm (either manually or using an automated external defibrillator (AED)):  while analysing heart rhythms, the pulse MUST be palpated; this will determine whether the rhythm is pulseless or not; if they do not have a pulse, the ALS algorithm should be followed.  heart rhythms during cardiac arrest may be split into shockable and non-shockable:  shockable – ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT) – approximately 20% of all cardiac arrests (both out of and inside hospital)  non-shockable – asystole (As) and pulseless electrical activity (PEA) – approximately 80% of all cardiac arrests.  the algorithm then splits depending on which heart rhythm is currently occurring; it is possible for the heart rhythms to change from shockable to non-shockable and vice versa during CPR, so it is important to continue monitoring and change treatment as appropriate. Ventricular fibrillation on II-lead ECG:  Shockable rhythms:  once a rhythm has been identified as either VF or pVT, a practitioner should restart chest compressions while the defibrillator is prepared  warn all practitioners (except the person delivering chest compressions) to ‘stand clear’ and to remove oxygendelivery devices as appropriate  the designated person will choose an energy level for the defibrillator (minimum of 150 J for the first shock and subsequent shocks should be higher than this) and begins to charge the device

DR. JAM  once the defibrillator is charged, tell the person performing chest compressions to stand clear and when possible, deliver the shock  after the shock has been delivered, immediately restart CPR in a ratio of 30 : 2 chest compressions to rescue breaths (unless the patient is already being ventilated) – do NOT pause at this point to reassess rhythm or check for a pulse  continue CPR for 2 minutes and then co-ordinate a brief pause to reassess the heart rhythm – if VF/pVT persists then repeat the steps as above to deliver a second shock  if VF/pVT continue to persist despite a second shock, repeat the steps as above to deliver a third shock AND give adrenaline (1 mg of 1 : 10 000 IV) and amiodarone (300 mg IV) while performing the next 2 minutes of CPR  continue to repeat the cycle of 2 minutes of CPR – rhythm/pulse check – defibrillation sequence if required  give a further 1 mg of adrenaline IV every alternate shock sequence (approximately every 3–5 minutes)  if an organised electrical activity compatible with cardiac output returns during a rhythm check, then immediately check for ROSC (return of systemic circulation) by looking for: signs of life, central pulses and end-tidal CO2, if possible:  if there are signs of ROSC then immediately begin post-resuscitation care  if there are NOT signs of ROSC then switch to the non-shockable algorithm. ECG trace showing an example of VT with broad-complex tachycardia and regular rhythm:  Non-shockable rhythms:  PEA is defined as cardiac arrest in the presence of electrical activity (other than ventricular tachyarrhythmia) that would normally be associated with a palpable pulse; so no specific ECG trace correlates with PEA (ECG may look completely normal)  once PEA or asystole has been identified as the underlying heart rhythm then CPR should be started immediately at a rate of 30 : 2 chest compressions to breaths

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  as soon as IV access is established, adrenaline (1 mg of 1 : 10 000 IV) should be given  continue CPR (30 : 2) until an airway is secured and the patient can be continuously ventilated and receive continuous chest compressions  recheck the heart rhythm after 2 minutes  if electrical activity compatible with a pulse is seen check for a pulse/signs of life:  signs of life present – immediately begin postresuscitation care  no signs of life present – continue CPR, re-check the rhythm every 2 minutes and administer adrenaline (1 mg IV) every alternate 2-minute cycle of CPR (every 3–5 minutes)  if electrical activity shows VF/pVT then switch to the shockable side of the ALS algorithm  it is especially important to look for and treat reversible causes of cardiac arrest (four Hs and four Ts) in the presence of PEA/asystole.  Asystole – this ECG trace shows an example of asystole demonstrating total cessation of electrical activity from the heart; the line is not usually completely flat and will show a level of undulation as seen here:  Prognosis  Immediate initiation of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) can double or quadruple survival from an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.  Defibrillation within 3–5 minutes of collapse can produce survival rates of up to 50–70%.  Around 20% of patients who undergo an in-hospital cardiac arrest will survive and be able to return home.  Prevention is key – an estimated 80% of patients show deterioration in clinical signs in the few hours preceding cardiac arrest.

DR. JAM Cardiac Failure Heart failure occurs when there is insufficient cardiac output to meet the circulatory demands of the body in the absence of mechanical obstructions to the circulation.  Overview Key Facts  Heart failure occurs when there is insufficient cardiac output to meet the circulatory demands of the body in the absence of mechanical obstructions to the circulation.  It can be defined by anatomy (left, right, or biventricular), ejection fraction (systolic and diastolic) or time course (acute and chronic).  Heart failure may be precipitated by valvular disease.  The NYHA (New York Heart Association) system classifies severity and the Driving and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) restrictions may apply (see other information). Epidemiology  Heart failure affects more than 40 million people globally.  Worldwide, prevalence ranges from 2% of all adults and up to 10% of those aged > 65; this rises to over 10% in those aged > 75 years.  In the United Kingdom, the prevalence ranges from 1 in 15 between ages 75 and 84 to 1 in 7 in those aged > 85.  It is thought that half of all heart failure patients have preserved ejection fraction. Aetiology Cardiac:  ischaemic heart disease (most common)  hypertension  cardiomyopathy  valvular heart disease  pericardial disease  arrhythmias, eg atrial fibrillation (AF)  congenital heart disease. High-output states:  anaemia  beri-beri  thyrotoxicosis  phaeochromocytoma  liver failure  sepsis

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Paget disease  arteriovenous (AV) malformations and fistulae. Other:  volume overload, eg end-stage kidney disease, nephrotic syndrome  obesity  drugs, eg alcohol, cocaine, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), beta blockers/Ca2+ channel blockers. Pathophysiology Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HF-PEF):  Also known as diastolic heart failure (although use of this term is declining); it should be considered in dyspnoeic patients with no signs of fluid overload.  May occur alone or in combination with systolic heart failure.  The main problem is impaired cardiac relaxation due to increased ventricular stiffness from a range of causes, resulting in poor cardiac filing and elevated diastolic pressures.  This results in signs of fluid overload and peripheral oedema, typical of right-sided or biventricular failure because the blood effectively backs up into the circulatory system.  This backed-up blood then leads to volume overload and the systemic signs observed. Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HF-REF):  Also known as systolic heart failure, this is defined as an ejection systolic fraction < 35–40%.  Impaired contractility of cardiac myocytes leads to reduced cardiac output and higher ventricular end-diastolic volumes/pressures. This pressure is transmitted backwards into the pulmonary vasculature, causing pulmonary oedema and breathlessness, typical of left-sided failure, and is often worse when supine.  In severe cases, this can lead to concurrent right-sided failure, leading in turn to signs of fluid overload and peripheral oedema.  Clinical Presentation  Dyspnoea.  Orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (PND).  Nocturnal cough.  Fluid retention.  Fatigue and decreased exercise tolerance.  Syncopal episodes.  Tachycardia/tachypnoea.  Displaced apex beat.  S3/S4 gallop rhythm.

DR. JAM  Hepatomegaly/raised jugular venous pressure (JVP).  Bibasal crepitations.  Haemoptysis.  Peripheral oedema.  Differential Diagnosis Conditions causing breathlessness:  chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)  asthma  pulmonary embolism  lung cancer  anxiety  pulmonary hypertension  myocardial infarction (MI). Conditions causing peripheral oedema:  prolonged inactivity or venous insufficiency causing dependent oedema  nephrotic syndrome  drugs (eg dihydropyridine, Ca2+ channel blockers, NSAIDs)  hypoalbuminaemia (from renal or hepatic disease)  pelvic tumour. Other conditions:  obesity  severe anaemia or thyroid disease  bilateral renal artery stenosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  B-type natriuretic peptide is measured as the main diagnostic blood test, with a level > 2000 pg/ml requiring a 2-week echocardiogram to be done (and six weeks if between 400 and 2000 pg/ml).  It is secreted by the cardiac myocytes and elevated levels are observed when they are overstretched, as is seen in heart failure.  Other bloods may uncover a cause, for example renal/liver/thyroid function tests, lipid profile, glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c).  The electrocardiogram may show signs of previous MI, ventricular enlargement, and abnormal rhythms (AF or complex ventricular arrhythmias).  Echocardiogram:  reduced ejection fraction (EF) in systolic heart failure  changes in left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) and LV systolic wall tension  features of LV dysfunction: reduced fractional shortening, LV enlargement, paradoxical septal motion  cardiac wall stiffness/reduced contractility.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differentials may be ruled out using chest X-rays, urinalysis, and peak flow/spirometry.  Management Non-pharmacological:  Stop offending medications that precipitate heart failure, eg NSAIDs and chemotherapy.  Optimise co-morbidities, eg diabetes, hypertension, peripheral artery disease and hyperlipidaemia.  Pneumococcal and influenza vaccine. Pharmacological:  Loop diuretics, eg furosemide (do not change mortality).  Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors/angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) (CONSENSUS, SOLVD, ATLAS, Val-HeFT, VALIANT and CHARM studies showed significant improvements in mortality and morbidity).  Beta-blockers (COPERNICUS, MERIT-HF and CIBIS-II showed improved mortality/morbidity).  Aldosterone receptor antagonists, eg spironolactone (RALES and EMPHASIS-HF).  Consider anti-platelets and statins.  Hydralazine and nitrates.  Digoxin - recommended for worsening/ severe heart failure despite first-line treatment for heart failure (on specialist advice.  Ivabradine (selectively inhibits funny current in the sinus node to slow sinus rhythm). Surgical:  Cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT).  Implantable cardiac defibrillator (ICD).  LV assist device.  Cardiac transplantation. Treatment with ICD or CRT for people with heart failure who have left ventricular dysfunction with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less (according to NYHA class, QRS duration and presence of LBBB).  Prognosis  The overall 5-year survival rate is 60% for those with an ejection systolic fraction (ESF) <40% whereas it is 95% for those with an ESF > 50%.  The 5-year mortality rate is approximately 50%.  Of those admitted to hospital 40% die or are readmitted within one year.  Poor prognostic indicators include:
