IV Dyspnoea at rest -60 Coarctation Of The Aorta Coarctation of the aorta (CoA) is an aortopathy, a disease of the aorta and severe narrowing at the site of the regressed ductus arteriosus, which connects the aorta to the pulmonary artery in utero.  Overview Key Facts  Coarctation of the aorta (CoA) is an aortopathy, a disease of the aorta and severe narrowing at the site of the regressed ductus arteriosus, which connects the aorta to the pulmonary artery in utero.  If severe, aortic blood flow is impaired, causing heart failure and metabolic acidosis.  It is life-threatening in early life.  Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) can keep the ductus arteriosus patent to allow right-to-left shunting while awaiting surgery.  Surgery is the standard treatment. Coarctation of the aorta: Epidemiology  1 in 2 500 deaths.  Higher rates in males and Caucasians.

DR. JAM Aetiology  CoA arises as an impairment in the vessel media development of the left fourth and sixth arches.  Associations of Coarctation  Cardiac:  bicuspid aortic valve (and thus AS ± AR) in 10–20%  patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)  ventricular septal defect (VSD)  mitral valve disease.  Non-cardiac:  berry aneurysms (circle of Willis)  Turner syndrome  renal abnormalities.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentation of coarctation include:  hypertension  radiofemoral delay of arterial pulse  absent femoral pulses  mid-systolic or continuous murmur (infraclavicular)  subscapular bruits  rib notching on chest X-ray  post-stenotic aortic dilatation on chest X-ray  leg cramps  muscle weakness  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for CoA include:  dilate cardiomyopathy  hypertrophic cardiomyopathy  aortic stenosis  hypertension.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnoses and investigations for coarctation of the aorta are as follows:  collateral development can be significant and audible posteriorly and may cause ‘notching’ of ribs on chest Xrays  barium swallows may demonstrate oesophageal compression from the post-stenotic dilatation of the aorta

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  echocardiography may be sufficient  magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is definitive  chest X-ray may show signs of congestive cardiac failure.  Management Pharmacological:  PGE1 can keep the ductus arteriosus patent to allow right-toleft shunting to the descending aorta while awaiting surgery. Surgical:  Treatment can be surgical or percutaneous.  End-to-end anastomosis is the preferred surgical technique, but restenosis can occur.  Balloon dilatation of the coarctation is typically focused on recurrent coarctation after surgery.  Prognosis  Complications may occur despite repair with 30% of patients with surgically corrected coarctation remaining significantly hypertensive with end-organ harm.  Heart failure, re-coarctation at a new site in the aorta.  Aneurysm formation at the site of repair.  Poor prognosis of left untreated. Coronary Artery Bypass Grafts Coronary artery bypass grafts are procedures that aim to reroute blood flow around a narrowed coronary artery in order to improve blood supply to the myocardium.  Overview Key Facts  Coronary artery bypass grafts (CABGs) are procedures that aim to reroute blood flow around a narrowed coronary artery in order to improve blood supply to the myocardium.  Coronary ‘targets’ are identified by coronary angiography, and a surgical strategy regarding on-pump or off-pump and the conduits is devised.  A ‘standard’ triple bypass involves grafting:  the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) to the left anterior descending (LAD) artery  a portion of the harvested long saphenous vein from the aorta to the circumflex artery

DR. JAM  a portion of the harvested long saphenous vein from the aorta to the distal right coronary artery  recently, saphenous vein grafts are being replaced with radial artery grafts. Indications for CABG  More than 50% narrowing of a coronary artery plus:  angina refractory to medical management  ST Depression on an exercise electrocardiogram (ECG)  left-main stem narrowing  severe triple vessel disease  angina with left ventricular dysfunction. Principles of coronary artery bypass grafting  The usual incision is a median sternotomy, although ‘minimally invasive’ procedures are sometimes performed via left anterolateral thoracotomy.  The IMAs are usually harvested before opening the pericardium.  The pericardium is opened and stay sutures placed in order to lift the heart forwards.  The heart is cannulated for cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) in the standard way.  CPB is initiated, an aortic cross-clamp applied and cardioplegia administered to stop the heart.  Previously planned coronary ‘targets’ are identified by direct examination of the coronary arteries.  Bottom-end anastomoses: conduits are anastomosed end to side on to the coronary targets using continuous 6/0 or 7/0 Prolene® sutures. It helps to wear loupes for this procedure.  The aortic cross-clamp is removed, the heart rewarmed and weaned from bypass.  Top-end anastomoses: with the heart now beating, a side-biting clamp is applied to the ascending aorta and circular punches taken from it, to which the ‘top ends’ of the vein grafts are anastomosed.  De-airing: a small needle is placed into the grafts to enable trapped air to escape in order to prevent air-embolic myocardial infarction (MI).  Protamine is given and the heart decannulated.  Drains are placed in the pericardium, and the pleurae if open.  The median sternotomy is closed in the standard fashion, taking care to avoid entrapment of the new grafts.  Procedure Saphenous vein harvest  The long saphenous vein runs from anterior to the medial malleolus to its junction with the femoral vein in the groin.  The key surgical landmarks for saphenous vein harvesting are:

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  at the ankle: the vein is immediately anterior to the medial malleolus. As it runs superiorly, in its first few centimetres, it becomes more posterior such that, at 5 cm above the superior margin of the medial malleolus, the vein lies at the midpoint of the medial malleolus in the anteroposterior (AP) plane  at the knee: the vein lies approximately one handbreadth posterior to the medial border of the patella  at the groin: the vein lies 1 cm medial to the midinguinal point.  As the vein contains valves, when harvesting the conduit, it is essential to mark its ends so that it can be oriented correctly for blood to flow to the coronary anastomosis. Procedure for saphenous vein harvesting  Make a small incision 5 cm proximal to the medial malleolus and at its midpoint in the anteroposterior (AP) plane (ideally, the incision is made after palpation of the vein, but this is not always possible); take great care not to puncture the vein itself with the skin incision.  Having identified the vein, extend the incision with scissors proximally up the leg; take care not to create a large flap of devitalised skin, which will increase the risk of wound infection. The amount of vein harvested will vary with the operative strategy. A rule of thumb is that one graft requires one scissorlength of the vein. This may need to be altered if the heart is dilated. Bear in mind that the vein shrinks in length when harvested.  Carefully dissect off the fine layer of fascia overlying the vein.  Carefully ligate each and every vein branch, however small, with fine silk (remember that ligatures will soon be exposed to arterial pressures).  Handle vein graft very carefully throughout to avoid spasm.  When the required length has been exposed, and its branches divided, cannulate the distal end with a Hamilton–Bailey cannula (and tie it into place).  Clamp the proximal end and excise the vein.  Flush the vein with heparinised blood.  Double-ligate the two vein ends remaining in the leg.  Close soft tissues in layers to obliterate dead space (can accommodate haematoma and lead to wound infections). Saphenous vein harvesting:

DR. JAM Left internal mammary artery (LIMA) harvest  The LIMA–left anterior descending artery (LAD) artery graft is now almost ubiquitous in CABG surgery because the late patency and survival data are so compelling.  The LIMA harvest should be undertaken with care because the vessel is very easy to injure, and non-use of the vessel results in a serious reduction of the patient’s chance of survival.  The IMAs arise from the subclavian artery and run parallel and lateral to the sternum, giving off intercostal branches. The most superior is the superior intercostal branch, which supplies the first and second interspaces. The IMAs run anterior to the internal thoracic fascia. Procedure: LIMA Harvest It helps to wear magnifying loupes for this procedure.  Perform median sternotomy.  Insert a special retractor to lift the left hemisternum relative to the right hemisternum (IMA is viewed from the opposite side of the table as if the surgeon were peering through a letterbox).  The details of the technique vary between surgeons, but most aim to create a pedicled (not a skeletonised) IMA graft, complete with associated fascia.  Take care not to injure the phrenic nerve as it crosses the IMA at the first rib.  Incise the internal thoracic fascia medial to the IMA with diathermy.  Take care not to touch the IMA while retracting the fascia to display the arterial branches.  Clip and divide the branches in turn.  Keep diathermy at a low setting and a good distance from the artery to avoid damaging it.  Eventually, when enough branches have been divided, the artery will be freed from the chest wall.  Divide the lateral fascia to free the pedicle.  Place a non-crushing bulldog clamp on the IMA proximally.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Clamp the distal end of the IMA with artery forceps and divide with scissors.  Ligate the distal end of the artery (staying on the chest wall) with a heavy suture. Radial artery harvest  Late occlusion in saphenous vein grafts has prompted the wider use of arterial conduits, in the hope of extending the proven benefits of late patency of IMA grafts to other coronary territories.  The radial artery is extremely prone to spasm – indeed, early experience with the conduit from the 1970s was very discouraging for exactly this reason.  More recently, radial artery grafts have enjoyed a renaissance that is attributable to better surgical technique and vasodilating drugs, particularly in young patients or those who have poor saphenous veins.  Patients are screened pre-operatively with the Allen test to ensure adequate collateral ulnar flow; it is important to know the Allen test as a medical student. Patients with high functional requirements of their hands are usually excluded from radial artery harvesting.  The non-dominant arm is normally used as the radial artery donor. Procedure: Radial artery harvest It helps to wear magnifying loupes to perform this procedure. Preparation  Place an oxygen saturation monitor on the index finger of the operated arm.  The arm, exposed from wrist to mid-upper arm, is prepared and draped on a board that is separate from the main operating table.  Landmarks are the radial pulse and the brachial pulse incision. Incision  Make an incision from 2 cm distal to the brachial pulse to the radial pulse and deepen through the subcutaneous fat, taking great care not to puncture the artery in its distal, subcutaneous part.  Throughout the procedure, absolutely meticulous haemostasis is required in order to retain good views of the artery. Procedure  Divide the fascia overlying the brachioradialis medial to the lateral antebrachial nerve of the forearm. Retract the muscle laterally to reveal the radial artery.  Taking care not to touch the artery, handling it only via the associated fascia, divide the fascial covering of the radial artery on the lateral side. Ligate and divide the branches using titanium

DR. JAM clips. Great care must be taken not to injure the superficial radial nerve which lies deep to the artery at this stage.  The medial border is then dissected free, ligating and dividing numerous branches.  Lift the artery from its bed, and ligate and divide the few posterior branches.  The procedure is almost complete. As a double-check of the pre-op Allen test, the artery is occluded between the fingers, and the trace from the oxygen saturation monitor on the patient’s finger is watched. If this remains pulsatile, the artery may be safely removed.  Remaining ends of the radial artery in the arms must be double ligated to prevent blood loss.  The artery is harvested and flushed with heparinised blood mixed with a vasodilator substance. The Allen Test Aim: To assess the adequacy of the ulnar artery blood supply to the hand:  the examiner’s fingers press hard on both the radial and ulnar pulses so as to stop the flow  the patient opens and closes his hand in order to exsanguinate it (the hand becomes white)  pressure is released from the ulnar artery only  if colour returns to the hand, the ulnar artery is likely to be adequate to supply the hand.  Complications Summary of complications of CABG  Immediate  bleeding  low cardiac output syndrome  myocardial infarction  neurological complications.  Early  pneumonia  sternal infections  leg infections  renal failure  atrial dysrhythmias  upper GI bleed and perforation.  Late  recurrent stenosis. Bleeding

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Bleeding may be due to:  ‘surgical’ causes:  dehiscence of the operative site  ligatures falling off side branches of coronary grafts  leakage from cannulation sites.  ‘non-surgical’ causes:  coagulopathy arising from CPB, and clotting factor consumption  generalised ‘microvascular ooze’.  When bleeding occurs within the confines of the pericardium, there is the potential for tamponade, even when blood loss is relatively slow.  Emergency re-opening of the thorax in the event of tamponade may be required to avoid cardiac arrest. Low cardiac output syndrome  This is caused by:  poor ventricular function  incomplete revascularisation  inadequate myocardial protection.  It is managed by:  maintenance of sinus rhythm (medically or with pacing)  optimised preload and afterload using fluid and monitoring (eg with a pulmonary artery catheter)  maintenance of haematocrit of 30% (eg with packed red cell infusion)  optimised oxygenation and correct acidosis  inotropes (if all the above have been optimised and cardiac output is still poor)  vasodilators to reduce afterload  investigation with transthoracic echocardiography and/or transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE)  intra-aortic balloon pump (to assist systolic emptying by reducing cardiac afterload while maintaining a mean arterial pressure for cerebral and coronary perfusion). Myocardial ischaemia and infarction  This is due to poor flow through the conduit, which is caused by:  tight anastomosis  arterial graft spasm  poor run-off (small distal coronary artery)  ventricular hypertrophy causing increased myocardial ischaemic watershed area.  It is managed by:  optimised oxygenation, haematocrit and haemodynamics

DR. JAM  nitrates  intra-aortic balloon pump. Neurological Complications  Cognitive and psychological abnormalities may be detected in up to 40% of patients’ post-bypass. Most return to normal; 1% have a cerebrovascular accident (CVA).  The risk of complications is increased by:  age > 70  emergency cardiac surgery  arteriopathy (peripheral vascular disease, atherosclerosis, carotid occlusive disease, previous transient ischaemic attack (TIA) or CVA)  prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass  intraoperative or perioperative circulatory arrest  postoperative atrial fibrillation.  Neurological complications are caused by:  co-existing carotid artery disease  hypoperfusion (intraoperatively or perioperatively).  They are managed by:  checking for carotid disease preoperatively  scheduling prior or simultaneous carotid endarterectomy if indicated  maintaining mean pressure of > 80 mmHg while on bypass. Note that peripheral neurological complications are caused by conduit harvest. Sternal Infections  Sternal infections are related to:  diabetes  peripheral vascular disease  obesity  bilateral IMA harvest  emergency re-opening  poor sterile technique.  Signs and symptoms are:  sternal click on movement or coughing  pain  sternal instability on examination (with a finger placed either side of the sternal wound ask the patient to cough. Movement between the two sides denotes instability)  discharge and/or wound breakdown  movement of wires on chest X-ray.  Sternal infections are caused by:  staphylococci (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA))  sometimes infections can spread by hand from other sites (eg from leg wounds following vein harvest).  Management includes:  involvement of microbiologists  sternal debridement and rewiring  occasionally plastics involvement and flap placement  long-term antibiotics. Leg Infections  Leg infections are related to:  diabetes  peripheral vascular disease  obesity  haematoma  poor sterile technique.

DR. JAM  Leg infections are caused by:  staphylococci (MRSA).  Management includes:  dressings  antibiotics, intravenous (IV) or oral, depending on the severity of the infection  incision and drainage of abscess areas. Renal failure  There is usually an underlying disease, with acute insult:  pre-existing renal dysfunction due to hypertension  diabetes and/or small-vessel disease  low cardiac output states.  Management includes:  management of any underlying cause, eg low cardiac output  cessation of nephrotoxic drugs  early renal team referral  depending on severity – just fluid management or haemofiltration or dialysis. Atrial dysrhythmias  Causes of atrial dysrhythmias include:  electrolyte imbalance  poor ventricular function  atrial distension by fluid overload  sepsis  drugs.  Atrial dysrhythmias are managed by:  acute life support if there is patient compromise  correction of electrolytes  rate control  rhythm control. Upper GI Bleed and perforation  These are related to:  surgical stress  prolonged intensive therapy unit (ITU) stay  past history of peptic ulcer disease  anticoagulation.  They are caused by:  Helicobacter pylori.  They are managed by:

High Altitude Medicine Altitude illness describes a number of conditions which can occur if individuals ascend rapidly to a high altitude (usually > 2500 m but susceptible individuals may experience it at lower altitudes),  Overview Key Facts  Altitude illness (AI) describes a number of conditions which can occur if individuals ascend rapidly to a high altitude (usually > 2500 m but susceptible individuals may experience it at lower altitudes),  High altitude is an elevation > 1500 m.  Altitude illness includes:  acute mountain sickness (AMS).  high altitude cerebral oedema (HACE).  high altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE).  AMS occurs in up to 25% of individuals climbing to altitudes of 2000–3000 m and up to 50% of individuals climbing to altitudes of 3500–4500 m.  AMS is far more common than HACE or HAPE.  Severe altitude illness can be a life-threatening condition and requires urgent treatment.  Risk factors include:  fast rate of ascent  greater altitude reached  history of altitude illness  individuals with a residential altitude < 900 m  pre-existing CVS conditions (eg congenital heart disease, angina).  As altitude increases, air pressure decreases – reduced O2 delivery into and around the body.  Individuals who ascend gradually can usually acclimatise to the reduction in O2 levels.  If the ascent is too fast, the body doesn’t get chance to acclimatise and altitude illness may occur. AMS HACE HAPE  headache  gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms  altered consciousness  ataxia  breathlessness  orthopnoea  wet cough  haemoptysis

DR. JAM  weakness  fatigue  dizziness (6– 10 h postascension).  confusion (~2 h post-ascension).  wheeze  chest tightness (~2 h post ascension).  Individuals climbing altitude may commonly get non-altitude illness headache (eg exhaustion, dehydration or hangover).  It is also important to rule out:  hypoglycaemia  hyponatraemia  hypothermia in patients with symptoms of altitude illness.  All three forms of altitude illness are diagnosed based on clinical findings – severity of illness is related to severity of symptoms.  Travelers who exhibit potential symptoms of altitude illness should not be left unsupervised.  AMS treatment includes:  stopping further ascension and resting  simple analgesia and anti-sickness medication  descending if symptoms do not improve or deteriorate over 1–2 days.  HACE/HAPE require urgent medical treatment – descend as soon as possible for further treatment.  Early descent for altitude illness may be aided by:  supplementary O2  portable hyperbaric chambers  medication including dexamethasone or nifedipine.  The main way of preventing altitude illness is through careful planning – advise avoiding large ascensions in altitude and plan sleeping altitudes accordingly.  Acetazolamide may be taken to help prevent altitude illness in individuals with a moderate-to-high risk.  Severe altitude illness or death is very rare and is avoidable in most cases. Epidemiology  An estimated 9–25 % of unacclimatised individuals who ascend to altitudes of 2000–3000 m develop AMS.  This increases to 35–50 % in individuals ascending to heights of 3500–4500 m.  AMS is much more common than HACE or HAPE.  HACE and HAPE are extremely rare in altitudes < 2800 m and incidence is only ~1–2 % in altitudes of 4000–5000 m. Aetiology  AI occurs when individuals ascend too rapidly and are unable to acclimatise to the changes in O2 levels.  It usually occurs in altitudes > 2500 m but can occur at lower altitudes (especially in individuals who are more susceptible).  The main risk factors can be split into those relating to the trip and those relating to the individual:

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Trip – rate of the ascent, the absolute change in altitude, and the altitude at which a person sleeps.  Individual – previous history of AI, normal residence below 900 m, exertion of arrival at altitude, and preexisting cardiovascular conditions (eg congenital heart disease or angina). Pathophysiology  Altitude illness can be split into:  AMS  HACE  HAPE.  As altitude increases, the barometric (air) pressure decreases.  The fraction of inspired O2 in the air remains the same (FiO2 = 21 %).  As a result, individuals are unable to take in as much O2 at altitude – reduced delivery of O2 around the body and to the tissues.  Individuals who ascend gradually can usually acclimatise to the reduction in O2 levels and do not become sick.  Acclimatisation happens by:  reduced renal bicarbonate excretion to correct respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation occurs due to hypoxia)  kidneys stimulated to produce erythropoietin – relative polycythaemia increases O2 carriage in the blood  increased 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (DPG) production shifts the O2 dissociation curve to the right to allow increased O2 offloading at tissues.  If the individual’s ascent is too rapid, then the body does not get chance to acclimatise, and AI may occur.  AMS and HACE are both neurological manifestations of altitude illness – it islikely that they are on a spectrum of the same disease, with HACE being a more severe form of AMS.  HACE and HAPE are severe but uncommon and usually occur together.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms of AMS don’t usually occur on immediate ascent, they tend to present 6–10 hours after reaching altitude (> 2500 m). AMS  AMS is defined as new-onset headache in an unacclimatised individual who has recently arrived at altitude, and 1 or more of the following:  GI symtoms (anorexia, nausea and vomiting)  dizziness  fatigue  weakness.  These criteria are a guide and generally any new symptoms which occur after ascending to altitude should be considered altitude illness until proven otherwise.

DR. JAM  AMS is usually self-limiting if further ascent is delayed – usually resolves within 1–3 days. HACE  HACE very rarely occurs and is usually only seen when altitudes > 4500 m are reached.  It is characterised by cerebral oedema which can present with:  reduced consciousness or loss of consciousness  new onset of confusion  new onset ataxia.  It is commonly preceded by AMS so it is important to look for these features.  HACE and HAPE usually occur ~2 days after ascent to altitude (> 3000–4000 m). HAPE  HAPE is the respiratory form of altitude illness.  Initially, symptoms include feeling breathless on exertion and a dry cough.  These can progress into:  breathlessness at rest  orthopnoea (breathlessness when lying flat)  wet cough  blood-stained sputum  wheezing  chest tightness.  HAPE may occur in the absence of AMS or HAE.  HACE and HAPE usually occur ~2 days after ascent to altitude (> 3000–4000 m).  Headache at high altitude is very common, although it is used as part of the diagnostic criteria.  Differential Diagnosis  The symptoms of AMS can easily be confused with other conditions, including:  headache – exhaustion, dehydration, hangover, migraine etc  GI symptoms – gastroenteritis, Traveller's diarrhoea, preexisting GI conditions  weakness and/or fatigue – exhaustion, anaemia etc.  It is important to monitor patients displaying any of these symptoms (having recently climbed at altitude), as AMS can develop into a more severe, life-threatening illness.  Other diagnoses to rule out include:  hypoglycaemia  hyponatraemia  hypothermia.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  AMS, HACE and HAPE are all clinical diagnoses – severity is usually subjective based on the intensity of symptoms.  Many high altitude settings are in remote locations with minimal access to healthcare facilities – investigations may be difficult to perform.  Simple examination may help in diagnosis:  Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) in patients who may have developed HACE  percussing and auscultating the chest in suspected HAPE.  Management  Many high altitude settings are in remote locations with minimal access to healthcare facilities – treatment options may be limited.  Travelers displaying any signs or symptoms of altitude illness should not be left alone as their symptoms may progress and become life-threatening. AMS  Travellers who have developed AMS should stop further ascent (may take 1–3 days for sickness to resolve).  It is important that they rest and take simple analgesia (paracetamol or ibuprofen) as required.  Anti-sickness medication may also help symptoms.  If symptoms of AMS do not improve or deteriorate over 1–2 days of rest, then individuals should descend. HACE/HAPE  Travellers exhibiting symptoms of HACE and HAPE require urgent medical attention and should descend as soon as it is safe to do so.  Some experienced travellers may carry medical supplies which can aid descent:  oxygen cylinders  portable hyperbaric chamber (increases barometric pressure to allow greater inhalation of O2)  nifedipine or dexamethasone – both have been proven to help in prophylaxis and treatment of altitude illness. Prevention:  The majority of preventative measures focus on ensuring the ascent is gradual and that patients sleep at an appropriate altitude to what they have gained (eg once over 3000 m, sleep elevation should not increase by > 500 m each day).  Preventative medication may be useful in individuals with moderate-to-high risk of developing altitude illness.  Acetazolamide 125 mg twice-daily (BD) is recommended (should start one day before ascent and continue for two days after reaching highest altitude) – contraindicated in pregnant women.

DR. JAM  Individuals should undergo a trial period of ~2 days on acetazolamide before climbing as there are numerous side effects:  polyuria  paraesthesia  nausea  vomiting  headache.  Other risks are present when climbing altitude and these should also be accounted for:  blisters  dehydration  sun exposure  Traveller's diarrhoea  hypothermia or cold injury.  Prognosis  Severe altitude illness or death as a result of altitude illness is avoidable in the majority of individuals who are climbing altitude. Hyperlipidaemia Hyperlipidaemia describes raised serum levels of plasma cholesterol and/or triglycerides.  Overview Key Facts  Hyperlipidaemia describes raised serum levels of plasma cholesterol and/or triglycerides.  Hyperlipidaemia, especially hypercholestolaemia (total and high-density lipoproteins (HDL) cholesterol), is associated with cardiovascular disease.  HDL is inversely associated with ischaemic heart disease (HDL is cardioprotective).  A total cholesterol : HDL ratio > 4.5 is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease.  A simplistic way to think of low-density lipoproteins (LDL) and HDL is that the HDL are packed densely and, as such, do not occupy as much space as the LDLs which, by their nature of being ‘bigger’, occlude the vessels more easily.  Intervention trials have shown a reduction of LDL cholesterol of 1 mmol can reduce cardiovascular events by up to 21% and mortality rate by 12%.  Causes are divided into primary and secondary:  primary hyperlipidemias can be grouped according to the simple lipid profile, primary hypercholesterolaemia,

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI primary hypertriglyceridaemia, primary mixed hyperlipidaemia  secondary causes need to be excluded, have a variety of causes and should be excluded and/or managed as appropriate.  Management includes:  dietary intervention, which can reduce cholesterol levels by up to 30%  increased physical activity levels  lipid lowering drugs.  β-Hydroxy β-methylglutaryl-Coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase inhibitors, or statins, are the pharmacological lipidlowering drug of choice which have been shown to reduce incidence of cardiovascular events. Epidemiology  Two-thirds of the United Kingdom population have a serum cholesterol level greater than 5.2 mmol/l (1).  Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia has a prevalence of around 1 in 500 (2).  Population studies have consistently demonstrated a strong relationship between both total and LDL cholesterol and coronary heart disease. HDL is protective.  A total cholesterol : HDL ratio 4.5 is associated with an increased risk. Intervention trials has shown a reduction of LDL cholesterol of 1 mmol reduces cardiovascular events by 21% and reduces the mortality rate by 12%.  Triglycerides are also associated with cardiovascular risk; very high triglyceride levels are also associated with pancreatitis, lipaemic serum and eruptive xanthomas.  Untreated primary familial hypercholesterolaemia results in coronary heart disease in 50% of men by the age of 50 and 30% of women by the age of 60. Aetiology  The condition may be classed as primary, which can be grouped according to the simple lipid profile and is usually due to a genetic cause; or secondary due to another underlying cause.  Secondary hyperlipidaemias are usually mixed, but either elevated cholesterol or triglycerides may predominate the clinical picture.  Factors Modifying HDL Levels:  Decreasing:  familial deficiency of HDL  hyperandrogenic state  post-pubertal males  obesity  hypertriglyceridaemia  diabetes mellitus  sedentary states  cigarette smoking.

DR. JAM  Increasing:  familial hyperlipoproteinaemia  low triglyceride levels  thin habitus  exercise  oestrogens  alcohol.  Causes of Secondary Hyperlipidaemia:  Predominantly increased triglycerides:  alcoholism  obesity  chronic kidney disease  diabetes mellitus  liver disease  high-dose oestrogens.  Predominantly increased cholesterol:  hypothyroidism  renal transplant  cigarette smoking (reduces HDL)  nephrotic syndrome  cholestasis. Pathophysiology  Cholesterol and triglycerides are insoluble in plasma and circulate bound to lipoproteins; therefore, they can be deposited within the vessels, leading to atheromatous plaque formation.  Lipoproteins consist of lipids, phospholipids and proteins.  The protein components of lipoproteins are called apolipoproteins (or apoproteins) and they act as cofactors for enzymes and ligands for receptors.  There are four major lipoproteins:  chylomicrons: large particles that carry dietary lipid (mainly triglycerides) from the gastrointestinal tract to the liver. Lipoprotein lipase acts on chylomicrons to release free fatty acids for energy metabolism  very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL): carries endogenous triglyceride (60%), and cholesterol (20%), from the liver to the tissues. The triglyceride core of the VLDL is also hydrolysed by lipoprotein lipase to release free fatty acids.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI The VLDL remnants are called intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL)  LDL: formed from the IDLs by hepatic lipase. LDL contains a cholesterol core (50%) and lesser amounts of triglyceride (10%). LDL metabolism is regulated by cellular cholesterol requirements via negative feedback control of the LDL receptor  HDL: carries cholesterol from the tissues back to the liver. HDL is formed in the liver and gut and acquires free cholesterol from the intracellular pools. HDL is inversely associated with ischaemic heart disease.  The LDL Receptor  Circulating LDL is taken up by the LDL receptor.  Cells replete in cholesterol reduce LDL-receptor expression.  When inhibited, the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase causes a fall in cellular cholesterol and an increase in LDL-receptor expression, thereby controlling the rate of new cholesterol synthesis.  Lipoprotein (a)  Lipoprotein (a) (Lp(a)) is a specialised form of LDL. Lp(a) inhibits fibrinolysis and promotes atherosclerotic plaque formation. It is an independent risk factor for ischaemic heart disease. Lipid metabolism:  Clinical Presentation  Most cases are found incidentally during blood testing, such as when determining cardiovascular risk profiles or if the patient has had other associated cardiovascular symptoms.

Lipid type Target levels Total cholesterol < 5 HDL > 1 LDL < 3 Non-HDL < 4 Triglycerides < 2.3  Management  For patients with hyperlipidaemia:  perform a cardiovascular risk assessment  use clinical findings alongside the measured lipid profile and the patient’s family history to judge the possibility of a familial lipid disorder  arrange specialist review of patients with a total cholesterol of 9 mmol or more/non-HDL cholesterol of 7.5 or more  arrange urgent specialist review if the patient has a triglyceride level of more than 20 mmol/l that is not a result of excess alcohol or poor glycaemic control. Non Pharmacological:  Treatment of hyperlipidaemia can reduce the risk of coronary heart disease by 30%.  In most cases, hypercholesterolaemia will respond to dietary intervention (up to 30% reduction) and statin therapy.  The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends that patients may be given advice regarding diet, exercise and lifestyle modification and have their risk of cardiovascular disease retested.  Mixed or isolated hypertriglyceridaemia may respond to diet and a fibrate. Pharmacological: If lifestyle modification is ineffective or inappropriate, offer statin treatment after cardiovascular risk assessment.  Statins: (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors)  widely used  reduces cardiovascular event widely used to lower cholesterol and have been shown to reduce cardiovascular events  NICE recommends starting with a statin and aim for a reduction in LDL by 50%  offer atorvastatin 20 mg for individuals with a QRISK2 assessment 10% or more, for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease  high-intensity statin therapy is appropriate for patients with FH.  Ezetimibe:

Primary Hypercholesterolaemia (without Hypertriglyceridaemia)  Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH)  a monogenic disorder resulting from LDL-receptor dysfunction  diagnosis is made by Simon Broome criteria - if positive, a specialist referral is required. 1. Tendon xanthomas (plaque deposition within tendons) in a patient or a first-degree relative (parent, sibling, child), or in a second-degree relative (grandparent, uncle, aunt), and elevated cholesterol concentrations as defined below:

DR. JAM Total cholesterol (mmol/L) LDL-C (mmol/L) Child > 6.7 > 4.0 Adult > 7.5 > 4.9 2. DNA-based evidence of an LDL-receptor mutation, familial defective Apo B100, or a PCSK9 mutation.  There are many different mutations in different families, all resulting in LDL-receptor deficiency/dysfunction and producing isolated hypercholesterolaemia.  Heterozygote prevalence is 1/500; homozygous FH is rare.  Other typical clinical features are Achilles tendon xanthomas (can also occur in other extensor tendons) and xanthelasma.  All patients with FH should have lipid-lowering therapy titrated upwards until there has been at least a 50% reduction in LDLcholesterol.  Untreated FH results in coronary heart disease in 50% of men by the age of 50 and 30% of women by the age of 60. Primary Hypertriglyceridaemia (without Hypercholesterolaemia)  Polygenic hypertriglyceridaemia is analogous to polygenic hypercholesterolaemia. Some cases are familial, but the precise defect is not known. There is elevated VLDL confer - even greater cardiovascular risk than LDL.  Lipoprotein lipase deficiency and apoprotein CII deficiency are both rare. They result in elevated triglycerides due to a failure to metabolise chylomicrons when they remain within the circulation for a prolonged period of time.  These patients present in childhood with eruptive xanthomas, lipaemia retinalis, retinal vein thrombosis, pancreatitis and hepatosplenomegaly.  Chylomicrons can be detected in fasting plasma. Primary Mixed (or Combined) Hyperlipidaemia  Familial polygenic combined hyperlipidaemia results in elevated cholesterol and triglycerides.  The prevalence is 1/200.  There is premature atherosclerosis.  Remnant hyperlipidaemia is a rare cause of mixed hyperlipidaemia (palmar xanthomas and tuberous xanthomas over the knees and elbows are characteristic). It is associated with apoprotein E2: there is a high cardiovascular risk. LDL-lowering Apheresis (Plasma Exchange)  LDL apheresis can lower plasma LDL by up to 65% after each treatment.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  This procedure involves the extracorporeal removal of LDL in a process similar to renal dialysis.  The treatment is lifelong and performed weekly to fortnightly.  It can be used to lower LDL-cholesterol in homozygous FH patients who have not responded to drug treatment or have evidence of coronary heart disease.  It can also be used in exceptional cases for patients with heterozygous FH, ie progressive coronary heart disease, despite maximal medical and surgical intervention.  Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors should not be used in patients undergoing LDL apheresis due to the increased risk of anaphylaxis.  Liver Transplantation  Patients who have had maximal medical treatment and LDL apheresis can be considered for liver transplantation.  The new liver provides functionally normal LDL receptors, thereby reducing plasma cholesterol levels. Hypertension Hypertension is a major risk factor for conditions such as stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, chronic kidney disease and premature death.  Overview Key Facts  Hypertension (HTN) is a major risk factor for conditions such as stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, chronic kidney disease and premature death. It is one of the most important preventable causes of morbidity and mortality in the United Kingdom (UK).  HTN is defined as a blood pressure (BP) >140/90 mmHg.  Approximately 30% of the adult population have hypertension in the UK; the prevalence is around 70% in patients in their eighth decade of life.  A 2 mmHg increase in BP increases the risk of mortality from ischaemic disease by 7% and 10% mortality from stroke. It is also a risk factor for heart failure, chronic kidney disease, cognitive decline and premature death.  Blood pressure >180/120 is severe and needs to be referred for assessment.  Ambulatory and home blood pressure monitoring are used to help diagnose HTN.  Treatment includes: angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), calcium channel blockers (CCB), diuretics, thiazides.

DR. JAM  Complications include end organ damage: retinopathy, renal disease. Epidemiology Overall, 30% of the UK adult population have hypertension, with the prevalence increasing with age to 70%. Aetiology  Over 90% of hypertension is classed idiopathic (primary) or essential hypertension. Aetiology of essential hypertension is poorly understood and may be as a result of numerous genetic and environmental factors.  Secondary hypertension:  approximately 5% of all cases are due to renal disease, 3% due to primary hyperaldosteronism and <1% has either an alternative rare endocrine or other causes  endocrine disease:  Conn syndrome  thyroid dysfunction  phaeochromocytoma  acromegaly  Cushing syndrome.  Pre-eclampsia/HTN in pregnancy.  Drugs: antidepressants, combine oral contraceptive pill. Pathophysiology The pathophysiology of essential hypertension is multifactorial. Major risk factors are:  obesity/being overweight  high dietary salt intake  low physical activity  stress  age  family history  ethnicity  sex – male > female. Secondary hypertension:  Renal disease accounts for most cases of secondary hypertension.  The pathogenesis involves stimulation of renin release with activation of the renin angiotensin aldosterone (RAA) system, reduced natriuretic capacity (in advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) and disorganisation of intrarenal vascular structures.  Most forms of renal disease are complicated by hypertension, exceptions are patients with chronic pyelonephritis who have salt wasting (typically normal blood pressure despite advanced CKD).

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Although cases of renal artery stenosis are associated with hypertension, the stenosis will be causative only in the minority of patients.  Coarctation of the aorta: hypertension is seen in the upper limbs only.  Cushing syndrome, phaeochromocytoma, acromegaly and apparent mineralocorticoid excess are all rare causes, the mechanisms of hypertension are related to the pathophysiological processes of the underlying cause.  Clinical Presentation HTN is usually asymptomatic. History and physical examination may highlight an underlying cause for secondary HTN.  Diagnosis/Investigation The National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines suggest that in patients with possible hypertension:  take up to three BP measurements, recording the lowest  it is important not to talk while the BP is being measured as this cause the patients BP to rise  offer ambulatory blood pressure monitoring if BP >140/90. Home blood pressure monitoring is an alternative if ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) is not tolerated  ABPM: average of 14 measurements to diagnose HTN  HBPM: record for 4–7 days. Use an average of the readings  multiple readings are taken because BP fluctuates during the day so much that it is important to be sure that treatment is warranted.  24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring Limited availability and relative expense of ambulatory BP monitoring prevent its use in all hypertensive patients. Specific areas of usefulness include:  assessing for ‘white coat’ hypertension  borderline hypertensive cases who may not need treatment  evaluation of hypotensive symptoms  identifying episodic hypertension (eg in phaeochromocytoma)  assessing drug compliance and effects (particularly in resistant cases)  nocturnal BP dipper status (non-dippers are at higher risk). Investigation of suspected phaeochromocytomas:  three 24-hour urinary catecholamine derivatives of all drugs on a vanilla-free diet (and off all drugs)  urinary metadrenalines may also be measured.

DR. JAM  Classification of hypertension Stage 1 HTN:  Clinic BP 140/90 or above AND  Subsequent ambulatory blood pressure monitoring / Home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) BP 135/85 or above. Stage 2 HTN:  Clinic BP 160/100 or above AND  ABPM/HBPM 150/95 or above. Severe HTN:  Clinic BP >180 systolic/100 diastolic or higher. Further tests that are indicated in patients with confirmed hypertension:  assess cardiovascular risk and consider modifying other risk factors eg cholesterol  urine: albumin creatinine ratio, look for haematuria  fundoscopy  biochemistry: glucose, electrolytes, eGFR, lipid profile  electrocardiogram.  Hypertensive retinal changes/hypertensive retinopathy Chronic hypertension causes:  arteriosclerotic changes, eg copper and silver wiring, due to hyalinisation of vessel walls  arteriovenous (AV) nicking, due to circulation changes resulting in venous dilatation around AV crossing. Changes related to more current blood pressure changes include:  focal or generalised arteriole narrowing, due to muscle spasm in vessel wall  cotton-wool spots are due to precapillary occlusion causing retinal ischaemia  haemorrhages, which can be deep and blotchy or superficial and flame-shaped  hard exudates cause reduced acuity  disc oedema occurs in malignant or accelerated phase hypertension due to vasoconstriction and choroidal ischaemia. May be associated with transient visual obscurations. Keith, Wagener and Barker Classification of Hypertensive Retinopathy:  Grade 1 – arteriolar attenuation.

Hypertension In Pregnancy Hypertension in pregnancy is high blood pressure that develops during pregnancy, which can lead to complications like preeclampsia and affect both maternal and fetal health.  Overview Key Facts Hypertension (HTN) in pregnancy includes gestational hypertension and pre-existing (essential) hypertension:  Gestational HTN:  develops after 20 weeks and may be transient or chronic  pre-eclampsia is pregnancy-induced HTN plus proteinuria and/or oedema:  it is considered to be a disease of the placental tissue  hence delivery of the placenta should resolve the disease; however, it can develop postnatally as well as following delivery.  eclampsia is the occurrence of one or more convulsions superimposed on pre-eclampsia.  Pre-existing HTN is hypertension that has been detected prior to pregnancy or at booking (before 20 weeks):  SBP > 140  DBP > 90  Patients can however develop superimposed preeclampsia in addition to pre-existing chronic HTN. Epidemiology • Around 5% of women are affected in their first pregnancy. • Rates are higher in those with type II diabetes. • Pre-eclampsia is the underlying cause of 12-25% of small gestational age (SGA) births and intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR).

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI • Worldwide, pre-eclampsia and its similar conditions are the number one cause of maternal mortality. Aetiology  Moderate risk factors for pre-eclampsia:  1st pregnancy  age > 40  BMI > 30  family history of pre-eclampsia  pregnancy interval of > 10 years  multiple pregnancies.  High risk factors:  chronic pre-existing HTN  HTN or pre-eclampsia/ eclampsia in a previous pregnancy  renal disease  autoimmune disease  diabetes. Pathophysiology  The mechanism of pregnancy induced hypertension and preeclampsia remains unclear, however current theories suggest that it may be as a result of poor placental perfusion, which occurs due to abnormal placentation.  Poor placentation, and in particular a lack of spiral artery remodelling, leads to higher systemic blood pressures being required to adequately perfuse the placenta.  Instead of a high flow and low resistance placental circulation, the lack of spiral artery remodelling leads to high resistance and low flow.  Normal placentation:  trophoblast invades the myometrium and spiral arteries (uterus) which destroys the tunica muscularis media  spiral arteries are therefore left dilated and unable to constrict, hence there is high flow and low resistance to the circulation.  Pre-eclampsia (abnormal placentation):  incomplete spiral artery remodelling causes high resistance, and low flow circulation is seen between the uterus and placenta  this is because the walls of the spiral arteries are still muscular and so constrict  blood pressure rises as a result  hypoxia occurs leading to oxidative stress due to under perfusion  a systemic inflammatory response occurs leading to endothelial dysfunction (blood vessels leak). Eclampsia:  Seizures in pregnancy or within ten days of delivery with at least two of these features:  proteinuria + one of either  thrombocytopenia or  raised AST /ALT.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Check for proteinuria – urine dipstick, then 24-hour urine analysis to quantify.  Monitor for organ dysfunction using blood tests:  full blood count (FBC) – low platelets and low haemoglobin (Hb)  urea and electrolytes (U+E) – raised urea, creatinine, and urate  liver function tests (LFTs) – raised alanine transaminase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST).  Ultrasound (USS) examination is used to assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume – with umbilical artery doppler velocimetry – at 28-30 weeks and 32-34 weeks.  Blood tests for pre-eclampsia:  low pregnancy associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A).  Liquor volume – evidence of fetal kidney function.  Integrated testing – a combination of independent risk factors, history, PAPP-A, uterine artery doppler at 12 weeks is most effective early predictive test.  Management  Management aims to:  prevent progression to eclampsia  minimise chance of maternal or fetal complications occurring. Non-pharmacological:  Stop teratogenic or contraindicated drugs (eg ACE inhibitors) in patients with existing hypertension.

Infective Endocarditis Infective endocarditis is an infection of the endocardial surface of the heart.  Overview Key Facts  Infective endocarditis (IE) is an infection of the endocardial surface of the heart.  IE is most commonly caused by bacterial infection affecting damaged or prosthetic heart valves.  IE can lead to valve insufficiency, heart failure, pericarditis and myocardial infarction.  Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci are noted to be the most common causes.  The most common location is the mitral valve.  Symptoms can be non-specific including malaise and tiredness. Fever and a new murmur should be investigated for IE.  Diagnosis is made using an echocardiogram.  Length of treatment is usually 4–6 weeks of antibiotics.  Empirical treatment for native valve endocarditis, unless staphylococcal infection is suspected, is intravenous amoxicillin (2 g every four hours) with gentamicin (1 mg/kg twice daily).  For prosthetic valve endocarditis, vancomycin and gentamicin plus rifampicin (300–600 mg every 12 hours) are currently recommended.  The condition is usually fatal if not diagnosed and managed rapidly.  The mortality rate is 30% with IE caused by staphylococci and 6% by sensitive streptococci.

DR. JAM Epidemiology Incidence is 1.7–6.2 cases per 100 000 patient-years. Aetiology  IE is most commonly caused by bacterial infection affecting damaged or prosthetic heart valves.  Organisms may originate from dental disease, intravenous lines, surgical intervention and intravenous drug use.  Almost any pathogenic organism may be implicated, particularly in immunocompromised patients.  Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause off endocarditis overall (both acute and sub-acute).  Other common causes include Streptococci (particularly, viridans-type streptococci, the most common cause of subacute endocarditis) , followed by coagulase negative Streptococci such as S.epidermidis and S.lugdenesis  Streptococcal endocarditis presents more indolently than staphylococcal endocarditis.  Right-sided staphylococcal endocarditis often occurs in intravenous drug users.  Endocarditis is less commonly caused by the HACEK group of organisms (around 5% of all cases):  Haemophilus aphrophilus and H. paraphrophilus  Actinobacillus hominis  Cardiobacterium hominis  Eikenella corrodens  Kingella kingae and K. denitricans.  Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections requires surgical intervention  Enterococci are less commonly implicated.  The following organisms are associated with culture negative endocarditis  Brucella  Bartonella  Coxiella burnetti (Q fever)  Chlamydia  Legionella  Mycoplasma  Whipples disease (Trophyerma whipplei  Fungal organisms can also cause an infective endocarditis (subacute).  Marantic (metastatic-related) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)-related (Libman–Sacks) endocarditis are causes of non-infective endocarditis. The following conditions are associated with an increased risk of endocarditis:  acquired valvular heart disease with stenosis or regurgitation

It is the identification of these vegetations that allows you to make the diagnosis.  An echocardiogram should be routinely performed in patients with S. aureus bacteraemia or candidaemia, in view of the higher likelihood of endocarditis.  In those with chronic or subacute presentations, three sets of blood cultures should be taken, with at least six hours between them, to confirm continuous bacteraemia.  Obtaining blood cultures while the patient is pyrexial increases the chance of capturing the causative organisms.  A transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE) is indicated if there is a prosthetic valve, or if the TTE is of poor quality, positive or negative in the context of continuing clinical suspicion.  If blood cultures are negative, serology for Coxiella and Bartonella spp. should be done, followed by serology for Chlamydia, Legionella and Mycoplasma spp. if these are negative, and Brucella sp. if there is a history of potential exposure. Long QT Syndrome Long QT syndrome is characterised by a prolonged QT interval on the ECG and it increases the risk of sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachyarrhythmias.  Overview Key Facts  Long QT syndrome is characterised by a prolonged QT interval on the ECG and it increases the risk of sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachyarrhythmias.  Prolonged QTc is defined as QTc > 440 ms in men and > 460 ms in women, but as a generic guide > 450 ms:  a QTc > 500 predisposes patients to develop torsades de pointes.  Long QT syndrome can be congenital (eg Romano–Ward syndrome) or acquired (secondary to drugs or electrolyte imbalances).  Many patients with long QT syndrome will be asymptomatic; it may be detected as an incidental finding on electrocardiogram (ECG).  Usually managed by correcting the cause, avoiding predisposing medications and prevention of arrhythmias by medication or pacemaker/implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD).

DR. JAM  The Schwartz score is used for the diagnosis of long QT syndrome. This takes into consideration clinical and ECG features to determine the likelihood of a patient having an inherited long QT syndrome.  Treatment involves avoiding activities that may trigger an arrhythmia (eg stress), use of beta-blockers or ICD insertion for patients at high risk of cardiac arrest.  Prognosis is usually good if treated and prevented. If left untreated, there is a 50% chance of death within 15 years. Epidemiology  Long QT syndrome affects 1:2000 to 1:5000 people, more commonly affecting women. Aetiology Congenital causes (account for 90–95% of cases)  Romano–Ward syndrome (autosomal dominant):  LQT1 – most common subtype of Romano–Ward syndrome:  usually triggered by swimming.  LQT2 – 2nd most common subtype of Romano–Ward syndrome:  usually triggered by stress/emotional event or auditory stimulus.  LQT3:  patients often suffer cardiac events while sleeping at night.  Jervell and Lange–Nielson syndrome (autosomal recessive):  associated with sensorineural deafness in both ears.  Anderson–Tawil syndrome:  presentation triad:  prolonged QT interval  periodic paralysis  characteristic facial and skeletal abnormalities.  Timothy syndrome:  features:  prolonged QT  syndactyly  structural heart abnormalities  features of autism spectrum disorder. Acquired causes – drugs  Antiarrhythmic drugs:  amiodarone  sotalol  procainamide.  Antipsychotics:  haloperidol.  Antidepressants:

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  citalopram.  Antibiotics:  erythromycin  trimethoprim.  Antihistamines:  terfenadine.  Antifungals:  ketoconazole  fluconazole. Acquired causes – electrolyte abnormalities  Hypokalaemia.  Hypomagnesaemia.  Hypocalcaemia. Pathophysiology  The QT interval represents depolarisation and repolarisation of the ventricles.  Prolonged QT means it takes a longer time for repolarisation and a longer action potential, which in turn can lead to arrhythmias:  eg torsades the pointes – after depolarisations occur before the cells have fully repolarised because of the prolonged time thus leading to arrhythmias.  Clinical Presentation  Many patients with long QT syndrome will be asymptomatic. It may be detected as an incidental finding on ECG.  Cardiac syncope may be associated with palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath and cyanosis.  Differential Diagnosis  Differntial diagnoses include:  Brugada syndrome  vasovagal syncope  seizures  torsades de pointes  hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Long QT syndrome is commonly unknown until a cardiac event has happened (syncope or cardiac arrest) or a seizure. Otherwise, it is diagnosed by measuring the QT interval length on a 12-lead ECG.  QT interval is measured from the beginning of QRS complex to end of T wave.  QTc is the QT interval divided by the square root of the RR interval.

JAM Marfan Syndrome Autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissue.  Overview Key Facts  Autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissue.  Characterised by musculoskeletal deformity resulting from loss of elastic tissue in addition to lens subluxation, root aneurysms and aortic dissection.  Surgical intervention may be required for aortic dilatation to prevent dissection.  Other manifestations, eg lens subluxation, require treatment from other members of a multidisciplinary team (MDT). Epidemiology  Estimated prevalence of 3 in 10 000 in the European population.  Life expectancy is prolonged by early surgery and is now similar to that of the general population. Aetiology  Caused by mutations in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene:  75% of mutations are autosomal dominant and inherited  25% of cases occur due to spontaneous mutations and are associated with older paternal age. Pathophysiology  Mutation in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene results in the production of abnormal fibrillin protein.  This causes mechanical instability and loss of elasticity of connective tissues.  Medial degeneration of the aortic wall, loss of smooth muscle cells and cystic medial necrosis all contribute to aortic dilatation and therefore an increased risk of dissection, aneurysm and rupture.  Abnormalities in the fibrillin-1 protein also cause a loss in the structural integrity of the skin, lenses of the eye and lungs.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentation:  family history – Marfan syndrome, aortic dissection/aneurysm  tall stature and/or long limbs  wide arm span to height ratio  high level of the pubic bone  high arched palate

Mitral Regurgitation Mitral regurgitation is a heart condition characterised by the leaking of blood backwards through the mitral valve with each heartbeat, which can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, shortness of breath, and heart palpitations and may require treatment depending on the severity.  Overview Key Facts  Valvular disease encompasses those pathologies which selectively affect the valves of the heart.

DR. JAM  These diseases result in different patterns of sounds called murmurs which can be used to help diagnose a patient on clinical examination.  The murmur is caused by turbulent blood flow within the heart.  Disease is often classified according to the valve affected and its particular affliction, eg stenosis or regurgitation.  The four main valvular disorders are stenosis and regurgitation of the left-sided heart valves (aortic and mitral valve).  Mitral regurgitation describes the inability of the mitral valves to meet and close as per normal, leading to leakage of blood back into the left atrium during ventricular contraction.  The murmur of mitral regurgitation is a pansystolic murmur that is heard loudest at the apex and radiates to the axilla.  The apex may be displaced laterally and may be described as thrusting in cases of severe regurgitation.  Potential causes of mitral regurgitation include causes such as:  degenerative causes, eg age-related mitral regurgitation (most common cause)  regurgitation secondary to underlying mitral valve prolapse  connective tissue disorders, such as Ehlers–Danlos syndrome.  Papillary muscle rupture, which could occur in the setting of a myocardial infarction, or infection in the setting of rheumatic fever or infective endocarditis, can also cause mitral regurgitation.  Presentation may be:  acute – with rapid progression of pulmonary oedema, which requires urgent surgical intervention  chronic – often initially asymptomatic but over the years will lead to heart failure and progressive dyspnoea.  Management is dependent on the acuteness of presentation, patient symptoms, signs of pulmonary hypertension, severity of regurgitation and left ventricular function.  Initial medical options for acute mitral regurgitation include:  nitrates  diuretics  sodium nitroprusside  positive inotropic agents  intra-aortic balloon pump.  Urgent surgical intervention with valve repair or replacement is the definitive treatment of choice for acute regurgitation.  Elective surgery is recommended for patients who are:  symptomatic  have features of pulmonary hypertension or fluid overload  asymptomatic but have a declining ejection fraction.  Valve replacement may be with a metallic or tissue valve.  Acute mitral regurgitation has a poor prognosis without treatment.  With chronic regurgitation, the best prognosis is in those who have asymptomatic disease with early surgical intervention.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Epidemiology  Mitral regurgitation is present in 2% of the whole population.  Very mild mitral regurgitation can be present in healthy individuals.  Moderate-to-severe regurgitation of the mitral valve is the second most common form of valvular disease following aortic stenosis.  It is the second most common valvular condition that requires surgery following aortic valve disease.  The condition is independently associated with:  women  low body mass index  increasing age  history of ischaemic heart disease (particularly myocardial infarction)  renal dysfunction  mitral stenosis  prior mitral valve prolapse. Aetiology  Causes of mitral regurgitation include:  myxomatous degeneration (most common and related to age)  functional, secondary to ventricular dilatation  mitral valve prolapse  ischaemic papillary muscle rupture  congenital heart diseases  collagen disorders  rheumatic heart disease  endocarditis. Pathophysiology  Mitral regurgitation describes retrograde flow from the left ventricle back into the left atrium, due to failure of closure of the mitral valves.  The increased blood volume in the left atrium causes an increased preload into the left ventricle during diastole.  This causes left ventricular volume overload.  In chronic cases, compensatory ventricular remodelling occurs, allowing maintenance of cardiac output and even an initial increase in ejection fraction in some cases.  Over time, volume overload causes ventricular dilatation, widening of the mitral annulus and diminished closing of leaflets, leading to further worsening of regurgitation.  Volume overload will eventually be so great that there will be dilatation and decreased contractility.

Mitral Stenosis Mitral stenosis is a heart condition characterised by the narrowing of the mitral valve, which can restrict blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle, leading to symptoms such as fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain, and palpitations and may require treatment depending on the severity.  Overview Key Facts  Valvular disease encompasses those pathologies which selectively affect the valves of the heart.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  These diseases result in different patterns of sounds called murmurs, which can be used to help diagnose a patient on clinical examination.  The murmur is caused by turbulent blood flow within the heart.  The disease is often classified according to the valve affected and its particular affliction, eg stenosis or regurgitation.  The four main valvular disorders are stenosis and regurgitation of the left-sided heart valves (aortic and mitral valves).  Mitral stenosis is the thickening of the mitral leaflets that may occur at the cusps, commissures or chordal level, to cause an obstruction of blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle.  Two-thirds of patients with the condition are women.  Thickening of the valves leads to reduced flexibility and an inability to open fully to allow blood to pass through.  Mitral stenosis may be caused by numerous conditions; however, most cases are due to rheumatic heart disease.  In rheumatic heart disease, antibodies form against streptococci and these also bind to the heart valve surface leading to stenosis.  Symptoms may include:  dyspnoea which is progressive and may occur with minimal activity  haemoptysis  dysphagia (due to left atrial enlargement)  palpitations (atrial fibrillation is invariable and increases thromboembolic stroke risk 17-fold).  On auscultation of the heart there will be a mid-late diastolic murmur:  best heard with the patient in the left lateral position  with the bell of the stethoscope.  Other signs of mitral stenosis may include:  malar flush  low pulse pressure  loud first heart sound  a long diastolic murmur with apical thrill (rare)  S1 will be loud in early disease but soft in severe mitral stenosis  (Due to valve leaflets becoming significantly more calcified)  very early opening snap (closer to S2); this may be lost if the valves are immobile  right ventricular heave or loud P2  pulmonary regurgitation (Graham Steell murmur)  tricuspid regurgitation.  Mitral stenosis is diagnosed when the valve area is < 2 cm2. It is considered severe when < 1 cm2.  Increased pulmonary pressures lead to pulmonary oedema, when heart rates increase and pulmonary hypertension.

JAM  Medical management of symptoms may include diuretics or long-acting nitrates to help dyspnoea.  Beta-blockers may help increase exercise tolerance.  Rate control may also be beneficial.  Anticoagulants are indicated in patients with atrial fibrillation.  Operative intervention is, however, the definitive treatment; options include:  percutaneous intervention with balloon valvuloplasty  surgical intervention such as open valve replacement or limited mitral valvotomy (now rarely performed in developed countries).  Prognosis  Prognosis is dependent on symptomatology at presentation:  in asymptomatic patients, the survival rate at 10 years is high  in cases with advanced symptomatology 10-year survival is poor, and if pulmonary stenosis is present and severe, the survival average is 3 years.  Complications that lead to mortality include thromboembolic events, infection, pulmonary stenosis and progressive cardiac failure.  Prognosis is greatly improved with operative intervention. Myotonic Dystrophy Myotonic dystrophy is the second most common type of muscular dystrophy.  Overview Key Facts  Myotonic dystrophy is the second most common type of muscular dystrophy.  Myotonic dystrophy is normally inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and there are two main types:  type I (DM1, a mutation in DMPK gene)  type II (DM2, a mutation in CNBP gene).  Myotonic dystrophy tends to present in the mid-20–30s with progressive muscle weakness and may present with other symptoms such as cataracts, heart block and intellectual disability.  The diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and genetic testing.  There is no cure for myotonic dystrophy, with only supportive treatment available.  Screening for complications should be performed.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Epidemiology  About 70 000 people have a muscular dystrophy in the UK.  The second most common type of muscular dystrophy is myotonic muscular dystrophy:  1 in 8000 people. Aetiology  Autosomal-dominant genetic inheritance:  50% chance of being passed onto the next generation. Pathophysiology  Type I:  mutation in the DMPK gene:  the long arm of chromosome 19  DMPK is part of cell communication.  trinucleotide repeat expansions of the cytosine-thymineguanine (CTG) triplet:  5–37 repeats = normal  > 50 repeats = symptomatic.  altered messenger RNA affects normal protein production  anticipation:  symptoms come on earlier and more severe as it is passed onto the next generation.  congenital myotonic dystrophy type I:  inherited from the mother.  Type II:  mutation in the CNBP gene:  chromosome 3  regulates protein production and activities of other genes.  tetranucleotide repeat expansions of cytosine-cytosinethymine-guanosine (CCTG):  the number of repeats is not correlated with the severity of the disease or the age of onset.  Type I and type II are the main types but there are also other types of myotonic dystrophy.  Clinical Presentation  Patients commonly present with the following signs and symptoms in their second to third decade of life but can also present at any other time.  The main presentation is progressive muscle weakness, tightness and wasting.  The severity is variable.  Type I:  affects the jaw, neck, shoulders, elbows and hips:

JAM  myotonia  weakness.  insulin resistance – type II diabetes  cataracts  cardiac problems  in men:  early balding  infertility.  may be congenital and present at birth.  Type II:  milder than type I  overlapping symptoms.  Differential Diagnosis  Duchenne muscular dystrophy.  Spinal muscle atrophy.  Peripheral neuropathy.  Myositis (polymyositis, dermatomyositis).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Myotonic dystrophy can be investigated in a few ways.  History and physical examination:  most important to identify any family history and their current presentation.  Genetic testing to detect DMPK or CNBP genes:  definitive test  chorionic villus sampling  amniocentesis.  Blood test:  creatine phosphokinase.  Imaging:  electromyography.  Management Non-pharmacological  The main treatment is supportive.  Support groups.  Mobility:  physiotherapy:  muscle strengthening  flexibility.  physical aids:  wheelchair

Pharmacological  There is no medication available to reverse muscular weakness.  Pharmacological management aims to prevent and treat complications.  Analgesia.  Cardiac medication:  ACE inhibitors  beta-blockers.  Testosterone replacement therapy (if required). Surgical  Surgical treatment is indicated for associated problems:  cataract  pacemaker for cardiac problems.  Prognosis  The prognosis depends on the specific type of myotonic dystrophy.  It may shorten life expectancy if it involves cardiac and respiratory function.  Type II myotonic dystrophy is milder and people tend to have a normal lifespan. Orthostatic Hypotension Orthostatic hypotension (postural hypotension) is defined as a fall in blood pressure within three minutes of standing.

DR. JAM  Overview Key Facts  Orthostatic hypotension (postural hypotension) is defined as a fall in blood pressure within three minutes of standing.  The incidence of orthostatic hypotension increases with age.  Clinical presentation is varied. Many patients will be asymptomatic. Common symptoms of cerebral hypoperfusion include dizziness, light-headedness and tunnel vision.  Some patients may present with syncope.  Management involves assessing and addressing the underlying cause (eg antihypertensives and diuretics). Otherwise, options may include medications such as oral fludrocortisone.  Patient education is vital to inform patients of triggers, how to recognise symptoms and steps to take to prevent syncope and falls.  Possible complications include blackouts, musculoskeletal/head injury and psychosocial consequences, including fear of falling. Epidemiology  Approximately a third of patients in the Emergency Department with syncope are diagnosed as having a ‘situational, orthostatic or vasovagal’ cause.  Prevalence – it exists in approximately 5% of those < 50 years to approximately 30% of those > 70 years old.  It can occur in more than half of those with Parkinson’s. Aetiology Causes of orthostatic hypotension Causes of orthostatic hypotension Drugs  GTN  Antihypertensives  Alpha-blockers (eg tamsulosin)  Tricyclic antidepressants  Diuretics  Levodopa/dopaminergics  Alcohol (most common polypharmacy cause of orthostatic hypotension in older patients is antidepressant + antihypertensive co-prescription) Conditions Cardiac  Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTs)  Arrhythmias, eg AF  Valvular, eg aortic stenosis  Cardiomyopathy (especially dilated)  Myocardial infarction (MI)  Pericarditis  Heart failure Neurological  Vasovagal syncope  Parkinson’s disease  Sympathectomy

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Spinal cord lesions  Guillain–Barré syndrome Endocrine  Diabetes  ↓ Aldosterone  ‘Dumping syndrome’ following gastrectomy States  Hyponatraemia  Dehydration  Blood loss  Loss of tolerance, ie following prolonged bed rest Other  Anaemia (especially pernicious)  Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)  Pregnancy  General factors for increased risk of orthostatic hypotension – older age, polypharmacy, multiple comorbidities and frailty. Pathophysiology  Blood pressure (BP) control when standing is normally due to an autonomic stress response (eg baroreceptor activation and ↓parasympathetic activity) combined with the typical mediators of blood pressure (ie ↑peripheral vascular resistance, ↑cardiac contractility, ↑heart rate, intravascular volume). Problems with any of these aspects can cause a postural drop in BP.  Neurological causes can reduce autonomic function.  Causes that instigate hypovolaemia (eg dehydration, diuretics, vasodilators) are a common risk factor for orthostatic hypotension.  There is also a normal reduction in baroreceptor reflex activity with increasing age; this especially occurs in those with hypertension, due to tolerance from prolonged higher pressures.  Straining during faecal excretion/urinating (micturition syncope) can lead to postural hypotension due to vagal nerve stimulation directly activating parasympathetic responses.  The symptoms of dizziness or blackouts occur due to cerebral hypoperfusion resulting from hypotension.  Clinical Presentation  Many with orthostatic hypotension are asymptomatic.  Symptoms can include (often worse in the morning):  blackouts  falls  light-headedness  headache  dizziness  weakness  tunnel vision  palpitations

DR. JAM  clinical history and examination important in eliminating suspicions of a serious cause, eg MI, pericarditis, Parkinson’s.  Differential Diagnosis  Orthostatic hypotension is a clinical finding.  Other causes of syncope and similar presentations include hypoglycaemia, epilepsy and anxiety/somatisation.  Key clinical examinations – cardiovascular and neurological.  Diagnosis/Investigation Definition Fall in systolic BP ≥ 20 mmHg (or ≥ 30 mmHg in hypertensives) and/or diastolic BP ≥10 mmHg (within three minutes of standing)  Diagnosis of simple orthostatic hypotension made by the presence of the above and the ruling-out of other causes. Investigation  For diagnosis:  lying or sitting to standing BP measurement:  if unable to confirm with this, but history convincing, further referral needed.  if asymptomatic – further investigation may not be needed.  For aetiology/differential assessment:  general observations:  if neurological cause – reactive tachycardia is often small, eg < 15 bpm increase.  ECG  24-hour BP monitoring  EMG/nerve conduction studies  tilt table testing  Valsalva manoeuvre  carotid sinus massage  ear examination.  Management  If an emergency presentation of potential syncope, first manage this, ie ABCDE approach, stabilisation and injury assessment. Otherwise  Establishing the aetiology and addressing it is of primary importance.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Managing the symptoms, improving life quality and preventing injury are more important than ‘treating’ blood pressure figures alone.  If asymptomatic – management/investigation may not be needed. Non-pharmacological  Patient information, including avoiding symptom triggers, eg sitting before standing from lying down, eating smaller meals regularly, increasing salt intake (unless hypertensive), avoiding strong caffeinated drinks, ensuring adequate hydration (ie ≥ 2 litres per day), tilting head at night when sleeping, compression stockings.  Possible referral to falls clinic to assess and address compounding risk factors in older patients.  Ensure safety – especially in older patients or those who live alone.  Driving safety – may need to stop driving until aetiology found and managed.  May need work adjustments. Pharmacological  Medication review is needed to reduce polypharmacy and stop/change precipitating medications.  Constipation management important, eg to reduce ‘straining’ and sitting periods.  Medication following second-degree care referral if the above measures are not enough.  Commonly first line: Fludrocortisone (used ‘off-label’, ensure enough sodium intake) ± Midodrine (more effective in neurological causes)  Others:  dihydroxyphenylserine (aka DOPS – converted in body noradrenaline)  octreotide (dosing before meals – for reducing postprandial hypotension).  Prognosis  Possible complications – blackouts, musculoskeletal/head injury, psychosocial consequences of this, including fear of falling.  Outcome following assessment and treatment tends to be good, unless due to a chronic condition (eg Parkinson’s, diabetes).  A significant number of patients sadly will not have the exact cause detected.

DR. JAM Pacemakers Pacemakers are used to return the heart to a normal sinus rhythm, whereas defibrillators are used to identify life-threatening ventricular tachycardias and terminate them before causing haemodynamic compromise.  Overview Key Facts  There are two main types of implantable cardiac devices:  pacemakers  defibrillators.  Both work by providing electrical current to the heart in order to mimic normal cardiac function.  Pacemakers are used to return the heart to a normal sinus rhythm, whereas defibrillators are used to identify lifethreatening ventricular tachycardias and terminate them before causing haemodynamic compromise.  Radio frequency ablation can also be used to terminate electrical foci which lead to abnormal electrical signalling within the myocardium, leading to abnormal rhythms.  Indications include:  supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)  atrial fibrillation (AF)  atrial flutter.
