Pathophysiology  Temporary Pacing  Pacing electrodes placed in the right ventricular apex cause activation from the right ventricle.  Temporary pacing for emergencies such as heart block is typically ventricular only.  Post-cardiac surgery, this employs epicardial pacing wires placed peri-operatively and may be atrial or ventricular (appendage and apex respectively) to optimise cardiac output.  Permanent Pacing  Permanent pacing can be ventricular only or atrioventricular to preserve atrioventricular (AV) synchrony.  Naming conventions are based on chamber paced, chamber sensed and pacemaker response to sensing, eg VVI means ventricular pacing, sensing and inhibition.  Dual chamber pacemaker (DDD) is increasingly used with dual pacing capabilities which can allow sophisticated pacing behaviour.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Most are also rate-responsive now (denoted ‘R’) – they use movement or physiological triggers (eg respiratory rate or QT interval) to increase heart rates.  Therefore, they reduce the occurrence of pacemaker syndrome and act more physiologically for patients.  Heart Failure  There are several synonymous terms for pacing in patients with cardiac failure including:  cardiac resynchronisation therapy  biventricular pacing  multisite pacing.  The atria and right ventricle are paced normally and additionally a pacing electrode is placed in a tributary of the coronary sinus on the lateral aspect of the left ventricle.  The two ventricles are paced simultaneously or near simultaneously with a short AV delay.  The aim is to optimise AV delay and reduce inter- and intraventricular asynchrony.  This therapy is known to reduce mortality, to improve exercise capacity, to improve quality of life and to reduce hospital admissions.  Implantable Cardiac Defibrillators  These devices detect life-threatening tachyarrhythmias and terminate them by overdrive pacing or counter-shock.  Implanted in a similar manner to permanent pacemakers.  Current evidence supports use in secondary prevention of cardiac arrest and specific primary prevention (eg individuals with LV impairment those with familial syndromes such as arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia, Brugada syndrome and long QT variants).  Diagnosis/Investigation  In temporary pacing, left bundle branch block (LBBB) morphology may be seen on electrocardiogram (ECG) due to the nature of electrode placement.  If pacing leads to septal perforation, right bundle branch block (RBBB) morphology may be present.  In heart failure, pacing is indicated when all of the following are present:  New York Heart Association (NYHA) Classification 3/4  QRS > 130 ms  left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) < 35% with dilated ventricle

DR. JAM  patient on optimal medical therapy (diuretics, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition (ACEI) and beta-blockers).  Management Surgical  Radio frequency ablation is a resistive, heart-mediated protein membrane disruption causing cell lysis and thus interrupting electrical pathways in cardiac structures.  Excellent results are obtained in the treatment of accessory pathways (which when activated can cause additional ectopic beats or even inco-ordinate atrioventricular function), atrial flutter and with complete AV nodal ablation or modification.  Ventricular tachycardia is technically more difficult to treat as the myocardium is much thicker than atrial.  Isolation of pulmonary veins by ablation therapy is now an established technique to treat AF.  Current cure rates around 85% but more than one procedure is required in half the cases.  Complete heart block and pericardial effusions are rare complications of radio frequency ablation.  Prognosis  Symptoms related to impairment of cardiac output or change in peripheral resistance caused by suboptimal pacemaker settings.  It can be caused by subtle differences in AV synchrony which causes loss of the atrial ‘kick’ – a major contributor to cardiac output.  Patients may become dizzy, hypotensive or develop signs of heart failure, they may also report fatigue which may be marked given the change from their previous functional status.  Optimisation is now a routine clinical activity to ensure this does not occur.  Other Indications for Referral to Electrophysiologist Condition When to Refer Potential Treatment SVT More than one episode Radio frequency ablation Atrial flutter More than one episode Radio frequency ablation Atrial fibrillation Highly symptomatic, refractory to or intolerant of drug therapy Radio frequency ablation Ventricular fibrillation Unless there is an obvious reversible cause, eg STImplantable cardioverterdefibrillator (ICD)

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI segment elevation MI (STEMI) Ventricular tachycardia Unless obvious reversible cause Radiofrequency ablation or ICD Ischaemic cardiomyopathy Ejection fraction > 30% on optimal medical therapy Primary prevention ICD NYHA Classic III–IV heart failure, QRS > 130 ms, ejection fraction < 35% On optimal medical therapy Heart failure pacing Pericardial Effusion Pericardial effusion is the abnormal accumulation of fluid around the heart, which can lead to symptoms like chest pain and shortness of breath.  Overview Key Facts  The pericardium consists of a serous layer and a fibrous layer between which is pericardial fluid.  This encloses the pericardial cavity consisting of the heart and great vessel roots.  The serous layer acts as a lubricant to allow the heart to move freely within the pericardium.  Normally, there is approximately 50 ml of fluid in between the two layers of the pericardium which helps to protect the heart and allow it to beat freely within the mediastinum.  This level of fluid may increase due to numerous pathological underlying causes, including infection, malignancy and trauma.  Pericardial fluid can slowly increase by up to 2 litres, which can be accommodated by pericardial stretching and thus without raising intrapericardial pressure.  This is known as pericardial effusion.  The fluid may be a transudate, exudate or blood.  Classic symptoms include chest pain, dysphagia, hoarseness or dyspnoea (these may be absent in slow build-up of effusion).  A large effusion can lead to mufﬂed heart sounds, loss of apical impulse, occasional pericardial rub, small ECG complexes and eventually electromechanical dissociation.  However, if a small volume of fluid (eg 200 ml) develops acutely, it can significantly limit ventricular filling, reduce cardiac output and elevate intracardiac pressures:  this is cardiac tamponade, a medical emergency that requires urgent intervention.

DR. JAM  The best diagnostic test is an echocardiogram to confirm and quantify the effusion; other tests will be required to diagnose the underlying cause.  Treatment depends on the size and acuteness of onset of the effusion and underlying cause. Epidemiology  Epidemiology of pericardial effusion is directly related to the epidemiology of the underlying causes. Aetiology  Aetiology:  infection, eg coxsackievirus, tuberculosis  mediastinal radiotherapy  pericardial malignancy  drugs, eg hydralazine  post-viral or bacterial pericarditis  following severe uraemic pericarditis  trauma and/or post-cardiac surgery  connective tissue disease  recurrent pericarditis  aortic dissection  iatrogenic (ablation/pacemaker)  ventricular rupture  anticoagulation. Pathophysiology  A slowly developing pericardial effusion of up to 2 litres can be accommodated by pericardial stretching, without raising the intrapericardial pressure.  In contrast, if a small amount of intrapericardial fluid (even 200 ml) accumulates rapidly, it can significantly limit ventricular filling.  Increases in intrapericardial pressure impairs the filling of the ventricles.  Ventricular filling pressure increases to accommodate it.  When pericardial pressure rises above ventricular filling pressure, cardiac output is reduced.  Systemic venous return is also reduced and blood pools in the venous circulation.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations for pericardial disease include:  classic symptoms include chest pain, dysphagia, hoarseness or dyspnoea (these may be absent in slow build-up of effusion)  a large effusion can lead to mufﬂed heart sounds, loss of apical impulse, occasional pericardial rub, small ECG complexes and eventually electro-mechanical dissociation

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  tachycardia/tachypnoea  Kussmaul's sign  Ewart's sign – cardiac tamponade leading to compression of lingular lobe thus causing bronchial breathing at the left lung base  right-sided heart failure – raised jugular venous pressure (JVP), ascites, hepatomegaly (non-pulsatile), oedema, cachexia  diastolic pericardial knock after S3  precipitation of atrial fibrillation.  Other key features may include:  Beck’s triad – comprising raised JVP, reduced BP and muffled heart sounds  pulsus alternans – variable left ventricular output and right ventricular ﬁlling  pulsus paradoxus – exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic BP  electrical alternans on ECG – ‘swinging QRS axis’  globular cardiac enlargement on chest radiograph.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for pericardial effusion include:  cardiomyopathy  pericarditis  cardiac tamponade  pulmonary embolism (PE)  pneumothorax  acute coronary syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation Bloods  Full blood count and blood cultures (look for raised white cell count or cytopenia as a sign of underlying disease).  Renal function tests and electrolytes, thyroid function tests.  Check autoantibodies, eg rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody.  B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and troponins may be elevated in the acute setting.  C-reactive protein (CRP)/erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) may also be raised. Electrocardiogram (ECG)  Low ECG complexes.  Electrical alterans.  Electromechanical dissociation.

DR. JAM Chest X-ray  Globular cardiac enlargement.  Pericardial effusion may be visualised. Echocardiogram  Collapse of cardiac chambers within cardiac tamponade.  Fluid surrounding the heart in pericardial effusion and pericarditis.  Echogenic bright bands in fibrotic constrictive pericarditis.  The density of the fluid present may indicate the underlying cause, eg haemopericardium due to trauma.  Some complicated cases may benefit from CT/MRI/biopsy; especially if secondary to malignancy or compression from a mediastinal mass.  Pericardial effusion on echo (PE): Pericardial fluid aspiration for analysis  Protein level, cell count, culture.  Smear for acid-fast bacilli in suspected TB infection, especially in patients with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).  Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels if elevated may be highly suggestive of malignant effusion.  Management Non-pharmacological and pharmacological  Interim and supportive measures include:  ABCDE approach as these patients can become critically unwell

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  oxygen may be required if there is any circulatory compromise  volume expansion/fluid resuscitation may be required if there is dehydration/hypovolaemia  positive inotropes  treatment of the underlying condition may reduce the amount of fluid present and prevent recurrence. Surgical  Pericardiocentesis may be required in cases of large effusions and also to aid diagnosis.  Percutaneous pericardiotomy – surgical pericardial windows may be necessary for chronic (eg malignant) effusions.  Pericardial sclerosis is an alternative to pericardiotomy.  Prognosis  Prognosis is dependent on the underlying cause.  Around one-third of large effusions may develop into cardiac tamponade, which is a medical emergency.  Larger effusions are often associated with more serious pathology.  Smaller, chronic effusions are often well tolerated by the patient.  Rarely, repeated episodes may lead to fibrosis and thickening of the pericardium:  when this occurs, it can lead to constrictive pericarditis which prevents adequate diastolic filling of the heart. Pericarditis The pericardium consists of a serous layer and a fibrous layer between which is pericardial fluid.  Overview Key Facts  The pericardium consists of a serous layer and a fibrous layer between which is pericardial fluid.  This encloses the pericardial cavity consisting of the heart and great vessel roots.  The serous layer acts as a lubricant to allow the heart to move freely within the pericardium.  Pericarditis describes inflammation of this pericardium.  Viral infections, bacterial sepsis, fungal infections and tuberculosis (TB) may all cause acute pericarditis.  Other causes include:

DR. JAM  acute myocardial infarction  malignancy  autoimmune disease  granulomatous disease  hypothyroidism, drugs such as hydralazine  trauma  radiotherapy.  Viruses are believed to be the cause of pericarditis in up to 85% of cases worldwide; the most common cause in the developed world is coxsackie B virus.  Other viral causes include adenovirus, echovirus and influenza viruses.  TB is the most common cause in the developing world.  Pericarditis presents with anterior pleuritic chest pain, which is worse on inspiration and relieved by sitting forward.  Patients may have a temperature on presentation, or describe a recent viral-type illness.  Examination may expose pericardial friction rub, which is pathognomonic of pericarditis:  this is best heard when the patient is upright and leaning forward (often described as the sound of walking on fresh snow).  The presence of ST-elevation on the electrocardiogram (ECG) is also indicative of this diagnosis.  The diagnosis can be made based on the triad of chest pain, pericardial friction rub and ECG changes.  There may be associated cardiac tamponade, evidenced by tachycardia, low blood and pulse pressure and distended neck veins.  Acute viral pericarditis may occasionally be associated with accumulation of a pericardial effusion, which can present with breathlessness:  an echocardiogram is used to confirm this and look for evidence of haemodynamic compromise.  For viral pericarditis, management includes limitation of activity and pain relief with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).  In severe cases, oral prednisolone may be considered as a second-line therapy.  If patients are unable to take NSAIDs, colchicine is the alternative.  Prognosis varies according to the underlying cause.  Patients with viral or idiopathic causes usually recover within weeks of treatment without complications.  Recurrence of pericarditis occurs in 10–15% of patients with pericarditis within the first year. Epidemiology  Viruses are believed to be the cause of pericarditis in up to 85% of cases worldwide.  TB is the most common cause in the developing world and coxsackie B virus is a common cause in the developed world.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Aetiology  The origin of acute pericarditis may be due to:  infection (viral, bacterial or fungal)  inflammation (eg rheumatoid, related to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), scleroderma or vasculitis)  drugs (hydralazine)  myocardial infarction  uraemia  neoplasia  sarcoidosis  hypothyroidism  trauma  radiotherapy. Pathophysiology  The pericardium consists of a serous and a fibrous layer between which is pericardial fluid.  This encloses the pericardial cavity consisting of the heart and great vessel roots.  The serous layer acts as a lubricant to allow the heart to move freely within the pericardium.  Pericarditis describes inflammation of the pericardium, which may be acute or chronic.  Chronic pericarditis can be classed as effusive, constrictive or a mixture of both types.  Constrictive pericarditis causes:  infection, eg Coxsackie B virus, TB  mediastinal radiotherapy  pericardial malignancy  drugs, eg hydralazine  post-viral or bacterial pericarditis  following severe uraemic pericarditis  trauma and/or post-cardiac surgery  connective tissue disease  recurrent pericarditis.  Clinical Presentation  The typical presentation for pericarditis is:  dull central chest pain  aggravated by inspiration, coughing and lying flat  may radiate into the arms or abdomen  relieved by sitting forward (this reduces contact with the inflamed pericardium).  The patient may have a fever, cough or a history of a recent viral illness.  Other presentations may include symptoms of associated cardiac tamponade:

DR. JAM  dysphagia  dyspnoea  hoarseness. Examination findings  Pericardial friction rub (high-pitched scratching sound, best heard over the left sternal border during expiration):  pathognomonic for acute pericarditis and present in around 50% of cases  best heard when the patient is sitting up and leaning forward  the rub is described as being similar to leather rubbing against leather or walking on snow  serial examinations may be needed as a friction rub may be transient from one hour to the next.  Tachycardia/tachypnoea.  Signs of cardiac tamponade may also be present and include:  pulsus paradoxus (decrease in palpable pulse and arterial systolic blood pressure of 10 mmHg on inspiration)  hypotension  muffled heart sounds  jugular venous distention  Ewart's sign – cardiac tamponade leading to compression of lingular lobe thus causing bronchial breathing at the left lung base  right-sided heart failure – raised jugular venous pressure (JVP), ascites, hepatomegaly (non-pulsatile), oedema, cachexia.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for acute pericarditis include:  pericardial effusion  cardiac tamponade  pulmonary embolism (PE)  pneumothorax  chronic pericarditis. Constrictive pericarditis versus restrictive cardiomyopathy: Similarities Differences Raised JVP with prominent x+y descents Absence of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) in constrictive pericarditis Atrial fibrillation Absent calcification on chest X-ray Normal systolic function Restrictive cardiomyopathy will have conduction abnormalities on ECG and prominent apical impulses

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis of pericarditis can be made based on the triad of chest pain, pericardial friction rub and ECG changes.  The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines have defined the diagnosis of acute pericarditis as two out of four of the following:  pericarditic chest pain  pericardial rub  new widespread ST elevation or PR depression  pericardial effusion (new or worsening).  A common complication of pericarditis is the development of pericardial effusion; an echocardiogram is used to confirm this and look for evidence of haemodynamic compromise. Bloods  B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and troponins may be elevated in the acute setting.  If troponin levels are significantly elevated, this can suggest myocardial involvement; patients should have BNP levels measured and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to quantify myocardial inflammation.  Inflammatory markers, such as white cell count (neutrophils/lymphocytes) and C-reactive protein (CRP)/erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) will be raised in pericarditis. Electrocardiogram (ECG)  Rhythm and conduction abnormalities are not typical in pericarditis unless the myocardium is involved.  Four temporal stages of ECG changes associated with pericarditis are recognised:  stage I: diffuse concave-upward ST-segment elevation with concordance of T waves; ST-segment depression in aVR or V1; PR-segment depression; low voltage; absence of reciprocal ST-segment changes  stage II: ST segments return to baseline; T-wave flattening  stage III: T-wave inversion  stage IV: gradual resolution of T-wave inversion. An ECG showing pericarditis:

DR. JAM Chest X-ray  Global cardiac enlargement.  Pericardial effusion.  In chronic constrictive pericarditis, there may be calcification of the pericardium seen on X-ray. Echocardiogram  Fluid surrounding the heart in pericardial effusion and pericarditis.  Echogenic bright bands in fibrotic constrictive pericarditis.  Some complicated cases may benefit from CT/MRI/biopsy; especially if secondary to malignancy or compression from a mediastinal mass. Management  For viral pericarditis, NSAIDs are the mainstay of treatment for the reduction of both inflammation and pain.  Treatment duration should be guided by symptoms and blood tests (CRP), but normally it is for 1–2 weeks’ duration.  If patients are unable to take NSAIDs, colchicine is the alternative.  Colchicine may also be used as an adjunct for pericarditis and is especially useful in cases of recurrence.  Corticosteroids should only be used as second-line due to the risk of drug dependence.  Patients should be advised to reduce physical activity for a minimum of three months from initial onset.  Treatment of the underlying cause is the mainstay of treatment for other secondary causes.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Most patients with viral or idiopathic pericarditis recover fully within a few weeks, without any complications.  Prognosis of pericarditis due to other causes depends on the underlying cause.  Development of constrictive pericarditis is highest for those with causes due to bacterial aetiologies, such as TB.  Between 15% and 30% of patients with apparently idiopathic acute pericarditis may have recurrent attacks and this is considered to be an autoimmune phenomenon. Prosthetic Valves The most common valvular surgery is valve replacement with prosthetic valves.  Overview Key Facts  The most common valvular surgery is valve replacement with prosthetic valves.  Prosthetic valves may be indicated for valvular heart disease, such as valve stenosis or regurgitation, congenital defects and infective valve destruction.  Valve prostheses may be metal or tissue (typically porcine or bovine).  Mechanical valves are more durable but tissue valves do not require full life-long anticoagulation, unlike their metallic counterparts.  The choice of valve will depend on numerous factors, including patient age, life expectancy, bleeding risk and patient preference.  All valve replacements have a residual transvalvular gradient across them; for mechanical valves, this can cause loud murmurs – ie an aortic valve replacement may still have a loud aortic stenosis ejection systolic murmur.  There are many types of mechanical valves:  ball and cage  single tilting disc  bileaflets.  Tissue valves can be homograft (cadaveric) or allograft (porcine or bovine).  Prosthetic valves can become infected (endocarditis), with mortality up to 60%:  usually, colonisation by Staphylococcus epidermidis if occurring within 6 months of implantation  septal abscesses may cause PR elongation  vegetations may cause new murmurs or muffle old ones

DR. JAM  mild haemolysis may also occur, which can be detected in urine (urobilinogen).  Anticoagulant-related bleeding and thromboembolic disease are also major complications that can be experienced by patients with prosthetic valves.  Bileaflet valve:  Ball and cage mechanical valves:

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Prosthetic valves can become infected (endocarditis), with mortality up to 60%.  Infection is usually by Staphylococcus epidermidis by 6 months colonisation.  Septal abscesses may cause PR elongation.  Vegetations may cause new murmurs or muffle old ones.  Mild haemolysis may occur, which can be detected in urine.  Anticoagulant-related bleeding and thromboembolic disease are also major complications that can be experienced by patients with prosthetic valves. Pulmonary Embolism A Pulmonary Embolism occurs when one or more emboli (most commonly a blood clot in the a deep vein – deep vein thrombosis) become lodged in the pulmonary arterial system.  Overview Key Facts  A Pulmonary Embolism (PE) occurs when one or more emboli (most commonly a blood clot in the a deep vein – deep vein thrombosis) become lodged in the pulmonary arterial system.  This causes obstruction of the artery, leading to respiratory dysfunction.  Can be either provoked (transient risk factors such as immobilisation, oral contraceptives, pregnancy) or unprovoked (no clear identifiable risk factor or permanent risk factors, such as malignancy or clotting disorder).  The condition can range from being asymptomatic to severe respiratory distress and shock leading to death.  Any signs of haemodynamic instability warrant urgent admission and management.  WELLS score is used to determine investigation method in suspected cases. Epidemiology  Can be difficult to determine as can be asymptomatic.  Estimated rate of 60-70 per 100 000. Aetiology  Thrombotic source (most common):  deep vein thrombosis (DVT).  Non-thrombotic source:  tumours, fat, amniotic fluid, sepsis, air.  Provoked (transient risk factors present):

DR. JAM  trauma, surgery, combined oral contraceptive pill, hormone replacement therapy, pregnancy, period of immobilisation.  Unprovoked  either unidentifiable risk factor or persistent risk factor that isn’t easily correctable  eg V Leiden mutation, coagulopathy, malignancy. Pathophysiology  Embolus travels to the arterial system and becomes lodged in the pulmonary artery.  Perfusion of the lung tissue is therefore prevented.  This area become dead space as it is still being ventilated.  Pulmonary arterial pressure increases and cardiac output decreases.  Alveoli can collapse and worsen hypoxemia.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms:  chest pain  cough  haemoptysis  dizziness.  Signs:  tachycardia  hypoxia  pyrexia  raised jugular venous pressure  pleural rub  extra heart sounds (a tricuspid regurgitation murmur, widely split second heart sound)  pleural rub  gallop rhythm  hypotension.  All female patients with unprovoked PE’s require a thorough breast examination at first appropriate opportunity to identify any potential breast malignancies.  Differential Diagnosis  Acute coronary syndrome.  Aortic dissection.  Oesophageal rupture.  Pneumothorax.  Endocarditis.  Pneumonia.  Pericarditis.  Acute heart failure.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Musculoskeletal chest pain.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Bloods: Full blood count (FBC), arterial blood gases (ABG), clotting screen, B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) (right ventricular strain), Troponin T.  Chest X-ray – often normal, helpful to rule out other respiratory pathology.  ECG – may show sinus tachycardia, ST segment and T wave abnormalities, right axis deviation/right heart strain. S1Q3T3 not often seen (in 5-10% of PEs).  Calculate two-level PE Wells’ score (as per NICE):  If score > 4 points, PE likely. Next offer:  immediate CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) or  if CTPA cannot be performed, immediate interim parenteral anticoagulant therapy followed by CTPA.  If score < or = 4, then PE unlikely. Next offer:  a D-dimer test. If D-dimer test is positive, offer:  immediate CTPA or  if CTPA cannot be performed, immediate interim parenteral anticoagulant therapy followed by CTPA.  A ventilation/perfusion single photon emission computed tomography (V/Q SPECT) can be considered for patients with renal failure/allergic to contrast/pregnant.  Once PE has been managed adequately, potential underlying causes should be investigated as required in patients with unprovoked PE.

DR. JAM  Management NICE recommends immediate admission in patients with signs of haemodynamic instability/ those who pregnant or post-partum, or 2-level Wells score of above 4 points. Initial management includes:  Oxygen via mask  Sit patient upright.  Analgesia  Urgent CTPA. Pharmacological: Treatment for confirmed PE or whist awaiting CTPA if not immediately available (interim anticoagulation): No renal impairment, active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome or haemodynamic instability:  Oral anticoagulant treatment (apixaban, or rivaroxaban).  If not suitable then:  Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) for at least 5 days, followed by dabigatran or edoxaban, or LMWH concurrently with a vitamin K antagonist for at least 5 days or until INR is at least 2.0 on two separate readings, then a vitamin K antagonist alone  Fondaparinux.  Unfractionated heparin may be used instead of apixaban or rivaroxaban in cases of renal impairment (determined by creatinine clearence levels) Patients with active cancer  consider a direct acting oral anticoagulant (DOAC), or LMWH/or LMWH concurrently with a vitamin K antagonist for at least 5 days or until INR is at least 2.0 on two separate readings and then a vitamin K antagonist alone.  Patients with antiphospholipid syndrome - LMWH concurrently with a vitamin K antagonist for at least 5 days or until INR is at least 2.0 on two separate readings, then a vitamin K antagonist alone Patients with haemodynamic instability  Thrombolytic therapy – first line for massive PE  considered if there is haemodynamic instability  can be given into a peripheral vein or directly into the pulmonary arteries (catheter-directed thrombolyis  streptokinase, urokinase, rt-PA. Surgical:  Embolectomy (not offered by many centres).  Inferior vena cava filter can be considered if:

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  patient can’t receive anti-coagulants (remove filter when they can receive anticoagulants)  recurrent PEs despite adequate anticoagulation (permanent filter).  Follow up  The choice of treatment will depend on factors such as:  the licensed indication of the treatment  the presence of co-morbidities  contraindication to treatment  patient preference and the preference of the person.  Specialists will usually make clinical decisions on the duration of treatment, which dependent on if the PE is classed as provoked or unprovoked:  provoked PE – treatment is usually continued for 3 months, and then re-reviewed (3 - 6 months for those with active cancer)  unprovoked PE - usually treated for beyond 3 months (often 6 months), duration determined by the patient's risk of further thromboembolism versus the risk of bleeding.  Early mobilisation is recommended.  Provide information on anticoagulation treatment and PE, and provide anticoagulation card and information regarding monitoring.  Discuss possible adverse effects.  Give advice regarding activity, modifications for dental treatment and surgery and implications if trying to become pregnant.  Smoking cessation advice should be offered.  Prognosis  If left untreated there is a high mortality and morbidity rate.  Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) is a rare complication of PE to be aware of.  over the course of months or years, emboli are replaced by fibrous tissue  this causes chronic obstruction of the pulmonary arterial vasculature; increases in pulmonary arterial pressure, and can lead to right heart failure.  Recurrence risk depends of whether the PE was provoked or unprovoked.  in unprovoked cases patients are at increased risk of a recurrence as the risk factor cannot be removed.

DR. JAM Pulmonary Hypertension Pulmonary hypertension is characterised by a progressive increase in resistance in the pulmonary circulation, eventually leading to right heart failure (cor pulmonale).  Overview Key Facts  Pulmonary hypertension is characterised by a progressive increase in resistance in the pulmonary circulation, eventually leading to right heart failure (cor pulmonale).  It is important to determine whether pulmonary hypertension is secondary to an underlying condition that may be treatable.  The most common cause of secondary pulmonary hypertension is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Airway rigidity leads to increased circulatory pressures to maintain blood flow.  Diagnosis is made by catheterisation to measure the pulmonary pressure.  Treatment is dependent on the underlying cause, but includes:  symptom management  supportive therapy, and  pulmonary vasodilators.  Definitive treatment is transplantation.  Prognosis for untreated primary pulmonary hypertension is poor with the average survival being three years.  With new therapy options, survival rates in treated patients are improving. Epidemiology  Primary pulmonary hypertension (PPH) is a rare disease with an incidence of 2 000 000 per year.  Prevalence is estimated to be between 10–50 cases per million population.  It is a disease of children and young adults.  Women : men ratio is 2 : 1. Aetiology World Health Organisation (WHO) Venice Classification of Pulmonary Hypertension  WHO Group 1: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension  idiopathic/sporadic  familial – associated with a specific gene mutation – bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 2 (BMPR2)  associated with pulmonary venous or capillary disease  associated with systemic diseases, including:  collagen vascular disease (eg scleroderma)  human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  cirrhosis.  drugs/toxins (eg anorexigens)  portal hypertension  congenital heart disease with shunting left to right (atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect)  persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborn babies.  WHO Group 2: Pulmonary Hypertension Associated with Left Heart Disease  atrial or ventricular disease (dilated cardiomyopathy, ischaemic heard disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)  valvular disease (eg mitral stenosis or aortic stenosis)  extrinsic compression of the central pulmonary veins.  WHO Group 3: Pulmonary Hypertension Associated with Lung Diseases and/or Hypoxemia  COPD  interstitial/fibrotic lung disease  obstructive sleep apnoea  alveolar hypoventilation disorders  chronic high altitude  chronic hypoxia (polio, myasthenia).  WHO Group 4: Pulmonary Hypertension due to Chronic Thrombotic and/or Embolic Disease  pulmonary emboli of proximal arteries  obstruction of distal pulmonary arteries  embolisation of thrombus, tumour, ova, parasites or foreign material  in-situ thrombosis  sickle cell disease.  WHO Group 5: Pulmonary Hypertension caused by Disorders Directly Affecting the Pulmonary Vasculature  inflammatory – schistosomiasis, sarcoidoisis  pulmonary capillary haemangiomatosis  glycogen storage disease. Pathophysiology  Primary Pulmonary Hypertension (PPH)  PPH constitutes < 1% of all cases of pulmonary hypertension and is characterised by a mean pulmonary artery pressure > 25 mmHg at rest, in the absence of another demonstrable cause.  One in ten cases is familial.  PPH is associated with connective tissue disease, vasculitis and HIV infection, and also the use of appetite suppressants (eg fenfluramine).  The pulmonary arteries become dilated and abnormally thickened; there is dilatation of the proximal pulmonary vessels with thick-walled, obstructed, ‘pruned’ peripheral vessels.  As a consequence of the high pulmonary pressure, the right ventricle undergoes marked hypertrophy.

DR. JAM  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations for pulmonary hypertension are as follows:  patients present with gradually worsening exertional dyspnoea  in the later stages, angina of effort and syncope occur  fatigue is common and disproportionate to exertion  dry cough  haemoptysis  cyanosis – central  right ventricular heave  loud P2  tricuspid regurgitation  peripheral oedema/ascites  chest pain/angina.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for pulmonary hypertension include:  cardiomyopathies  pulmonary stenosis  congestive cardiac failure  portal hypertension  obstructive sleep apnoea.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Rule out other causes of breathlessness.  Electrocardiogram (ECG) – abnormal ECG more likely in severe disease but a normal ECG does not rule out PAH.  may show P pulmonale, right axis deviation, RV hypertrophy, RV strain, right bundle branch block, and QTc prolongation.  Spirometry:  identify any underlying respiratory disease.  Chest radiograph:  prominent vasculature – central pulmonary arterial dilatation  enlarged right atrium and ventricle  normal CXR doesn’t exclude PAH.  Echocardiogram should always be performed when PAH is suspected.  peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity key finding.  Further imaging:  ventilation perfusion scan – to look for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension or  high resolution computed tomography (CT) – for diagnosis/prognosis

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  CT pulmonary angiogram.  Other tests to consider:  bloods: BNP, HIV testing, immunological testing, full blood count, liver function test, urea and electrolytes, clotting  pulmonary angiogram  exercise test: gives functional and prognostic information  right heart catheterisation: directly measure pulmonary pressure to confirm diagnosis  MRI  overnight oximetry: used when considering sleep disordered breathing. Image below is an example of a side-selective pulmonary artery angiogram (A and B right pulmonary artery, C and D left pulmonary artery) in digital subtraction technique of a patient with CTEPH:  Panels A and C represent anterior-posterior projections, panels B and D represent lateral projections.  Management Non-pharmacological:  Advise avoidance of strenuous exercise.  Recommend contraception/advice regarding the risks of high morbidity and mortality during pregnancy in women of childbearing age. Pharmacological:  Treatment of PPH would usually be undertaken at a specialist centre. The chief aspects involve:

DR. JAM  anticoagulation (to avoid thrombus formation in situ in the pulmonary arteries and pulmonary embolism)  digoxin, even in patients with sinus rhythm  ambulatory supplemental oxygen for some  prostacyclin (PGI2), a potent pulmonary and systemic vasodilator, is used particularly to bridge patients to transplantation. The drug has an extremely short half-life and has to be given by continuous intravenous infusion, usually through a tunnelled central venous catheter. It is also very expensive  phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors (sildenafil/tadalafil) slow progression and may have some reversal of pathology.  endothelin receptor blockade (eg bosentan)  calcium channel antagonists have been used to lower pulmonary (and systemic) pressure  diuretics are helpful in the management of right heart failure to reduce circulating fluid within the vascular space  continuous ambulatory inhaled nitric oxide is being developed to provide good pulmonary vasodilatation, but without systemic effect. Surgical:  Pulmonary endarterectomy.  Balloon pulmonary angioplasty – for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension who cannot undergo endarterectomy surgery.  Atrial septostomy.  Heart-lung transplantation.  Prognosis  Untreated, the median survival is approximately three years.  Prognosis in treated individuals varies depending on underlying cause, speed of diagnosis and existing comorbidities.  The introduction of new and more effective therapies over the last 20 years has greatly improved survival rates and morbidity in patients with pulmonary hypertension. Restrictive Cardiomyopathy The term cardiomyopathies refers to a group of diseases that selectively affects the myocardial muscle layer of the heart.  Overview Key Facts  The term cardiomyopathies refers to a group of diseases that selectively affects the myocardial muscle layer of the heart.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  There can be few or no symptoms of cardiomyopathy at the early stages of the disease.  The main types are dilated, hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathy.  Restrictive cardiomyopathy is relatively rare and makes up only 5% of all cases of cardiomyopathy.  It is characterised by normal left ventricular cavity size and systolic function but with increased myocardial stiffness.  This leads to restricted filling of both ventricles in diastole.  Causes may be divided into myocardial and endomyocardial; in many cases no cause can be found (idiopathic).  Cardiac amyloidosis is another common cause in the West.  Restrictive cardiomyopathy produces identical symptoms to constrictive pericarditis and may be very difficult to differentiate.  Restrictive cardiomyopathy presents with signs of right-sided heart failure (cachexia, hepatomegaly, raised JVP, ascites and oedema).  Up to 75% of patients develop atrial fibrillation (AF); stagnation of blood due to AF may lead to thrombus formation.  Unlike constrictive pericarditis, surgery is of little use in restrictive cardiomyopathy; treatment involves managing symptoms and preventing consequences of heart failure, AF and arrhythmia.  Prognosis is variable and is dependent on the underlying cause.  Cardiac amyloidosis  Cardiac amyloidosis is the most common cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy in the West.  It is characterised by the deposition of abnormal protein (amyloid) in the cardiac tissue.  Protein deposition can be due to primary disorder (amyloid light-chain amyloidosis, a clonal plasma cell disorder with light chain production to form the fibrils).  It can also be secondary to any chronic inflammatory disorder.  Deposition and resultant fibrosis cause the ventricles to become thickened and stiff, with poor systolic and diastolic function.  Electrocardiograms (ECGs) show characteristic low-voltage QRS complexes and echocardiographic appearances of the myocardium are classically ‘speckled’.  Diagnosis is confirmed by cardiac biopsy with Congo red staining which demonstrates amyloid infiltration.  Cardiac involvement is a marker of poor prognosis in amyloidosis disease, with congestive heart failure, syncope, pulmonary hypertension and conduction problems being causes of death.  Treatment is palliative; negative inotropic drugs, such as diltiazem, should be avoided.

DR. JAM Epidemiology  Restrictive cardiomyopathy is relatively rare, accounting for 5% of all cardiomyopathies.  The condition is more common in older people and more often found in women.  The most common cause in the West is amyloidosis.  When it occurs in children, the cause is usually idiopathic.  Unlike hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, familial inheritance is not characteristic. Aetiology  Myocardial causes:  idiopathic  scleroderma  amyloid  sarcoid  haemochromatosis  glycogen storage disorders  Gaucher’s disease.  Endomyocardial causes:  endomyocardial ﬁbrosis  hyper-eosinophilic syndromes (including Lofﬂer’s)  carcinoid  malignancy or radiotherapy  toxin related. Pathophysiology  Increased stiffness of the myocardium causes ventricular pressures to rise precipitously with small increases in volume.  Accentuated filling occurs in the early diastole and terminates abruptly at the end of the rapid filling phase.  The atria typically dilate in response and may develop atrial fibrillation.  Infiltration of the conducting tissues with protein deposits (depending on the underlying cause) leads to conduction abnormalities including heart block.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations for cardiomyopathy include the following:  dyspnoea  syncope/pre-syncope/dizziness  angina  palpitations  orthopnoea/paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea  congestive heart failure  sudden cardiac death

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  oedema.  This presents in a similar way to restrictive cardiomyopathy, ie with signs of right-sided heart failure (cachexia, hepatomegaly, raised JVP, ascites and oedema) due to restriction of diastolic ﬁlling of both ventricles.  Differential Diagnosis  The main differential is constrictive pericarditis, which presents in a very similar way.  Other differentials to consider are:  other forms of cardiomyopathy  pericardial effusion  cardiac tamponade  pulmonary embolism (PE)  pneumothorax  chronic pericarditis.  Types of cardiomyopathy:  Diagnosis/Investigation  Investigations for restrictive cardiomyopathy are as follows:  bloods – include renal function, electrolytes, liver function tests, cardiac enzymes  electrocardiogram (ECG) is likely to show rhythm abnormality, up to 75% of patients will have AF, there may be ST/T wave abnormalities  cardiac catheterisation – increased right-heart pressures (similar results to that of constrictive pericarditis)  echocardiography findings include small ventricular chamber size, thickened left ventricular wall and small cavities; speckling may be present  cardiac catheterisation to monitor pressures

DR. JAM  cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) – can be used when an echocardiogram is inconclusive and may help differentiate from pericarditis  cardiac biopsy may be required to differentiate restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis and to help identify an underlying cause and is considered the gold standard for diagnosis of amyloidosis  investigations of a possible underlying cause should also be considered as appropriate, depending on the presentation, examination findings and initial investigation results.  High-magnification micrograph of senile cardiac amyloidosis; H&E stain; autopsy specimen (note positivity for Congo red staining):  Management  Often, underlying causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy do not respond to intervention, making management difficult in many cases.  There is no specific treatment for the condition.  Management is of heart failure, co-existing atrial fibrillation and existing or potential arrhythmias.  Management may also include treatment of underlying causes if identified.  Pacing, internal cardiac defibrillators and transplantation may be of value in some patients. Pharmacological  Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors.  Beta-blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers may be used for rate control in those with atrial fibrillation.  Amiodarone (can reduce ventricular arrhythmias in high-risk patients).  Avoid digoxin (if in sinus rhythm), nitrates, atropine, inotropes, diuretics (unless in left ventricular failure):  digoxin binds to amyloid fibrils and can reach toxic levels – even within therapeutic range.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Anticoagulation with warfarin or direct-acting oral coagulant may be indicated as atrial fibrillation incidence and rate of ventricular thrombogenesis is high. Surgical  Dual-chamber pacing.  Internal defibrillators should be considered in patients at high risk from sudden death.  Transplantation is the treatment of choice in most cases of restrictive cardiomyopathy in children and may be indicated in some adults.  Prognosis  The prognosis is often related to the underlying cause and can be very variable, but mortality rates at 5 years may be up to 70%.  Patients ultimately develop right-heart failure and pulmonary hypertension.  There is an increased risk of sudden cardiac death.  There is a significantly increased risk for thromboembolism, especially in patients with AF.  The prognosis is worse when the underlying cause is amyloidosis, which is especially difficult to treat. Rheumatic Fever Rheumatic fever occurs following group A streptococcal (pyogenes) infection due to a type II hypersensitivity reaction.  Overview Key Facts  Rheumatic fever occurs following group A streptococcal (pyogenes) infection due to a type II hypersensitivity reaction (molecular mimicry)  antibodies against streptococcus also bind to heart tissue and joints leading to its clinical picture.  Pancarditis usually occurs with valvular defects as long-term sequelae.  Cardiac histology shows Aschoff’s nodule. Aschoff's nodule:

DR. JAM  Penicillin and salicylates or steroids are the mainstay of treatment.  Duckett–Jones criteria are used for diagnosis.  Major Duckett–Jones criteria:  carditis  polyarthritis  chorea  erythema marginatum  subcutaneous nodules.  Minor Duckett–Jones criteria:  fever  arthralgia  previous rheumatic heart disease  high erythrocyte sedimentation rate/C-reactive protein  first degree heart block (prolonged PR interval).  Two major, or one major with two minor, are needed along with evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (raised antistreptolysin O titre, positive throat swab or history of scarlet fever).  Penicillin is the treatment of choice.  Clinical Presentation  Cardiovascular:  carditis occurs in about 50–60% of all cases of acute rheumatic fever  considered the most serious manifestation of rheumatic fever  characterised by pancarditis (endocardium, pericardium and epicardium)  usually, the mitral and aortic valves are affected, which can lead to valvular dysfunction  acute rheumatic fever usually presents as tachycardia and a cardiac murmur.  Joints:

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  arthritis occurs in 75% of patients with rheumatic fever and typically involves large joints such as the knees, ankles, wrists and elbows  affected joints return to normal in a few days, then another one or more become affected (migratory polyarthritis).  Skin:  subcutaneous nodule: a firm nodule 1 cm or more in diameter along the extensor surfaces of the tendons near bony prominences:  rare; present in < 1% of patients with rheumatic fever.  erythema marginatum: macular lesions with pale centres that do not itch:  occurs primarily on the trunk and extremities.  Central nervous system:  Sydenham’s chorea occurs in 10–15% of patients with rheumatic fever  presents as rapid, irregular and aimless involuntary movements of the arms, legs, trunk and facial muscles  usually disappears during sleep  can be diagnosed with ‘Milkmaid’s Grip’ sign or spooning and pronation sign, with supportive evidence of rheumatic fever.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The Duckett–Jones diagnostic criteria are still used as a guide to the diagnosis of rheumatic fever.  There are five major and four minor criteria.  The diagnosis can be made if the patient has two major criteria or one major and two minor criteria.  Major criteria:  migratory polyarthritis  carditis  subcutaneous nodules  erythema marginatum  Sydenham’s chorea.  Minor criteria:  arthralgia  fever  elevated acute-phase reactant (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein)  prolonged PR interval.  In around 80% of the cases, antistreptolysin O titre will be elevated.

DR. JAM  Management Non-pharmacological:  Bed rest is recommended in the acute phase (carditis).  Full activity should not be resumed until markers for inflammation and infection (acute-phase reactants) have returned to normal. Pharmacological:  Penicillin is the drug of choice to eradicate the infection.  Alternatively, erythromycin or a cephalosporin can be used in case of penicillin allergy.  Aspirin can be used in mild-to-moderate carditis.  Heart failure will require diuretics, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and digoxin.  Diazepam can be used in chorea (self-limiting).  Aspirin and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can be used in arthritis.  Surgical:  Surgery is needed in case of valvular repair (mitral valve) or replacement.  If medication has failed and heart failure is present, cardiac surgery could be considered.  Prognosis  The prognosis of rheumatic fever depends on the severity of cardiac involvement.  In cases of severe carditis, the prognosis is poor.  Patients with a history of rheumatic fever are at high risk of recurrence. Supraventricular Tachycardia Supraventricular tachycardia is a rapid heart rhythm originating above the heart's ventricles.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Cardiac arrhythmias include a group of conditions characterised by abnormal conduction of the electrical activity in the heart.  This may result in abnormal mechanical function of the heart.  Arrhythmias can be classed by:  rate – tachycardias (heart rate (HR) > 100 beats/min) or bradycardias (HR <60 beats/min)  the origin of the aberrant conduction – atrial, junctional (AV node) or ventricular  the duration of the QRS complex on electrocardiogram (ECG) – narrow or wide complex arrhythmias.  Supraventricular tachycardias (SVTs) are tachycardias that arise above the atrioventricular node.  The most common SVT is atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia (AVNRT):  it is more frequently seen in women and most commonly seen in people in their 20s and 30s.  Other forms include atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia, atrial tachycardia and those caused by accessory pathways, such as Wolf–Parkinson–White syndrome.  The definition does not usually include atrial fibrillation.  In some instances SVT may resolve spontaneously, or with vagal manoeuvres.  Management of persisting arrhythmia or recurrence depends on the type of arrhythmia and may involve one or more of the following:  anti-arrhythmic drugs  catheter ablation  implantable cardioverter defibrillators. Epidemiology  Incidence of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is approximately 35 cases per 100 000 patients, with a prevalence of 2.25 cases per 1000 in the general population. Aetiology  SVT risk factors:  heart disease and failure  thyroid disease  heart disease  chronic lung disease and smoking  alcohol and caffeine  drugs (eg cocaine and methamphetamines)  certain medications, including asthma medications and over-the-counter cold and allergy drugs  surgery  pregnancy

DR. JAM  Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome. Pathophysiology SVT pathophysiology  Atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia (AVNRT) involves a re-entry circuit in and around the AV node – ie there is more than one conduction pathway in close proximity to the AV node:  differential conduction in the tissue around the AV node allows a micro re-entry circuit to be maintained, resulting in regular tachycardia.  Atrioventricular nodal tachycardia (AVT) involves an accessory pathway between the atria and ventricles some distance from the AV node, eg Wolff–Parkinson–White (WPW) syndrome.  Accessory pathways connect the atrium and ventricles together bypassing the AV node and enabling retrograde conduction. This may predispose to unrestricted conduction of AF from atria to ventricles as a result of anterograde conduction through the pathway. This may lead to ventricular fibrillation.  WPW is present when a partial pathway-mediated preexcitation (B wave) is present on the resting ECG. Mechanism for atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia:  Atrial flutter:  a macro re-entrant circuit where the electrical activation circles the right atrium; this generates characteristic sawtoothed flutter waves, which typically have a rate between 250 and 350 bpm, with a ventricular response of 150 bpm (2 : 1 block)

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  the ventricular response may be slowed by increasing the vagal block of the AV node (eg carotid sinus massage) or by adenosine, which ‘uncovers’ the flutter waves on ECG.  Atrial fibrillation:  the source is from myocardial tissue in the entrance to four pulmonary veins  AF may be paroxysmal, persistent or permanent  loss of P wave on ECG with irregular ventricular rhythm.  Clinical Presentation  Irregular pulse.  Shortness of breath.  Palpitations.  Tachycardia/bradycardia.  Syncope.  Dizziness.  Chest pain.  Sequelae of emboli, eg stroke.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis of SVTs:  atrial fibrillation  atrial flutter  atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia (AVRT)  atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia (AVNRT)  sinus arrhythmia.  Other potential differentials:  ventricular tachycardia  torsades de pointes  ventricular fibrillation.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Bloods:  full blood count – look for anaemia  electrolytes (eg potassium/calcium/magnesium)  thyroid function tests  cardiac enzymes (if the patient describes chest discomfort)  digoxin levels should be taken in patients on digoxin.  ECG:  diagnosis of the type of arrhythmia via ECG is essential.  Other tests:

DR. JAM  chest X-ray may show signs of heart failure  transoesophageal echocardiogram may be indicated to look for mural thrombi or structural causes  24-hour Holter monitoring may be required for a diagnosis of paroxysmal episodes.  Management  Management depends on the following things:  the type of arrhythmia  acuteness of onset  haemodynamic stability  the underlying cause. Non-pharmacological  All patients should be assessed using the ABCDE approach.  Oxygen may be indicated if the patient is hypoxic.  Reversible causes should be identified and treated.  Vagal manoeuvres (SVT only):  Valsalva manoeuvre  carotid sinus massage  immersion of face in ice water.  DC cardioversion if haemodynamically compromised. Pharmacological  Resuscitation Council guidelines should be followed for managing arrhythmias.  The management depends on the rate, the stability of the patient and ECG features of the rhythm.  Tachycardias:  adenosine – slows the heart down by slowing conduction through the AV node  rate control (eg AF) – beta-blockers, digoxin or diltiazem  amiodarone, sotalol, flecainide and lidocaine for chemical cardioversion  isoprenaline and magnesium sulphate for torsades de pointes. Surgical  Pacing, temporary or permanent, for conditions including sick sinus syndrome, AV block, preventing tachycardia, chronic bifascicular block.  Radiofrequency ablation – useful to permanently treat accessory pathways and atrial flutter.  Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators – detects and terminates life-threatening tachyarrhythmias and can be used as primary and secondary prevention of cardiac arrest (eg in Brugada syndrome, long QT variants, LV impairment).

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  SVT is usually paroxysmal.  Episodes may occur regularly or very infrequently (sometimes years apart).  The duration of each episode may only be minutes or last for several months. Ventricular Fibrillation Ventricular fibrillation is a life-threatening arrhythmia caused by rapid and irregular electrical activity in the ventricles. The ventricles are not able to contract in a synchronised manner and the heart is unable to function as a pump.  Overview Key Facts  Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is a life-threatening arrhythmia caused by rapid and irregular electrical activity in the ventricles. The ventricles are not able to contract in a synchronised manor and the heart is unable to function as a pump.  VF results in cardiac arrest. The definitive management is early CPR and defibrillation, following resuscitation advanced life support (ALS) guidelines as a shockable rhythm.  Prognosis after resuscitation is dependent on the duration of CPR, time to defibrillation, haemodynamic stability and neurological recovery.  Prognosis is low in patients who experience ventricular fibrillation, the survival rate is between only 15% and 20% outside of hospital and between 40% and 50% in hospital. Epidemiology  25% of cardiac arrests are shockable rhythms (including VF and pulseless ventricular tachycardia/pulseless VT).  Of those who suffer out-of-hospital cardiac arrests, about 25– 30% are successful in achieving the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) but only 8% survive to go home after hospitalisation.  16.9% of in-hospital cardiac arrests are shockable rhythms (VF and pulseless VT):  of these, 49% survive to be discharged from hospital.  There is a 50% recurrence rate of having another episode of VF. Aetiology  There are many causes of VF:  cardiac causes:  coronary heart disease

DR. JAM  valvular disorders  cardiac tamponade  aortic dissection  brugada syndrome  long QT syndrome  cardiomyopathy.  respiratory causes:  pulmonary embolism  tension pneumothorax  aspiration.  neurological:  intracranial haemorrhage  seizures. Pathophysiology  The mechanism behind how VF works is still unclear.  There are two hypotheses:  multiple wavelet mechanism:  where there are numerous wavelets formed and reentry circuits causing the fibrillation of the ventricles  mother rotor mechanism:  where there is one re-entry circuit formed that leads to other unstable circuits leading to unsynchronised electrical activity.  When the heart goes into VF, the heart is not able to pump oxygen and blood to the rest of the body and this leads to hypoperfusion and possibly death.  Clinical Presentation  Before going into cardiac arrest, patients may experience chest pain, palpitations, fatigue, nausea and other symptoms.  However, most patients in VF present with a loss of consciousness and no pulse detected.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  ventricular tachycardia – polymorphic (torsades de pointes)  Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome  atrial fibrillation  supraventricular tachycardia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The main investigation in a cardiac arrest scenario is the rhythm strip on a defibrillator.  ECG features include:

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  irregular waves of varying amplitude  no P waves, QRS complexes or T waves  amplitude decreases over time (ie starts as ‘coarse’ VF before becoming ‘fine’ VF).  Other investigations should be considered to detect any reversible causes leading to the cardiac arrest, in particular, the 4 Hs and 4 Ts while attempting resuscitation:  hypoxia  hypothermia  hyperkalaemia  hypovalaemia  tension pneumothorax  tamponade  toxins  thrombosis.  Management Non-pharmacological  Resuscitation ALS guidelines:  call resuscitation team  CPR 30:2 and attach defibrillator  assess rhythm  once VF detected ⇢ shockable pathway  deliver 1 shock and then resume CPR for 2 minutes and repeat cycle with assessing rhythm.  Precordial thump is not usually recommended but can be considered if it can be done without delay while waiting for a defibrillator. Pharmacological  During resuscitation:  give adrenaline 1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes after alternate shocks:  withhold if there are signs of return of spontaneous circulation.  give amiodarone 300 mg IV after 3 shocks. Surgical  Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) post-resuscitation (for patients at risk of recurrent VF).  Prognosis  Prognosis is poor in patients who experience VF, and the survival rate is between only 15% and 20% outside of hospital and between 40% and 50% in hospital. However, with prompt defibrillation within 3–5 minutes, the Resuscitation Council (UK) states that survival rate could be between 50% and 70%.

DR. JAM  Good prognostic factors include short resuscitation time, early defibrillation, haemodynamic stability and quick neurological recovery. Ventricular Septal Defect Ventricular septal defect is the most common isolated congenital heart defect.  Overview Key Facts  Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common isolated congenital heart defect.  The septum is made of two parts:  a superior membranous component, which contains the atrioventricular node (AVN)  an inferior muscular component.  Most defects are small and treated conservatively.  Larger defects can present with poor feeding and reduced exercise tolerance.  Complications include pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger’s.  Medical management includes diuretics, and angiotensinconverting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors.  Surgery is needed for larger VSDs. Epidemiology  VSDs are the most common isolated congenital heart defect (2/1000 births; 30% of all congenital defects). Aetiology  Associated with conditions such as:  Edwards syndrome  Patau syndrome  Down syndrome  Turner syndrome, 22q11 deletion  Holt Oram syndrome  Fetal alcohol syndrome. Pathophysiology  Membranous VSDs can be more complicated due to the AVN and proximity of the aortic apparatus.  Large defects allow significant left-to-right shunt, causing elevated right heart pressures and consequently pulmonary hypertension.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Once Eisenmenger’s complex develops, the thrill and left sternal edge (LSE) murmur abate, and signs are of pulmonary hypertension regurgitation and right ventricular failure. Ventricular septal defect:  Clinical Presentation  Smaller VSDs may be asymptomatic.  Larger VSDs may present with poor feeding and poor exercise tolerance.  Murmur:  May be ejection systolic in very small or very large defects.  With large defects the aortic component of the second sound is obscured, or even a single/palpable S2 is heard; a mitral diastolic murmur may occur. The apex beat is typically hyperdynamic.  Parasternal heave and LSE murmur.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)  pulmonary stenosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Electrocardiogram:  left ventricular hypertrophy  biventricular hypertrophy

DR. JAM  pulmonary hypertension – right axis deviation, right ventricular hypertrophy, right atrial hypertrophy.  Chest X-ray:  cardiomegaly  enlarged pulmonary artery and hilar pulmonary arteries in pulmonary hypertension.  Echocardiogram:  can identify the size, amount, and locations of defects  can estimate pulmonary artery pressure and shunt volume.  Management Non-pharmacological:  spontaneous closure is more common in muscular defects. Pharmacological:  high calorie foods to support feeding  digoxin for its positive inotropic effect  heart failure  first line treatment is with diuretics  ACE inhibitors reduce the afterload. Surgical:  Indications for closure:  significant left-to-right shunt  associated with other defect requiring cardiotomy  elevated right heart pressure causing pulmonary hypertension  endocarditis  membranous VSD causing.  Surgery should occur earlier to avoid Eisenmenger, otherwise a combined heart/lung transplantation would be required.  VSDs can be repaired percutaneously and transcatheter endovascular closure of VSDs is done with echocardiographic and fluoroscopic guidance.  Prognosis  Most small VSDs close spontaneously.  Post-surgical outcome for VSDs is excellent and surgical mortality is approaching zero.  Prognosis is very poor in those that develop pulmonary hypertension or Eisenmenger.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Other Eisenmenger syndrome: Refers to any untreated congenital cardiac defect with intracardiac communication that leads to:  severe irreversible pulmonary hypertension  reversal of left-to-right shunts  cyanosis  long-standing left-to-right shunts (eg in large VSDs, atrial septal defect (ASDs) or PDAs) cause remodelling of the pulmonary microvasculature, with obstruction and pulmonary blood flow and raised pressures  this causes shunts to reverse, sending deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation, which is evident as cyanosis. Signs of development include:  clubbing and central cyanosis  decrease of original pansystolic (left-to-right) murmur  decreasing intensity of tricuspid/pulmonary flow murmurs  single S2 with louder intensity, palpable P2; right ventricular heave  appearance of Graham Steell murmur due to pulmonary regurgitation  pansystolic murmur and V waves due to TR. Causes:  VSD (Eisenmenger’s complex)  ASD  PDA. Complications of Eisenmenger syndrome:  right ventricular failure  massive haemoptysis  cerebral embolism/abscess  infective endocarditis (rare). Ventricular Tachycardia – Monomorphic Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is the most common form of ventricular tachycardia and is usually what people refer to when discussing ventricular tachycardia.

DR. JAM  Overview Key Facts  Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) is the most common form of ventricular tachycardia and is usually what people refer to when discussing ventricular tachycardia.  It is a regular broad QRS complex tachycardia that can lead to ventricular fibrillation or cardiac arrest.  Wide variation in clinical presentation (from mild symptoms to cardiac arrest) depending on the ventricular rate and underlying cardiac disease.  Stable VT is treated with amiodarone whereas unstable VT (with adverse features) will need to be managed following the resuscitation guidelines for adult tachycardia (with pulse).  Pulseless VT is managed as per the resuscitation guidelines for cardiac arrest with a shockable rhythm.  Prognosis (short term) is good with rapid treatment; longerterm prognosis depends on the underlying cause of the VT. Epidemiology  Ventricular tachycardia is more common in middle-age as people tend to develop heart disease later in life.  The exact incidence is unknown as VT tends to lead to ventricular fibrillation (VF) or overlaps with it.  25% of people presenting with a cardiac arrest are in shockable rhythms (including VF and pulseless VT). Aetiology  There are risk factors that can lead to VT:  coronary heart disease  cardiomyopathy  valvular heart disease  myocardial infarction  long QT syndrome  electrolyte abnormalities:  hypokalaemia  hypocalcaemia  hypomagnesaemia.  sympathomimetic agents can trigger VT:  eg cocaine. Pathophysiology  Ventricular tachycardia originates from a disturbance in electrical activity from the ventricles.  There is a re-entrance circuit in the ventricles that is causing it to beat faster than it should:  commonly due to heart disease – from previous scarring of the myocardium  scar tissue cannot conduct electrical activity properly leading into a circuit around the scar.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation  Wide variation in clinical presentation (from mild symptoms to cardiac arrest) depending on the ventricular rate and underlying cardiac disease.  Patients with VT may present in cardiac arrest.  However, short periods of VT may be asymptomatic or could present with palpitations, chest pain or feeling light-headed. Symptoms are due to a reduction in cardiac output.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  ventricular tachycardia – polymorphic  ventricular fibrillation  supraventricular tachycardia with bundle branch block.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Ventricular tachycardia is diagnosed on an ECG; the features seen are:  broad complex QRS (>120 ms)  tachycardia (>100 bpm – usually between 150 and 200 bpm)  AV dissociation  monomorphic VT:  regular pattern  one morphology seen.  If this progresses into cardiac arrest, other investigations should be considered to detect any reversible causes, in particular the 4 Hs and 4 Ts while attempting resuscitation:  hypoxia  hypothermia  hyperkalaemia  hypovolaemia  tension pneumothorax  tamponade  toxins  thrombosis. Example of ventricular tachycardia ECG:

DR. JAM  Management Non-pharmacological  Pulseless VT:  cardiac arrest management following ALS guidelines:  call resuscitation team  CPR 30 : 2 and attach defibrillator  assess rhythm  once VF detected ⇢ shockable pathway  deliver one shock and then resume CPR for 2 minutes and repeat cycle with assessing rhythm.  VT with adverse features (shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia or heart failure) – cardioversion:  synchronised shocks to prevent progression to VF. Pharmacological  Stable VT (ie no adverse features):  amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 minutes then amiodarone 900 mg IV over 24 hours.  Pulseless VT:  shockable rhythm – follow ALS guidelines:  shock + CPR  give adrenaline 1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes after alternate shocks  withhold if there are signs of return of spontaneous circulation  give amiodarone 300 mg IV after three shocks.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Treat reversible causes:  replenish electrolytes (magnesium, potassium).  Anti-arrhythmias – prevention:  beta-blockers. Surgical  Implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) post-resuscitation.  Catheter ablation for recurrent VT.  Prognosis  Prognosis is good if treated promptly.  Prognosis overall is based on the underlying heart conditions of the patient. Ventricular Tachycardia – Polymorphic Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is a broad complex tachycardia where there are numerous ventricular foci that lead to the polymorphic shape of QRS complexes that vary in their pattern.  Overview Key Facts  Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a broad complex tachycardia where there are numerous ventricular foci that lead to the polymorphic shape of QRS complexes that vary in their pattern.  The most common type of polymorphic VT is torsades de pointes (with a characteristic twisting of QRS complex around the baseline).  Management of stable torsades de pointes involves intravenous (IV) magnesium and correction of underlying electrolyte disturbances.  Patients with torsades de pointes may spontaneously revert back into sinus rhythm or may also progress to ventricular fibrillation. It is a life-threatening arrhythmia. Epidemiology  The exact incidence is unknown as VT tends to lead to ventricular fibrillation (VF) or overlaps with it.  25% of people presenting with a cardiac arrest are shockable rhythms (including VF and pulseless VT).  Torsades de pointes is more common in White women at any age.

DR. JAM Aetiology  Causes for bidirectional polymorphic VT:  digoxin toxicity.  Causes for torsades de pointes:  inherited  myocardial infarction  drug-induced  congenital long QT syndrome:  Romano–Ward syndrome  Jervell and Lange–Nielson syndrome.  electrolyte abnormalities:  low potassium/magnesium/calcium. Pathophysiology  Polymorphic VT is due to a ventricle repolarisation abnormality.  Torsades de pointes:  prolongation of QT interval indicates a longer time needed for myocytes to repolarise due to channelopathy affecting ion transport  this leads to premature after-depolarisations.  Clinical Presentation  Patients with polymorphic VT can present with symptoms such as light-headedness, palpitations, dizziness or sudden cardiac death. Like any other arrhythmia, there is a risk of polymorphic VT progressing to VF or cardiac arrest and one may present as unconscious. However, most episodes are short-lived and will spontaneously revert back into sinus rhythm.  Torsades de pointes can be triggered by exertion or stress.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  ventricular tachycardia – monomorphic  supraventricular tachycardia with bundle branch block  ventricular fibrillation  atrial fibrillation with pre-excitation.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Polymorphic VT is diagnosed on an ECG. Polymorphic VT used to be referred to by its French name torsades de pointes, however now torsades de pointes specifically refers to polymorphic VT with prolonged QT interval.  Torsades de pointes:  specific subset of polymorphic VT with prolonged QT interval  twisting of QRS complex – wave-like form.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Bidirectional VT:  associated with digoxin toxicity.  As it is classed as a broad-complex tachycardia the following features are present on the ECG:  broad QRS complex (>120 ms)  tachycardia (> 100 bpm)  AV dissociation  polymorphic pattern.  Polymorphic VT – torsades de pointes:  Management Non-pharmacological  Avoid stressful events.  Cardioversion.  Temporary transvenous pacing. Pharmacological  Magnesium IV is the drug of choice to terminate torsades de pointes:  1–2 g in 30–60 seconds  repeated in 5–10 minutes.  Avoid drugs that cause prolonged QTc:  anti-arrhythmic drugs:  amiodarone  sotalol

DR. JAM  procainamide.  antipsychotics:  haloperidol  antidepressants:  citalopram.  antibiotics:  erythromycin  trimethoprim.  antihistamines:  terfenadine.  antifungals:  ketoconazole  fluconazole.  medications that cause loss of potassium (diuretics):  indapamide.  Prevention of arrhythmia:  correct underlying electrolyte abnormalities – potassium supplements and magnesium supplements  beta blocker. Surgical  Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) if indicated.  Prognosis  Patients with torsades de pointes may spontaneously revert back into sinus rhythm or may also progress to ventricular fibrillation. It is a life-threatening arrhythmia.  If the cause is known and can be treated, the prognosis is good.

Cardiology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI

stem: Which one of the following antiarrhythmic agents works primarily by its action on SA and AV nodes?
explanation:
Verapamil
Calcium-channel blockers (class IV agents) act mainly on the sinoatrial (SA) and atrioventricular (AV) nodes (direct membrane effect), as these structures are almost exclusively depolarised by the slow calcium channels. They also reduce contractility of the heart – and so require caution in heart failure.

Amiodarone
Amiodarone is incorrect. Amiodarone (like sotalol) is a class III agent. Class III agents are predominantly potassium-channel inhibitors, which prolong repolarisation; this means action-potential duration is prolonged and therefore the refractory periods. They have little effect on conduction velocity. This means they are helpful in re-entrant arrhythmias.

Atenolol
Atenolol is incorrect. Atenolol and other beta blockers (class II agents) act by blocking the effects of catecholamines on β1-adrenergic receptors, which reduces sympathetic activity on the heart. By slowing conduction through the AV node they are particularly useful in controlling SVTs – but also impair theAInormal Tutor homeostatic mechanisms designed to control heart rate and contractility. Therefore, they impair the normal responses to blood loss or hypoglycaemia. In contrast, calcium-channel antagonists are less likely to do this.

stem: A 60-year-old man complains of dizziness and palpitations. He has a history of ischaemic heart disease. An electrocardiogram (ECG) shows tachycardia, broad QRS complexes, atrioventricular (AV) dissociation and the presence of capture beats. His heart rate is 140 bpm and his blood pressure is 90/50 mmHg. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Sustained ventricular tachycardia
The features described in the question are highly suggestive of sustained ventricular tachycardia. The diagnosis is by ECG which shows a tachycardia of 120 bpm or greater with three or more consecutive wide QRS complexes. A sustained ventricular tachycardia will last over 30 seconds, while an unsustained ventricular tachycardia will last less than 30 seconds and resolve spontaneously. Sustained ventricular tachycardia is almost always symptomatic.

Ventricular premature beats
Ventricular premature beats is incorrect. Broad QRS complexes may be seen in ventricular premature beats, but, following a premature beat, there is usually a compensatory pause. This condition is usually asymptomatic.

stem: A 60-year-old White man, with NYHA (New York Heart Association) class II heart failure, is taking an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and bisoprolol for his heart failure. He is also taking 50 mg of furosemide. He is generally well in himself. On direct questioning at his routine outpatient visit, he has noticed a severe deterioration in his exercise tolerance over the last year and he now sleeps in a chair downstairs because he finds it impossible to climb the stairs owing to shortness of breath. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 105/72 mmHg, pulse of 85 bpm and regular. There are bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest, and bilateral ankle swelling. Which one of the following drugs should be added to his list of medications with respect to his overall prognosis?
explanation:
Spironolactone
The European Society of Cardiology recommends the addition of spironolactone for improving the survival of patients who are in the transition from well-controlled class II to class III or IV heart failure; the mortality benefit is considerable. Given that the patient is having a worsening of symptoms despite ACE-I and beta blocker, spironolactone is the next most appropriate therapy for prognosis.

Digoxin
Digoxin is incorrect. Digoxin helps to relieve symptoms to some extent, and is more useful if the patient is in atrial fibrillation; however, there is no overt prognostic benefit with digoxin and, therefore, it is not the correct answer.
