stem: A 67-year-old Afro-Caribbean man with a history of hypertension comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review. He didn’t tolerate a calcium channel blocker due to ankle swelling, so has been commenced on indapamide as the ﬁrst intervention for his hypertension. After three months of treatment, his blood pressure (BP) is still elevated at 155/95 mmHg. His body mass index (BMI) is 33 kg/m2. His creatinine level is measured at 105 µmol/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation:
B Valsartan Treatment of hypertension is indicated in patients under the age of 80 with stage 1 hypertension (>140/90) and one of the following: target organ damage, established cardiovascular disease, renal disease, diabetes or a 10- year cardiovascular risk equivalent to 10% of greater.

The choice of initial drug treatment is different in the under-55s and the over-55s or black people of African or Caribbean origin. An angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) is ﬁrst-line treatment in the ﬁrst group, whereas a calcium-channel blocker is recommended in the latter. For the next step of treatment, angiotensin receptor blockers are preferred to ACE inhibitors in patients of Afro- Caribbean origin – for this reason valsartan is the preferred option in this case. A Amlodipine Amlodipine is contraindicated as the patient previously developed ankle swelling on a calcium antagonist. C Bendroﬂumethiazide Thiazide diuretics such as bendroﬂumethiazide are included in step three of the guidelines for management of hypertension, and should be added on top of an ACE inhibitor or ARB and calcium-channel blocker. D Atenolol Atenolol, is not recommended as a ﬁrst- or second-line antihypertensive agent, particularly in the obese population because of its association with impaired glucose tolerance. E Chlorthalidone Chlorthalidone, is a thiazide-like diuretic with a similar mechanism of action to indapamide. Since he remains hypertensive on indapamide, there would be little beneﬁt of adding another agent of the same class.

stem: A 65-year-old man, who is a known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patient, has been treated for recurrent chest infections over the last month with courses of co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin by his general practitioner (GP). On a review consultation the GP notices a quiet pan systolic murmur on auscultation and refers the patient for echocardiographic (ECHO) assessment. This shows a normal left ventricle with good function and trivial mitral regurgitation. The right ventricle is reported as at the upper limits of normal, with evidence of increased pressures and pulmonary regurgitation.
options: Amoxicillin 3 g orally prior to the procedure
Amoxicillin 1 g IV and gentamicin 120 mg IV prior to the procedure
Clindamycin 600 mg orally prior to the procedure
Amoxicillin 3 g orally prior to the procedure and 4 h following the procedure
explanation:
A No need for antibiotic prophylaxis This patient’s echocardiogram shows trivial mitral regurgitation (which is a normal ﬁnding) and pulmonary regurgitation which is secondary to elevated pulmonary pressures, most likely due to his chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Although antibiotic prophylaxis was previously indicated in cases of structural pulmonary valve disease, recent NICE guidelines (see weblink below) indicate that no antibiotic prophylaxis is required for dental procedures, stating that ‘Antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis is not recommended routinely for people undergoing dental procedures.’ B Amoxicillin 3 g orally prior to the procedure Antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer routinely recommended for dental procedures. Amoxicillin is active against Gram-positive bacteria such as Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus spp., Streptococcus spp., Streptococcus pneumoniae and Gramnegative bacteria including Escherichia coli, Haemophilus inﬂuenzae, Proteus mirabilis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Amoxicillin is also active against Helicobacter pylori but it is not effective against Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Serratia, Citrobacter and some Gram-negative aerobes. C Amoxicillin 1 g IV and gentamicin 120 mg IV prior to the procedure Antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer routinely recommended for dental procedures. Amoxicillin is active against Gram-positive bacteria such as Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus spp., Streptococcus spp., Streptococcus pneumoniae and Gramnegative bacteria including Escherichia coli, Haemophilus inﬂuenzae, Proteus mirabilis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Amoxicillin is also active against Helicobacter pylori but it is not effective against Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Serratia, Citrobacter and some Gram-negative aerobes. Gentamicin is bactericidal and is active against many strains of Gram-positive and -negative pathogens including species of Escherichia, Enterobacter, Klebsiella, Salmonella, Serratia, Shigella, Staphylococcus aureus, some Proteus and against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Gentamicin is often effective against strains of these organisms which are resistant to other antibiotics such as streptomycin, kanamycin and neomycin. Gentamicin is effective against penicillin- resistant Staphylococci, but rarely effective against Streptococci. D Clindamycin 600 mg orally prior to the procedure Antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer routinely recommended for dental procedures. Clindamycin is active against Bacteroides fragilis, P. jiroveci, Toxoplasma gondii, Clostridium, Corynebacterium acnes and Pneumocystis carinii. It is thus useful in the treatment of abdominal and pelvic abscess, respiratory tract infec-

tions including lung abscess, and skin and soft-tissue infections. E Amoxicillin 3 g orally prior to the procedure and 4 h following the procedure Antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer routinely recommended for dental procedures. Amoxicillin is active against Gram-positive bacteria such as Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus spp., Streptococcus spp., Streptococcus pneumoniae and Gramnegative bacteria including Escherichia coli, Haemophilus inﬂuenzae, Proteus mirabilis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Amoxicillin is also active against Helicobacter pylori but it is not effective against Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Serratia, Citrobacter and some Gram-negative aerobes.

stem: A 18-year-old man presents with a history of progressive cyanosis, haemoptysis, and episodes of syncope. On examination, he has a notably prominent left precordium and an ejection murmur in the second left intercostal space. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Atrial septal defect (ASD) with aortic regurgitation
explanation:
ASD with pulmonary hypertension
Here, one must consider the most common pathology in the light of clinical findings. It is unlikely that this man has an ASD and also has left-sided heart failure, otherwise his symptoms would reflect this scenario. His prominent left precordium suggests that the right ventricle is dilated and that he has increased right-sided pressures with increased turbulent flow through the pulmonary valve. He is young, so we think immediately about congenital diseases and their complications. It is important to know that haemodynamically significant ASDs can lead to pulmonary hypertension over time.

ASD with mitral stenosis
ASD with mitral stenosis is incorrect. Ostium secundum ASD in combination with rheumatic mitral stenosis (Lutembacher syndrome) can cause the same picture in advanced cases if there is pulmonary hypertension, but this is far less common.

stem: A 53-year-old woman who has had chemotherapy for metastatic breast cancer six months earlier comes to the clinic complaining of shortness of breath on exertion. Her BP is 125/78 mmHg, her pulse is 94 bpm and her apex beat is displaced to the anterior axillary line. Clinical results are given in the table below: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 119 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.0 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 190 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 160 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Cardiomegaly, increased shadowing consistent Chest X-ray with mild pulmonary oedema at both bases Which one of the following chemotherapeutic agents is most likely to be responsible for this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Doxorubicin
The clinical scenario is of a 53-year-old woman who had chemotherapy for metastatic breast cancer six months earlier. She now presents with shortness of breath, cardiomegaly (on CXR and displaced apex) and pulmonary oedema consistent with left ventricular failure. Cancer patients who are undergoing chemotherapy have an increased risk of developing cardiovascular complications. Anthracyclines and related compounds (e.g. doxorubicin, daunorubicin, idarubicin and mitoxantrone) are the most frequently implicated agents. Doxorubicin can be associated with heart failure, myocardial necrosis causing a dilated cardiomyopathy (reduced left ventricular ejection fraction) and tachyarrhythmias; Other common side effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, loss of appetite, myelosuppression, alopecia, missed menstrual periods, darkening of skin or nails, weakness, tiredness, eye redness, puffy eyelids, reddish colour to urine, tears, and sweat that may last for several days. Hypersensitivity reactions are also seen.

Docetaxel
Docetaxel is incorrect. Taxanes (eg paclitaxel and docetaxel) are the most commonly used chemotherapeutic agents. Docetaxel may be associated with arrhythmias and cardiac failure, although the likelihood is less than with doxorubicin. Other common side effects of docetaxel are anaemia, severe neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, infection, skin rash, alopecia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, weakness, pain, increased liver enzymes (bilirubin, AST, ALT, ALP), oedema, stomatitis, weight gain, myalgia, arthralgia, burning sensation, paresthesia, dysesthesia, nail depigmentation, nail hyperpigmentation, and thinning of nails. Taxane induced pneumonitis and hypersensitivity reactions are also seen.

Cisplatin
Cisplatin is incorrect. Platinum-based chemotherapies are usually associated with nerve damage (peripheral neuropathy). They are not associated with heart failure or cardiomyopathy. Other common side effects of cisplatin are nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, bone marrow depression and transient increase in liver enzymes. Hypersensitivity reactions are also seen.

Bleomycin
Bleomycin is incorrect. The most important side effect of bleomycin is interstitial pneumonitis. Bleomycin does not cause heart failure and cardiomyopathy.

Carboplatin
Carboplatin is incorrect. Carboplatin, like cisplatin is most likely to be associated with peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with a history of severe retrosternal chest pain of one day’s duration. The pain radiates to the back and left shoulder and increases with inspiration, coughing and changes in body posture. On examination, her blood pressure is 105/8 5 mmHg and her heart rate is 110 beats per minute (bpm). Her respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute. Her temperature is 38.1 °C. Her heart sounds are normal and a friction rub is heard during expiration. An ECG reveals ST segment elevation in both limb and chest leads and ST segment depression in aVR. She has a WCC of 14,000/ml, with left shift and ESR of 55 mm in the ﬁrst hour. A CXR is unremarkable. She responds well over the next few days to ibuprofen 800 mg four times per day along with colchicine and is discharged home. She presents ﬁve months later with low-grade fever and chest pain. She describes similar symptoms three months after the initial episode that responded to ibuprofen which she selfadministered. She is started on ibuprofen again and work-up for autoimmune screening is requested, which turns out to be negative. However, despite seven days therapy with ibuprofen, she experiences bouts of chest pain. What is the next step recommended in the management of this patient?
explanation:
D Colchicine Between 15 and 30% of patients with apparently idiopathic acute pericarditis may have recurrent attacks, and this is considered to be

an autoimmune phenomenon. Colchicine is useful both in acute episode and to prevent recurrence of pericarditis. B Prednisolone Prednisolone can be considered in patients who fail to respond to non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drug and colchicine therapy. It is reserved for patients who fail to respond to initial intervention because of the adverse effects of steroid therapy including weight gain, loss of bone mineral density and dysglycaemia. A Pericardial biopsy Pericardial biopsy in patients with recurrent pericarditis without effusion is unlikely to be revealing and is not needed. C Pericardectomy Pericardectomy is only indicated for recurrent pericarditis once medical interventions have failed. E Cyclosporin Cyclosporine is used in the treatment of recurrent pericarditis posttransplant, but colchicine is preferred as a ﬁrst-line agent in the non-transplant setting.

stem: A 35-year-old man who has not been subject to regular medical follow up is admitted via the Emergency department with increasing shortness of breath. On further questioning it transpires that a heart murmur was noted in childhood, but his parents refused to allow regular follow up, and over the past few months he has found it increasingly difficult to do his job as a builder. On examination his BP is 150/80 mmHg, pulse is 88/min and regular. He looks cyanosed at rest and is clubbed. There are bilateral crackles on auscultation of the chest, consistent with fluid overload. You find some old letters scanned into the computer which suggest he had a pansystolic murmur in childhood, which appears quieter / absent now. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ventricular septal defect
The clinical scenario is of a 35-year-old man with increasing shortness of breath. Because of this, he has found it increasingly difficult to do his job as a builder over the past few months. He was told about a heart murmur in childhood but has not been under regular medical follow up. On examination, his pulse = 88 bpm, regular (normal); B.P = 150/80 mmHg (high); he looks cyanosed at rest and is clubbed (cyanosis and cardiac cause of clubbing can be due to congenital cyanotic heart disease or Eisenmenger syndrome). On auscultation, the pansystolic murmur, loudest at the sternal edge (only three conditions produce a pansystolic murmur – mitral regurgitation (MR), tricuspid regurgitation (TR) and ventricular septal defect (VSD)), which is seen in childhood is not present, another feature of Eisenmenger’s. There are also bilateral basal crackles (consistent with fluid overload). The symptoms of increasing shortness of breath, untreated heart murmur in childhood, cyanosis,

stem: An 18-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department (ED) with severe chest pain that developed abruptly 30 minutes ago. She describes the pain as ‘tearing’ and says it radiates into her jaw. There is no past history of cardiovascular disease. The past history is signiﬁcant for primary amenorrhoea. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 170/110 mmHg in the right arm and 145/90 mmHg in the left. Her pulse is 120 beats per minute (bpm) and regularly regular, and she is afebrile. The patient appears in distress and you note a diastolic murmur, mufﬂed heart sounds and a raised jugular venous pressure (JVP). You also notice that the patient is of short stature and has a broad neck. An ECG is performed and reveals sinus tachycardia and widespread ST depression. A portable CXR is performed and reveals a widened mediastinum. You suspect aortic dissection. What is the likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
A Turner’s syndrome This patient ﬁts the description for Turner’s syndrome – Amenor-

rhoea, short stature and broad neck. The presenting complain of chest pain is highly suggestive of aortic dissection and is supported by the clinical ﬁndings of blood pressure difference, diastolic murmur (AR), mufﬂed heart sounds (effusion) and widened mediastinum. Turner’s syndrome is a chromosomal disorder resulting from the 45X karyotype. It is characterised by short stature, ovarian failure with primary or secondary amenorrhoea, webbed neck, cubitus valgus, a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, and aortic dissection in adulthood. Aortic dissection characteristically presents with a very abrupt onset of chest pain which differentiates it from the other differentials. The mediastinum is widened on the chest X-ray in many cases of aortic dissection. Around 2/3rds of dissections in Turner’s arise in the ascending aorta. Epidemiological data suggests that the incidence of aortic dissection is many times higher for young women with Turner’s versus age matched controls. The annual incidence is 15/100,000 years for those<20 years, and is 73-78/100,000 years for those 20-40 years of age. This is against an incidence of 6/100,000 years for those without Turner’s syndrome. C Noonan syndrome Noonan syndrome has similar external physical characteristics to Turner’s, although in females it is associated with normal fertility. It is associated with ASDs, VSDs and pulmonary stenosis. B Pseudoxanthoma elasticum PXE is a genetic condition that can cause early onset atherosclerosis. It typically causes cutaneous and ophthalmic changes which are not described in the case. It is caused by an autosomal recessive gene mutation in ABCC6 gene on chromosome 16. D Marfan syndrome Marfan’s syndrome is a connective tissue disease. Patients typically are tall and thin with long arms and legs. It is very commonly associated with aortopathy and can present with aortic dissection. E Osteogenesis imperfecta OI is a genetic disease affecting the bones. Patients will typically have short stature and blue sclera with varying involvement of their bones. This is not typically associated with cardiovascular disease.

stem: A 17-year-old man is brought to the Emergency department after collapsing whilst swimming with his girlfriend. A previous collapse from which he came round spontaneously is reported. She administered CPR and when the ambulance arrived he was found to be in VF. He was defibrillated and attained sinus rhythm. 12 lead ECG demonstrates QT prolongation and you suspect he may have congenital long-QT syndrome. Which of the following is the most likely defect?
options: Slow delayed rectifier potassium channel mutation
Rapid delayed rectifier potassium channel mutation
explanation:
Slow delayed rectifier potassium channel mutation
The clinical scenario is of a young man (17-years old) with a history of collapse while swimming. His girlfriend administered CPR and he was found to be in VF. He was defibrillated, attained sinus rhythm and 12 lead ECG demonstrated QT prolongation. He has had a previous collapse after a swimming trip from which he came around spontaneously. The history and ECG findings are very suggestive of congenital long QT syndrome. Long QT syndrome Type 1 (LQT1) is the most common type of LQTS (30-35% of all cases). The LQT1 gene is KCNQ1, which has been isolated to chromosome 11. KCNQ1 codes for the voltage-gated potassium channel KvLQT1 that is highly expressed in the heart. This is a slow delayed rectifier potassium channel mutation; hence this is the most likely mutation in this patient. It is believed that the product of the KCNQ1 gene produces an alpha subunit that interacts with other proteins (in particular, the minK beta subunit) to create the IKs ion channel, which is responsible for the delayed potassium rectifier current of the cardiac action potential.

stem: A 61-year-old man is admitted to the Cardiology Clinic after a collapse. He does not recall the circumstances surrounding the fall, but states that he has been getting chest tightness on exertion lately. This is his third such collapse in six months. He has a background of previous non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and has an ejection systolic murmur on auscultation. On examination, his lying blood pressure (BP) is 135/85 mmHg, while his standing (BP) is 133/80 mmHg. An ECHO reveals an ejection fraction of approximately 40%, moderate left ventricular (LV) systolic function, and moderate aortic stenosis (AS). An ECG is shown below: What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
D Permanent pacemaker (PPM) implantation This is a symptomatic trifascicular block, as demonstrated on the ECG. Trifascicular block is the combination of bifascicular block (right bundle branch block with either left anterior fascicular block or left posterior fascicular block) and atrioventricular node block. In symptomatic trifascicular block, where other causes are not suspected, Permanent pacemaker (PPM) implantation is required. This is particularly pertinent if complete heart block or second-degree heart block are also present. B No intervention required This is a symptomatic trifascicular block and requires a PPM; otherwise, it may lead to a fatal episode or further collapse. A Implantable cardioverter–deﬁbrillator (ICD) ICD is usually indicated in those who have had a life-threatening arrhythmia or who are at risk of such an arrhythmia, including Brugada syndrome, long QT or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. This is a symptomatic trifascicular block and requires a PPM. C Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) His history of exertional chest pain could be consistent with ischaemia (which in this patient would probably be due to his aortic stenosis), however, the ECG does not show a STEMI and there

are no signs of acute ischaemia, therefore there is no indication for PCI. E Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) While this patient has aortic stenosis, this is measured as moderate. They may eventually require a TAVI if the stenosis worsens. However, it is more likely that these collapses are secondary to trifascicular block shown on the ECG.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the clinic with shortness of breath and angina. She has a history of hypertension and type II diabetes for which she takes metformin and BD Mixed Insulin. On examination her BP is 155/92 mmHg. You notice reversed splitting of the second heart sound and bibasal crackles on auscultation of the chest consistent with cardiac failure. Which one of the following is the most likely finding on ECG?
explanation:
Left bundle-branch block
Reversed splitting of the second heart sound occurs when closure of the pulmonary valve occurs before the aortic valve. Conditions associated with reversed splitting of the second heart sound include left bundle-branch block, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and aortic stenosis. Of the options, left bundle-branch block is the most appropriate. The ECG would show a broad QRS complex (>120ms), tall R waves in the lateral leads (I, V5-6) and deep S waves in the right precordial leads (V1-3) and usually leads to left axis deviation. A fixed splitting of the second heart sound is associated with an atrial septal or ventricular septal defect.

QT prolongation
QT prolongation is incorrect. QT prolongation is a measure of delayed ventricular repolarisation and can predispose the myocardium to early after-depolarisations and subsequent re-entrant tachycardias. It does not typically produced any cardiac murmurs.

stem: A 46-year-old Asian man presented to the Cardiology outpatient clinic with breathlessness which has gradually increased over the past few weeks. He has previously underwent a coronary artery bypass graft surgery six months ago without complications and otherwise has no co-morbidities.. He had a respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min, pulse rate of 99 bpm and the jugular venous pressure (JVP) shows prominent x and y descents. There was also bibasal crepitations in both lung fields and mild pedal oedema. Auscultation of heart sounds during inspiration is associated with a drop in systolic blood pressure of 10-15 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Constrictive pericarditis
The history of recent cardiac surgery points us more towards a diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis, where fibrosis is seen around the areas of bypass grafting. Constrictive pericarditis can also follow infective pericarditis, tuberculosis and kidney disease. In the context of a known pericarditis or pericardial effusion, auscultation of heart sounds in inspiration that is associated with a drop in systolic blood pressure of >10 mmHg signifies pulsus paradoxus. This occurs when the effusion has normalised the wall pressures across all the chambers, so that the increased venous return to the right side of the heart in inspiration due to reduced intrathoracic pressure causes the septum to bulge into the left ventricle, thereby reducing stroke volume and blood pressure. This is a sign of impending circulatory collapse due to cardiac tamponade.

stem: Which one of the following patients would be best served by a permanent pacemaker (PPM)?
options: 40-year-old asymptomatic man with type I second-degree AV block and a maximum documented
40-year-old man with type II second-degree AV block and a ventricular rate of 45 bpm when awake
40-year-old man with Lyme disease with asymptomatic complete AV block
40-year-old man with chronic asymptomatic bifasicular block and first-degree AV block
40-year-old man, 3 days after suffering an acute anterior MI and having a persistent first-degree AV
explanation:
40-year-old man with type II second-degree AV block and a ventricular rate of 45 bpm when awake
and asymptomatic Type II second-degree AV block has a high chance of progressing to asystole (35%) each year, and is associated with sudden and unexpected haemodynamic instability. Consequently, urgent insertion of a PPM is appropriate even without symptoms (Class I indication). The indications for pacing can be complex and open to debate, and certainly require tailoring to the individual patient and clinical circumstances; but the 2013 ESC guidelines give clear advice and should be followed for exam questions. All five scenarios feature a 40-year old man with a persistent AV block (except one, which features a non permanent AV block).

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She is 12 weeks’ pregnant with her first child. A systolic murmur has been noted by her General Practitioner, who is concerned that she may have underlying congenital heart disease. On examination, her blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg, pulse is 65 bpm and regular. There is a systolic murmur. Echocardiogram reveals no evidence of ventricular hypertrophy or atrial dilatation, normal valves, and a small ventricular septal defect (VSD). Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention with respect to her pregnancy?
explanation:
Observation
Minor VSDs have no impact on outcomes in pregnancy, therefore, no intervention is required. Over an extended period of follow up (>10 years), around half of patients with a minor VSD have no significant problems; endocarditis is seen in around 10% of patients, and aortic regurgitation/left ventricular dilation in around 20%.

Oral nitrate
Oral nitrate is incorrect. Endogenous nitric oxide is upregulated in patients with VSD; supplementation with an oral nitrate isn’t of value in managing the condition here.

stem: A 25-year-old computer programmer suddenly develops dysphasia and right-sided weakness. He is obese with a BMI of 34 kg/m 2. You note that his left leg is swollen. His blood pressure is 155/85 mmHg, pulse is 85 bpm and regular. Which investigation would confirm the underlying cardiological diagnosis?
explanation:
Transoesophageal echocardiogram with bubble study
The patient in this scenario has had a sudden onset stroke. The ‘computer programmer’ career implies a sedentary lifestyle with the possibility of DVT. The implication is that he has had a paradoxical embolus. Patent foramen ovale: A young, otherwise healthy person who suddenly develops a stroke is likely to have a paradoxical embolism due to a patent foramen ovale (PFO) (or ostium secundum defect) PFOs are relatively common and may be present in 25–30% of the general population; however, the vast majority do not cause a problem PFOs greater than 4 mm and associated with shunting are more likely to be associated with systemic emboli. Diagnosis:

stem: You review a 26-year-old woman who attends the Cardiology Clinic with her husband. They wish to start a family, but they have been referred by their General Practitioner, as he is worried that the woman has a history of heart disease. Which one of the following cardiovascular conditions is an absolute contraindication to pregnancy?
explanation:
Primary pulmonary hypertension
Primary pulmonary hypertension rapidly worsens in pregnancy, and patients are advised not to become pregnant.

Atrial septal defect
Atrial septal defect is incorrect. Most women with an atrial septal defect can tolerate pregnancy without any problems.

Mitral valve prolapse
Mitral valve prolapse is incorrect. Increased monitoring is also recommended in patients with mitral valve prolapse, but again this is not an absolute contraindication to pregnancy.

stem: A 60-year-old woman visits her GP complaining of increasing shortness of breath. She has also suffered one fainting episode over the past month. Prior to this, she has been well without symptoms and was active. Clinical examination reveals a BP of 132/82 mmHg, and an ejection systolic murmur. ECG shows marked left ventricular hypertrophy with strain. Echocardiography shows a peak aortic valve gradient of 90 mmHg and decreased left ventricular systolic function. What is the correct management?
explanation:
Urgent aortic valve replacement (within 8 weeks)
The description is classical for aortic stenosis. This is the narrowing of the aortic valve, which is typically heard as a crescendo–descrendo murmur at the upper sternal edge. Echocardiography can interrogate severity: in the modern era, valve areas of ≤ 1 cm2 and a mean gradient over 40 mmHg (or peak flow velocity over 4 m/s) are considered severe. Gradients less than 20 mmHg are considered mild. Surgery for aortic valve replacement (AVR) is indicated in severely aortic symptomatic patients (angina, exertional breathlessness, syncope), as the risk of sudden death increases dramatically with the onset of symptoms. In patients with exertional syncope the risk of death in some series is 50% at 2 years. The risk of aortic valve surgery is < 5%. In this patient, with high-risk symptoms (syncope) and confirmed severe AS, it is appropriate to offer AVR at the earliest opportunity. Patients who are asymptomatic are typically not operated upon unless there is another indication for a cardiac operation – for example, coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG). Similarly, patients with moderate aortic stenosis who need to have CABG will often be offered simultaneous AVR, as the risk of re-do surgery at a later

stem: A 69-year-old man has been admitted to the Emergency Department with syncope. He feels hot, complains of nausea and then faints. His electrocardiogram (ECG) during the symptoms is normal. His brother suffers from adult-onset epilepsy. Which one of the following is the investigation most likely to reveal the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Tilt test
The patient is strapped to a tilt-table and tilted, head upright, at 70° for up to 45 min – blood pressure and cardiac rhythm are monitored throughout. In neurocardiogenic syncope, the patient classically maintains normal BP initially, until the sudden onset of syncope is associated with severe hypotension and bradycardia, often preceded by tachycardia. These features resolve with return to the supine posture. Some patients have a mainly vasodepressor response, with hypotension and little change in heart rate, whereas others have a marked cardioinhibitory response, with severe bradycardia or asystole of several seconds’ duration. Most patients exhibit a mixed response, and those patients with marked cardioinhibition also have a preceding vasodepressor response.

stem: A 54-year-old man suddenly develops weakness of the left side of his face and arm and difficulty in speech. This episode lasts for 15 minutes. He has a history of hypertension, which is well controlled on a calcium channel blocking agent. His brother had had a severe, disabling stroke at the age of 50. His cholesterol level is 5.8 mmol/litre. A CT scan performed the same day showed the presence of two old lacunar infarcts in the right middle cerebral artery territory. CT angiogram of the carotid system shows a 71% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery. Which one of the following factors is the strongest predictor of his being at a high risk of early recurrent stroke?
options: Presence of previous completed strokes on CT scan
explanation:
Presence of moderate carotid stenosis
This is the strongest predictor of risk from the options offered. This is a transient ischaemic attack (TIA) since the episode lasted less than 24 hours About 15–20% of patients with stroke have a preceding TIA The issue of subsequent stroke prevention is therefore paramount when managing such a ‘warning event’ The urgency of treatment of minor stroke or transient ischaemic attack should depend on the early risk of major stroke The risk of recurrent stroke during the first few days after a TIA or minor stroke is much higher than previously estimated

stem: A 72-year-old diabetic man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a 40-min history of central chest pain. The pain eases after an hour with bed rest. ECG shows mild anterior ST flattening. The troponin T level is slightly raised. What would be the optimal management of the underlying cause of his chest pain besides usual medical measures?
options: Discharge home with referral to the outpatients department
explanation:
Inpatient coronary angiography
This patient falls into the high-risk category of acute coronary syndrome, an NSTEMI; although there are insufficient data to calculate a GRACE score, it is clear that further invasive investigations are required. Patients with NSTEMI that are invasively managed had improved prognosis than those managed medically. Furthermore, although the immediate risk of death in NSTEMI is lower than that of STEMI during the initial inpatient stay, the prognosis over the next year is actually much worse. Therefore, aggressive management is appropriate, particularly when significant ECG. High-risk patients may have one or more of the following features: prolonged, ongoing (> 20 min) rest pain pulmonary oedema or angina with hypotension rest angina with dynamic ST changes > 1 mm raised troponin (I and T) age > 70 years

stem: A 17-year-old youth is brought to the GP by his mother. He was previously seen 2 weeks earlier suffering from acute pharyngitis. His teeth are in generally poor condition, but otherwise there is no previous medical history. On examination he is febrile with a temperature of 38.2 °C, and has a polyarthritis affecting his knees, ankles, wrists and elbows. He also appears to have subcutaneous nodules over his elbows, and mitral regurgitation on cardiovascular examination. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Rheumatic fever
The patient has characteristic features of rheumatic fever. Physical findings suggestive of rheumatic fever include: history of previous pharyngitis fever polyarthritis carditis (including the mitral regurgitation murmur) presence of subcutaneous extensor surface nodules. Laboratory testing suggestive of the diagnosis would include: a positive anti-streptolysin O titre (peaks at 4–5 weeks after a streptococcal throat infection)

stem: A 21-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department from a night club where he collapsed whilst dancing with his friends. He is known to have a history of Wolff–Parkinson–White (WPW) syndrome, and is awaiting electrophysiology studies with a view to ablation in the next few weeks. He has had two previous episodes of palpitations over the past year. His BP is 85/60 mmHg, with pulse 170 bpm (irregular). He has bilateral basal crackles consistent with heart failure. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.6 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 181 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ECG Fast atrial fibrillation (AF) Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Direct current (DC) cardioversion
This patient is in significant haemodynamic compromise, and therefore progression to DC cardioversion is the only appropriate next step.

Adenosine
Adenosine is incorrect. Adenosine should be avoided in AF associated with WPW because of the risk of slowing conduction outside the accessory pathway whilst having no effect on the accessory pathway itself, leading to a further increase in heart rate and worsening haemodynamic compromise

Digoxin
Digoxin is incorrect. Digoxin should be avoided in AF associated with WPW because of the risk of slowing conduction outside the accessory pathway whilst having no effect on the accessory pathway itself, leading to a further increase in heart rate and worsening haemodynamic compromise.

Flecainide
Flecainide is incorrect. Flecainide can be used in this situation providing there is no haemodynamic compromise, and would be an option if this patient had an adequate BP (although discussion with a cardiologist is advised first).

Verapamil
Verapamil is incorrect. Verapamil should be avoided in AF associated with WPW, because of the risk of slowing conduction outside the accessory pathway whilst having no effect on the accessory pathway itself, leading to a further increase in heart rate and worsening haemodynamic compromise.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents some 6 months after a Starr Edwards aortic valve replacement. He is increasingly short of breath and troubled by bilateral ankle swelling. He is currently taking furosemide 40mg, ramipril 5mg and warfarin. On examination his BP is 135/75 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular. There is an aortic murmur consistent with a prosthetic valve, bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest and pitting ankle oedema. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 89 g/l 135–175 g/l Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) 94 fl 76–98 fl White Cell Count (WCC) 8.0 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 207 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 18 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 111 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 75 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) 24 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Valve haemolysis
The clinical scenario is of a 67 year old man who presents 6 months after aortic valve replacement (Starr Edwards valve) with increasing shortness of breath and bilateral ankle swelling. He is on regular medication. On examination, pulse and blood pressure are normal (P=85 bpm, regular; B.P = 135/75 mmHg); he has an aortic murmur consistent with a prosthetic valve, bilateral basal crepitations and pitting ankle oedema. These clinical features are consistent with a diagnosis of heart failure secondary to haemolytic anaemia given the Hb and raised bilirubin with normal ALT. Out of the given options the most likely cause of hemolytic anaemia following aortic valve replacement is valve hemolysis due the prosthetic valve. Valve haemolysis is said to occur in around 30% of patients with a Starr Edwards valve. Although it rarely leads to significant anaemia (<1% cases), it seems likely in this case. Hemolytic anaemia is seen more commonly with mechanical heart valves than with bioprosthetic valves (porcine aortic valves are associated with a lower rate of haemolysis and therefore represent a potentially better choice for replacement). In patients with bioprosthetic valves, hemolysis is associated with paravalvular regurgitation or, less commonly, bioprosthetic structural degeneration. Patients usually present with anemia, heart failure, jaundice, dark urine, increasing serum LDH, and a new or changed regurgitant murmur. The peripheral smear shows variable numbers of schistocytes and smaller red cell fragments consistent with a microangiopathic process.

Dilative cardiomyopathy
Dilated cardiomyopathy is incorrect. Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is also a cause of heart failure and may lead to shortness of breath, bilateral ankle swelling and bilateral basal crepitations; however, there is nothing to suggest in the question that the patient has a history of DCM and aortic valve replacement is not a factor to cause DCM. Also DCM would not explain the blood findings of hemolytic anaemia and thus it is unlikely to be the cause of heart failure in this case.

Recurrent pulmonary emboli
Recurrent pulmonary emboli may lead to shortness of breath in a post-operative patient but it would not lead to the heart failure described in the question. A large pulmonary embolus may cause right heart failure (not left heart failure) but it is usually not seen with recurrent pulmonary emboli (which are usually small). There are no

Subacute bacterial endocarditis
Subacute bacterial endocarditis may develop in a patient with aortic valve replacement and lead to heart failure; however, it would present with fever and a pathologic murmur across the valve (in this case there is no fever and a aortic murmur which is consistent with prosthetic valve). Also subacute bacterial endocarditis would not explain the blood findings of haemolytic anaemia, thus it is unlikely to be the cause of heart failure in this case.

stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with syncope and is noted by the paramedic crew to be tachycardic and hypotensive. He is the subject of a ‘pre-alert’ because of his BP, and you check his notes on the Electronic Medical Records (EMR). He is apparently under investigation for tuberculous (TB) pericarditis. Which of the following signs would be most specific to cardiac tamponade?
explanation:
Muffled heart sounds
Beck’s triad is characteristically described as being associated with elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP), hypotension and diminished heart sounds. There are a number of other potential causes of elevated JVP and hypotension, but diminished heart sounds are more likely to be seen in cardiac tamponade.

Accentuated apex beat
Accentuated apex beat is incorrect. If anything, the apex beat is more likely to be diminishedChat by awith large effusion rather than accentuated in cardiac tamponade.

Tachycardia
Tachycardia is incorrect. There are other causes of tachycardia and it is not a consistent finding in cardiac tamponade.

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with exertional dyspnoea upon rushing upstairs or going to the local shops. She is in sinus rhythm at 80 bpm and her blood pressure is 160/80 mmHg without evidence of fluid overload. She is taking the maximum dose of an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEI) and furosemide (40 mg, once daily) for long-standing hypertension. Echocardiography confirms significantly impaired left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction, 35%). Coronary arteries and renal function are normal. Which additional medication should be considered for symptomatic and prognostic benefit?
explanation:
Bisoprolol
This woman has chronic heart failure (CHF) with compatible symptoms and objective evidence of left ventricular dysfunction at rest, as shown by reduced ejection fraction. There is overwhelming evidence for the long-term prognostic and symptomatic benefit of an ACEI in patients with CHF. In addition, clinical trials support the prognostic and symptomatic benefit of certain beta blockers in CHF patients, so this is the next appropriate therapy to start. In the UK, bisoprolol and carvedilol are the two agents licensed for use in this condition. Trials of bisoprolol and carvedilol suggest a reduction of ≈30% in mortality, particularly in patients with severe cardiac failure.

stem: An 80-year-old man presented to Accident and Emergency with gradually increasing confusion and shortness of breath. ECG showed 2:1 atrioventricular block with a ventricular rate of 40/min. In order to localise the site of the block, the physician made the patient do vagal manoeuvres, during which there were no changes in the block. He then gave 500 mcg of atropine and the conduction ratio worsened. Where is the likely site of the conduction block?
options: Unable to comment from the data given
explanation:
His–Purkinje system
Autonomic manoeuvres, such as carotid sinus massage or Valsalva, help to localise the site of block. This is because the AV node has good autonomic innervation and responds to increases in vagal tone, unlike the distal conducting system, which does not. Therefore, manoeuvres that increase vagal tone worsen an AV nodal block but not an infranodal block. In contrast, atropine improves AV nodal block (it will speed up heart rate), whereas it worsens block in the His–Purkinje system. In this case, the heart rate was unaffected by the vagal manoeuvre but worsened by atropine; therefore, the block can be located to the His–Purkinje system.

Left bundle branch
Left bundle branch is incorrect. As the block can be located to the His-Purkinje system this is not an appropriate choice.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the Emergency department with central crushing chest pain radiating down both arms. This has lasted for the past 2 hours and he is feeling faint and sweaty. On examination his BP is 90/50 mmHg, his pulse is 30/min. There are bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 301 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 12.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* Troponin 5.1 ng/ml <0.1 ng/ml ECG Complete heart block Which of the following is the most likely arterial segment to be occluded?
explanation:
Proximal right coronary
The clinical scenario is of a 54 year old man with central crushing chest pain radiating down both arms for 2 hours with light-headedness (feeling faint) and sweating (autonomic features). On examination, pulse is very low (P=30 bpm); B.P is also low (B.P = 90/50 mmHg) with bilateral basal crackles on auscultation. Blood investigations reveals high blood glucose (12.1 mmol/l) and very high troponin levels (5.1 μg/l); rest of the blood investigations are normal. ECG shows complete heart block. Proximal right coronary occlusion has the highest rate of AV block (24%) because this leads to involvement of both the AV nodal artery and the right superior descending artery – there are more chances of complete heart block with proximal RCA occlusion.

Distal right coronary
Distal right coronary artery is incorrect. Distal right coronary occlusion usually leads to first degree AV block (prolongation of the PR interval) and Mobitz type I (Wenckebach). It may also lead to complete heart block but the incidence is less than due to proximal RCA occlusion. Complete AV block (CHB) with inferior wall MI generally results from an intranodal lesion (lesion within the AV node) due to RCA occlusion. It is associated with a narrow QRS complex, and develops in a progressive fashion from first to second to third degree block. It often results in an asymptomatic bradycardia (40 to 60 beats/min) and is usually transient, resolving within 5-7 days; however in some cases RCA occlusion produces persistent complete heart block. These patients are symptomatic with a HR <40/min and usually resolve with revascularization but may require temporary/permanent pacing. Prognosis is favourable with respect to heart block associated with RCA occlusion/inferior wall MI (recovery is usual after revascularization). In contrast heart block associated with LAD occlusion/anterior wall MI carries a very poor prognosis due to the extent of the infarct.

Proximal left coronary
Proximal left anterior descending artery is incorrect. Complete heart block can be seen in massive anterior infarction, although more severe hypotension would therefore be expected.It occurs due to necrosis of the bundle branches travelling within the septum.

Circumflex
Left Circumflex artery is incorrect. Occlusion of the left circumflex artery which manifests as a lateral MI on the ECG, may affect the AV node directly in the 10% of individuals in whom it supplies the AV node and may lead to complete heart block, however this occurs much less commonly than in patients with RCA occlusion.

stem: Which one of the following is the commonest cardiovascular abnormality seen in an adult patient with Marfan syndrome?
explanation:
Aortic root dilatation
Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder that is inherited as an autosomal-dominant trait. There is considerable variation in its clinical manifestations. All of the options listed in the question could happen in Marfan syndrome, the most common feature however is aortic root dilatation: this occurs because the fibrillen gene defect means the arterial wall media is abnormal and weakened. The aortic root is exposed to the greatest pressure, making it liable to root dilatation and formation of a fusiform aortic aneurysm.

Aortic regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation is incorrect. Once aortic root dilatation occurs, there can be failure of coaptation of valve leaflets, leading to aortic regurgitation. This is not, however, the most common cardiovascular abnormality seen.

Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is incorrect. Mitral regurgitation can result from mitral valve prolapse, dilatation of a mitral valve annulus or mitral annular calcification; mitral valve prolapse is the second most frequent Chatfeature with AI in Tutor Marfans.

stem: Cardiac catheterisation is performed on a 25-year-old man with a systolic murmur but no symptoms. ECG and chest X-ray are normal. The findings are as follows (pressures mmHg): Aorta 125/70 left ventricle 120/12 Mean 8 Right ventricle 40/8 Pulmonary artery 44/14 Mean 13 Saturations (%): Aorta 97 Superior vena cava 70 Right atrium 70 Right ventricle 85 Pulmonary artery 84 What is the most likely cardiac diagnosis?
explanation:
Ventricular septal defect
Catheter data: you should be familiar with the intracardiac pressures and saturations. The accompanying figure shows typical saturations. The table shows pressures. In this case, aortic, left ventricular and right atrial pressures are normal. The right ventricular pressure is elevated and there are elevated pulmonary artery pressures. A mean pulmonary artery pressure of over 25 mmHg is consistent with pulmonary hypertension. The wedge pressure, which is an indirect measure of the left atrium pressure, is also normal. Note that wedge pressures are calculated by inflating a balloon in the small pulmonary arteries until the vessel is nearly fully occluded: the pressure-wave form then reflects the left atrium pressure, which could not otherwise be measured without puncturing the atrial septum. Normal pressure range (mmHg) Site (systolic/diastolic) Central venous pressure 3-8 Right ventricular pressure 15-30/3-8 Pulmonary artery pressure 15-25/4-12 Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (equivalent to left atrial 2-15 pressure) Left ventricular pressure 100-140/3-12

stem: A 75-year-old man with stable congestive cardiac failure presents with atrial fibrillation. He is haemodynamically stable with a ventricular rate of 72. He has a good functional state; chest X-ray shows clear lung fields. Echocardiography revealed a dilated left atrium and mild mitral regurgitation. Which drug option would be most beneficial for this patient?
explanation:
Rivaroxaban
Atrial fibrillation possesses a risk of stroke, which accumulates every year from diagnosis. Different risk calculators are available; however, for non-valvular AF, the CHA2DS2-VASc score should be used. In this case, the patient has only mild mitral regurgitation (MR) and not significant mitral stenosis; therefore the atrial fibrillation is a consequence of his age and congestive heart failure and it is appropriate to use the CHA2DS2- VASc score.Note that it is typical to observe mild MR in patients with congestive heart failure due to dilatation of the mitral annulus. He scored 3, based on his age and congestive heart failure, and therefore he should be anticoagulated. Therefore, the correct answer is rivaroxaban and not aspirin. Warfarin, apixaban, and dabigatran are possible alternatives. These newer agents do not require regular monitoring, which makes administration easier. In studies they appear to be as efficacious as warfarin with beneficial bleeding profiles; the difficulty is that there is no way of monitoring compliance because there is no readily available blood test.

stem: A 65-year-old man with stable angina complains of shortness of breath after walking two flights of stairs. He has normal left ventricular function on the echocardiogram and a positive exercise tolerance test (3 mm ST depression at stage III). Which one of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
explanation:
Atenolol
β-blocking agents are the cornerstone of the pharmacological management of chronic angina pectoris. They are well tolerated and reduce the frequency and duration of anginal episodes and improve exercise tolerance. They are also effective antihypertensive agents and prevent some arrhythmias. They act by competitively inhibiting catecholamine effects on the ß-adrenergic receptor; this reduces heart rate and improves coronary perfusion (by prolonging diastole), thereby reducing an exercise-induced rise in blood pressure and contractility. They are also associated with a positive outcome benefit.

Simvastatin
Simvastatin is incorrect. It is true patients with angina should receive statin therapy as a primary prevention strategy of myocardial infarction and death. However, Atenolol is the best first-line treatment modality of this gentleman’s angina.

stem: A 52-year-old man undergoes Bruce-protocol exercise testing 6 weeks after an uncomplicated inferior myocardial infarction. He had echocardiography before his exercise test, which demonstrated abnormal inferior wall motion. He is currently taking (all on a once-daily basis) aspirin (75 mg), simvastatin (40 mg), lisinopril (20 mg) and atenolol (25 mg). Resting heart rate is 72 bpm and blood pressure is 130/70 mmHg. He achieves 4 minutes 15 seconds, stopping secondary to chest pain and associated ST-segment depression in inferolateral leads. What would be the next stage in his management?
options: Add diltiazem and review in clinic
Increase atenolol (50 mg, once daily) and repeat the exercise test
Refer for a myocardial perfusion scan
explanation:
Refer for coronary angiography
The purpose of the exercise test post-myocardial infarction is risk stratification and patient self-confidence. That said, it is becoming used less frequently because of newer imaging methods (e.g. such as cardiac computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging). Patients who cannot undergo two stages of the Bruce protocol (< 6 minutes) are at a higher risk of adverse cardiovascular events. This youngish man has an early positive exercise test, as exemplified by symptoms and associated electrocardiographic changes. He should be referred for coronary angiography to accurately ascertain if he has prognostic disease warranting coronary artery bypass grafting (e.g. left main stem disease, proximal three-vessel disease or proximal two-vessel disease including the left anterior descending artery). Percutaneous intervention can also be considered if he has ongoing symptoms (likely in view of his symptoms upon exercise testing).

stem: A 28-year-old woman is listed for routine cardiac catheterisation. She is being investigated for probable pulmonary hypertension as she has symptoms of increased shortness of breath and probable mild right-sided heart failure, which have developed over the past 4 months. Which of the following would you expect to see on cardiac catheterisation?
explanation:
Mean pulmonary artery pressure 42 mmHg
Pulmonary hypertension is associated with MAP >25 mmHg at rest or >30 mmHg on exercise. Pulmonary hypertension is associated with symptoms of dyspnoea, tiredness, chest pain and peripheral oedema. Onset is typically gradual. Normal ranges: PULMONARY CAPILLARY WEDGE: normal mean pressure <12 mmHg PULMONARY ARTERY: normal systolic pressure <25 mmHg normal diastolic pressure <10 mmHg normal mean pressure <15 mmHg RIGHT VENTRICLE Normal systolic pressure <25 mmHg Normal diastolic pressure <5 mmHg.

stem: A 22-year-old cocaine addict presents with central crushing chest pain after apparently snorting three lines of the drug. He is pale and sweaty. His blood pressure is 180/110 mmHg. ECG shows anterior ST elevation consistent with myocardial infarction. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)
Cocaine use has recently been implicated as a cause of unstable angina. Three possible mechanisms by which cocaine induces myocardial ischaemia are: Increased myocardial oxygen demand Decreased myocardial oxygen supply secondary to vasospasm or coronary thrombosis Direct myocardial toxicity. Documented cocaine use should not be considered to rule out underlying significant coronary artery disease (CAD), as the drug may precipitate coronary vasospasm or acute myocardial infarction in the patient with atherosclerotic CAD. Where urgent angioplasty is available, this is preferable to thrombolysis as outcome studies show it to be superior.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with severe tearing back and chest pain that came on very suddenly. He has a past medical history of hypertension for which he takes ramipril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg, and he smokes 30 cigarettes per day. On examination he is in severe pain, his BP is 155/85 mmHg; he has bilateral upgoing plantars and 4/5 weakness affecting left-ankle dorsiflexion. He appears to have a pericardial rub. Which of the following features is most suggestive of dissecting aortic aneurysm?
explanation:
The pattern of pain described
The clinical scenario of an elderly man (70 years old) with severe tearing back and chest pain that came on suddenly is characteristic of dissecting aortic aneurysm. He has a history of hypertension (on medications) and he is a smoker. Both of these are risk factors for aortic dissection. On examination, his BP is high (155/85 mmHg); he has bilateral upgoing plantars, weakness of left ankle dorsiflexion (4/5) and a pericardial rub. The pattern of pain described - acute onset of severe tearing back and chest pain - is classical of aortic dissection. The symptoms and signs of aortic dissection depend upon the extent of dissection and the affected cardiovascular structures. the most common symptom is pain (occurring in 90% patients). The typical pattern is an acute onset of severe, sharp knife-like/tearing pain in the chest or/and the back that causes the patient to seek medical help within minutes to hours. The pain is described as unlike any pain experienced before. The location of the pain is typically described as anterior chest in ascending aorta (type A) dissection and back for descending aorta (type B) dissection, although this distinction isn’t invariable.

stem: A 50-year-old woman, who is already on ramipril, furosemide and bisoprolol for heart failure, decompensates and presents to the Emergency Department with pulmonary oedema. Her heart rate is 120 bpm and her blood pressure is 84/62 mmHg. She is given oxygen and diamorphine. There is marked peripheral pitting oedema. Which of the following actions is indicated in her further management?
options: Increase diuretics and maintain the current dose of beta blocker
Increase diuretics, reduce the beta blocker dose
Increase diuretics, increase the beta blocker dose
Increase diuretics, stop beta blockers permanently
Intravenous (IV) diuretics, stop beta blockers and restart beta blockers when her lungs are dry
explanation:
Intravenous (IV) diuretics, stop beta blockers and restart beta blockers when her lungs are dry
This patient has presented with pulmonary odema and hypotension on a background of heart failure. Following the latest ESC guidelines she should be given IV loop diuretics, oxygen if hypoxic, and IV opiate. As the systolic BP is below 85 mmHg, her beta blockers should be held and a non-vasodilating inotrope (such as dobutamine starting at 2.5 μg/kg per min) considered. The beta blockers should be restarted when she is stabilised and her pulmonary oedema resolved.

Increase diuretics, increase the beta blocker dose
Increase diuretics, increase the beta blocker dose is incorrect. The patient is is already hypotensive, so increasing the beta blocker would worsen this situation. The beta blocker should be stopped and a non- vasodilating inotrope should be added. It can then be restarted when the pulmonary oedema is resolved.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who is 26 weeks pregnant presents to the Emergency Department with increasing shortness of breath. She had previously asymptomatic mitral stenosis, but says her exercise tolerance has decreased significantly during the past few weeks. On examination, her BP is 143/73 mmHg, with pulse is 75/min and regular. She has a malar flush and her JVP is elevated. There is a mid to late-diastolic murmur, loudest when she is in the left lateral position. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism underlying the worsening in her symptoms?
explanation:
Increased circulating volume
Stroke volume increases by about 30% during pregnancy, heart rate by 15%. Systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure both fall during pregnancy. Balloon valvotomy is the treatment of choice for severe mitral stenosis in late pregnancy. Nitrates are also utilised for symptom relief where BP allows.

Decreased venous return
Decreased venous return is incorrect. Systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure both fall during pregnancy. Venous return is increased.

stem: As medical registrar on-call you are summoned to assist with a cardiac arrest on the coronary care unit. A 60- year-old man is being resuscitated having presented with unstable angina 3 days before. He has had three unsuccessful shocks for ventricular fibrillation. An anaesthetist is looking after his airway. He has large-bore intravenous access in his antecubital fossa. Which additional therapy would you consider first at this point?
explanation:
Amiodarone
Current recommendations for advanced life support in the UK are provided by the European Resuscitation Council and Resuscitation Council UK. In patients with refractory ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia (i.e. after three initial shocks), intravenous amiodarone should be considered. The standard dose used is a 300-mg bolus; if central access is available, then this is the desired route. If this is not the case, then large-bore peripheral access can be used.

Calcium chloride
Calcium chloride is incorrect. Calcium chloride is indicated during cardiopulmonary resuscitation if hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia or calcium channel block toxicity is present.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with cardiac-sounding chest pain which comes on at rest in the early hours of the morning. After extensive investigations (including angiography), his coronary arteries are shown to be in good condition and there is no clear ischaemic cause for his symptoms. He is a non-smoker with a normal cholesterol. A diagnosis of recurrent coronary vasospasm is made. Which of the following pharmaceutical agents would be best suited to manage his symptoms?
explanation:
Isosorbide mononitrate
The patient has recurrent coronary artery vasospasm, the symptoms of which comprise: angina-like chest pain during at rest, particularly in the early hours of the morning characteristic electrocardiographic changes during exercise testing normal coronary arteries on cardiac catheterisation inducible coronary artery spasm during the catheterisation, Nitrates are often effective in patients with this set of symptoms, as are a range of calcium antagonists (e.g. dihydropyridine, non-dihydropyridine agents).

Diazepam
Diazepam is incorrect. Benzodiazepines would not be helpful in this case.

stem: A 17-year-old male is referred to the Cardiology Clinic after a murmur was discovered at a screening medical to join the army. He has no past medical history and takes no regular medications. On physical examination; his blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg and heart rate 80 bpm. An echocardiogram revealed evidence of a small ventricular septal defect (VSD). Which of the following murmurs would you expect?
options: Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
Ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge
Late diastolic murmur at the apex
Late systolic murmur at the apex
Pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge
explanation:
Pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge
The loudness of the murmur seen in conjunction with a VSD is related to the turbulent blood flow that results from the defect. As such, a small VSD may be associated with a surprisingly loud murmur. The murmur tends to be heard throughout systole but, if the defect is in the muscular portion only, it may be shorter as the hole is closed as the muscle contracts. Moderate or worse lesions are associated with a palpable thrill.

Late diastolic murmur at the apex
Late diastolic murmur at the apex is incorrect. A late diastolic murmur starts after S2 and extends up to S1 with a crescendo configuration. This is associated with AV valve narrowing. Common causes include mitral stenosis, tricuspid stenosis, myxoma and complete heart block.

stem: A 25-year-old medical student noticed that he had a murmur when he tested his new stethoscope. On assessment in the Cardiology Clinic, he was found to have a harsh systolic murmur over his precordium, which did not change with inspiration. ECG showed features of biventricular hypertrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ventricular septal defect
Right-sided murmurs increase with inspiration (e.g. tricuspid regurgitation (TR)), whereas left-sided murmurs do not increase with inspiration. The clue to diagnosis is in the ECG finding: aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation produce left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), TR produces right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) and a ventricular septal defect (VSD) produces biventricular hypertrophy. Biventricular hypertrophy is classically described as having biphasic QRS complexes in V2–5 – which is known as the Katz Wachtel phenomenon and is classic for VSD. In other cases, biventricular hypertrophy on an ECG consists of features of LVH (S in V2 and the R in V5 > 35 mm) and features of RVH. RVH is seen as right axis deviation, tall biphasic QRS complexes in multiple leads and deep S waves in V5–6. Many VSDs are associated with a thrill (a palpable murmur) at the lower left sternal edge.

stem: A 20-year-old man is admitted for radiofrequency ablation for recurrent paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF). He has failed trials of both oral flecainide and then sotalol. On examination in the hospital, his BP is 110/70 mmHg, with pulse 65/min and regular; 12-lead ECG is unremarkable. Which of the following is the commonest site for radiofrequency ablation?
explanation:
Pulmonary veins
With regard to AF, radiofrequency ablation has a success rate approaching 85% when wide circumferential ablation is performed around the areas where pulmonary veins join with the atrium. The goal is to electrically isolate rapid electrical activity arising from within the veins, or adjacent to the pulmonary vein ostia, from the rest of the left atrium.

Superior vena cava
Superior vena cava is incorrect. Radiofrequency ablation can be used for ectopic beats that generate atrial fibrillation, but it is not the commonest site for ablation.

stem: A 30-year-old postman with hypertension who is usually in good health presents to the emergency department with sudden severe breathlessness and sweating. Chest examination reveals bilateral basal crackles. His condition improves with diamorphine and furosemide. His electrocardiogram (ECG) and cardiac enzymes are normal. He develops two further episodes of pulmonary oedema that respond well to diuretics. Investigations in the follow-up clinic reveal evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy on chest radiograph, but with a preserved ejection fraction on echocardiogram, and an elevated creatinine of 145 μmol/l. What is the most likely cause of the pulmonary oedema?
explanation:
Renal artery stenosis
The differential diagnosis of acute pulmonary oedema includes: severe left ventricular dysfunction paroxysmal arrhythmias three-vessel or left mainstem coronary disease. In the context of hypertension, the differential diagnosis also includes renal artery stenosis and phaeochromocytoma. Renal artery stenosis is more common than phaeochromocytoma in a 30-year-old and is therefore the correct answer in this scenario.

stem: A 18-year-old man attending the cardiology clinic requires dental treatment. He has a history of structural heart disease but is not taking any medication. On physical examination he is afebrile and well but a heart murmur is audible. His jugular venous pressure is not raised and there is no ankle oedema. Which one of the following is the most appropriate option for antibiotic prophylaxis?
explanation:
No action is required
NICE guidelines do not mandate use of antibiotics for prophylaxis, as there is little or no evidence to support their use. Original expert opinion supported the use of a single dose of 3 g amoxicillin, but this has now been replaced by advice suggesting use of antibiotics is the decision of the individual clinician based on benefit risk.

Amoxicillin
Amoxicillin is incorrect. Amoxicillin given as a single dose was the former intervention of choice with respect to antibiotic prophylaxis.

Erythromycin
Erythromycin is incorrect. Erythromycin is used as a prophylactic agent where it is required, in patients who are penicillin allergic.

stem: A 72-year-old man who visited his GP suffering from an infection 2 days earlier is admitted to the Emergency Department after suffering a collapse at the supermarket. His wife tells you that he suffered from a myocardial infarction some 6 years ago, but has otherwise been relatively well, taking aspirin, ramipril and atorvastatin as regular medications. She does not know the type of antibiotics he has been taking. On examination his BP is 120/71 mmHg and he is drowsy. His pulse is 70 bpm and regular. Clinical results are given in the table below: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 232 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 123 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Short runs of torsades seen on the monitor Which one of the following is the most likely causative antibiotic?
explanation:
Clarithromycin
Both macrolides, such as erythromycin and clarithromycin, and quinolones, such as ciprofloxacin and olfloxacin, may lead to QT prolongation, which pre-disposes to the development of torsades des pointes VT The problem may be exacerbated by co-administration with CYP-P450 inhibitors such as ketoconazole. Initial management involves withdrawal of the potential offending agent and electrolyte assay to exclude potential exacerbating factors such as hypomagnesaemia.

Cephalexin
Cephalexin is incorrect. Cephalosporins do not have a significant effect on the QT interval.

Co-amoxiclav
Co-amoxiclav is incorrect. Co-amoxiclav is not associated with any cardiovascular adverse events, the main concern of co-amoxiclav is cholestatic jaundice.

Metronidazole
Metronidazole is incorrect. Metronidazole is an inhibitor of aldehyde dehydrdogenase, the main concern with it’s use for many patients who take it is therefore the antibuse effect if they drink alcohol.

Oxytetracycline
Oxytetracycline is incorrect. Oxytetracycline is not associated with QT prolongation, main side effects of concern associated with tetracyclines include photosensitisation and gastro-oesophageal reflux.

stem: A 39-year-old female is admitted with pulmonary oedema, blood pressure 195/134 mmHg and fundoscopy showing retinal haemorrhages but not papilloedema. She has systemic sclerosis and asthma. Which one of the following agents would be the most appropriate immediate management?
explanation:
Intravenous sodium nitroprusside
Malignant hypertension is a rare condition characterised by very high blood pressures, with bilateral retinal haemorrhages and/or exudates or cotton wool spots, without the added requirement for papilloedema. All patients with malignant hypertension should be admitted for assessment, investigation and commencement of therapy under supervision. Malignant hypertension may be associated with hypertensive crises including LVF with pulmonary oedema, myocardial infarction (MI) and encephalopathy. In these patients rapid but controlled lowering of BP with intra-arterial BP monitoring on the ICU is indicated – aiming for a diastolic reduction of 10– 15% (or to 110 mmHg) within 1 h. A titratable IV agent is ideal, such as sodium nitroprusside

stem: A 70-year-old woman had a history of dyspnoea and palpitations for 6 months. An electrocardiogram (ECG) at that time showed atrial fibrillation. She was started on long term digoxin, diuretics and aspirin. She now presents with two short-lived episodes of altered sensation in the left face, left arm and leg. There is poor coordination of the left hand, but she tells you that this began around 6 months earlier. The echocardiogram (ECHO) was normal, as was a computed tomography (CT) head scan. Which one of the following is the most appropriate step in long-term management?
explanation:
Anticoagulation
This patient has had a stroke with a background of atrial fibrillation. Even prior to this stroke, her CHADS 2-VASc score was elevated and should have been considered for long-term anticoagulation. Anticoagulation Indications Guidelines state that anticoagulation is indicated in patients with any one of: prosthetic heart valve prior history of rheumatic heart valve disease prior history of stroke or transient ischaemic attack age older than 75 years hypertension or coronary artery disease with poor left ventricle (LV) function.

stem: A 50-year-old man with no previous cardiovascular history comes to the Emergency Department after referral from his GP. He attended the GP surgery with palpitations, which were extremely rapid and irregular. It is now 1100 h and he tells you the palpitations began at 3am after a heavy drinking session with a friend from work. There is no history of smoking, cardiovascular disease or previous myocardial infarction; he plays squash twice per week and cycles to work. On examination his BP is 125/77 mmHg and his pulse is 140 bpm, irregular. He is not in cardiac failure. Clinical results are given in the table below: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 4.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 210 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 120 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Chest X-Ray No cardiomegaly, no LVF ECG Fast atrial fibrillation, no Q waves Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy to chemically cardiovert him?
explanation:
Flecainide
In the UK the drugs most commonly used for cardioversion of atrial fibrillation are flecainide and amiodarone. Flecainide is the appropriate option in a structurally normal heart. Successful cardioversion is reported in up to 90% of patients given IV flecainide. Flecainide should be avoided in patients with a previous ischaemic cardiovascular history, as the CAST trial suggested that mortality was increased in patients given flecainide post myocardial infarction.

Adenosine
Adenosine is incorrect. Adenosine will not cardiovert atrial fibrillation as a general rule, and may be dangerous in patients with pre-excitation.

Bisoprolol
Bisoprolol is incorrect. Bisoprolol may have a role in maintaining sinus rhythm post cardioversion.

Digoxin
Digoxin is incorrect. Digoxin does not cardiovert.

Verapamil
Verapamil is incorrect. Verapamil may be employed to maintain sinus rhythm after successful electrical cardioversion.

stem: A 62-year-old man is assessed in a cardiovascular unit for angina symptoms. He has been suffering increasing chest pain over the past 3 months. Currently, he can walk only ≈35-45 metres on the flat before he starts to suffer pain. On examination, he has a blood pressure of 144/82 mmHg and a pulse of 74 bpm. There are no murmurs and his chest is clear. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 128 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 207 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 135 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l 2 mm ST depression in the anterior chest ETT leads after 4 minutes and 40 seconds Which one of the following agents is proven to impact on the risk of future cardiovascular events?
explanation:
Aspirin
Calcium antagonists, nitrates and potassium-channel activators have not been shown to affect the risk of future cardiovascular events. However, aspirin has been shown to reduce the risk of events across the spectrum of major adverse cardiac events (stroke, myocardial infarction and sudden cardiac death). Several studies have shown relative risk reductions of ≤50% for aspirin versus placebo. The CURE trial added clopidogrel to aspirin and demonstrated a further reduction in the risk of ischaemic cardiovascular events at the expense of an increased risk of bleeding events.

Diltiazem
Diltiazem is a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker. This subclass presents more negative chronotropic and inotropic effects than the dihydropyridine subclass. Also, diltiazem induces a significant reduction of atrioventricular conduction rate. Therefore, it is useful for acute and chronic treatment as well as for the prevention of atrial arrhythmias. Diltiazem is also an effective and safe antihypertensive agent. It also reduces the frequency of angina episodes and increases exercise tolerance. The extended-release formulation of diltiazem allows once-daily administration, thereby optimising antihypertensive and antianginal therapies.

GTN
GTN is effective for rapid relief of angina symptoms by vasodilatation.

Isosorbide mononitrate
Isosorbide mononitrate is a nitrate and relieves anginal symptoms by coronary vasodilatation.

Nicorandil
Nicorandil is a potassium-channel activator. It induces dilatation of coronary arteries in patients with ischaemic heart disease.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a history of previous myocardial infarctions comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review. His pre-appointment ECG reveals left bundle branch block, and sinus rhythm with a ventricular rate of 85/min. Which of the following is the most likely finding on auscultation?
explanation:
Reverse split 2nd heart sound
