Causes of reversed splitting of the 2nd heart sound include aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and ischaemic heart disease with left bundle branch block.

Ejection systolic murmur (ESM)
Ejection systolic murmur (ESM) is incorrect. ESMs are seen in aortic stenosis.

Quiet 2nd heart sound
Quiet 2nd heart sound is incorrect. A quiet 2nd heart sound is due to a poorly mobile aortic valve, such as with calcification.

stem: A 70-year-old man undergoes successful DC cardioversion (DCCV) for atrial fibrillation (AF). Which one of the following factors best predicts long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm following this procedure?
options: AF duration less than 6 months prior to cardioversion
explanation:
AF duration less than 6 months prior to cardioversion
AF with a shorter duration has the greatest chance of successful cardioversion, and maintence of sinus rhythm. After 6 months, success rates begin to fall and after 12 months, DCCV becomes unlikely to restore sinus rhythm for long periods. The presence of AF appears to trigger atrial remodelling, which creates anatomical and electrical conditions that favour further AF (leading to the expression ‘AF begets AF’).

Age over 75 years
Age over 75 years is incorrect. Age is much less important than the duration of AF.

Normal left ventricular function
Normal left ventricular function is incorrect. Cardioversion has a much higher success rate in patients with structurally normal hearts, but the left atrial size is a better predictor than left ventricular function (hence this option is false). Specifically AF is more likely to persist if LA diameter is > 5 cm. Patients with abnormal dilated ventricles are also less likely to remain in sinus rhythm.

stem: Which one of the following is a feature of coarctation of the aorta?
options: If it occurs proximal to the left subclavian artery, blood pressure elevation may be evident only in the
It is always associated with a continuous murmur
It is accompanied by a bicuspid aortic valve in around 50 to 80% of cases
It presents with the inability to augment cardiac output with exercise
Surgical correction usually resolves the hypertension
explanation:
It is accompanied by a bicuspid aortic valve in around 50 to 80% of cases
Note that the converse, the percentage of those with a bicuspid aortic valve who also have coarctation is much less, at around 20%. This is intuitive, as bicuspid aortic valve are present in between 0.5 and 2% (~1%) of the population.

If it occurs proximal to the left subclavian artery, blood pressure elevation may be evident only in the
left arm If it occurs proximal to the left subclavian artery, blood pressure elevation may be evident only in the left arm is incorrect. If it arises proximal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, blood pressure may be elevated only in the right arm.

It is always associated with a continuous murmur
It is always associated with a continuous murmur is incorrect. A continuous murmur may only be heard if the obstruction is severe.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a history of intermittent light-headedness. Clinical examination and 12- lead ECG are normal. Which one of the following, if present on a 24-h Holter ECG tracing, would be the most clinically important?
options: Heart rates of 40 bpm during sleep
explanation:
Supraventricular tachycardia
All the answers listed are common findings on Holter monitors. In this case, given the presentation of intermittent light-headedness – then supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) carries the most clinical significance. Diagnosis of the underlying cause of the SVT will be based on the presence or absence of P-waves and P-wave morphology. Patients can be taught valsalva exercises or carotid sinus massage to avert SVTs at home. Those who present in the Emergency Department should be given adenosine for acute cardioversion to sinus rhythm. Longer term management may require beta blockers to suppress episodes. Flecainide or sotalol may also be considered for prophylaxis.

stem: A 57-year-old man developed central crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm accompanied by sweating and syncope. He had a past medical history of hypertension and was a smoker. His wife drove him to the hospital but unfortunately whilst she was parking the car he suffered a cardiac arrest and died. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his cardiac arrest?
explanation:
Ventricular fibrillation
By far the commonest cause of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest is ventricular fibrillation. The strategy of early defibrillation and placement of automated defibrillators in public places is designed to minimise time to defibrillation and maximise chances of successful resuscitation.

Acute ventricular septal defect (VSD)
Acute ventricular septal defect (VSD) is incorrect. Acute VSD is less likely to occur in the immediate period of a myocardial infarction, and is usually seen a few days after the initial insult.

Cardiac tamponade
Cardiac tamponade is incorrect. Cardiac tamponade is less likely to occur in the immediate period of a myocardial infarction, and is usually seen a few days after the initial insult.

stem: The epsilon potential is seen on the ECG of patients with which one of the following?
explanation:
Right ventricular dysplasia
Epsilon potentials are only seen in arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), also called right ventricular dysplasia. They are not present in the other conditions and, as such, the remaining options are false. The figure below shows an epsilon wave.  Right ventricular dysplasia The epsilon potential is a marker of right-ventricular conduction delay, and appears as a sharp deflection or blip after termination of the QRS complex during the ST segment or upstroke of the T wave. Sometimes the blip can be buried in the end of the QRS It is seen in the right ventricular leads, V1 and V2 Fontaine named the waves ‘epsilon’ since epsilon follows delta in the Greek alphabet

stem: You are asked to see a 67-year-old man who has been admitted overnight following a road traffic accident. He sustained extensive bruising to his chest from the steering wheel. The nurses are concerned as he has become hypotensive and tachycardic. There is a history of a previous inferior myocardial infarction some 7 years ago, but nil else of note. On examination his BP is 90/50 mmHg, pulse is 95/min and regular. He looks peripherally shut down. There are muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus. Investigations – arterial blood gas - reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value pH 7.29 7.35–7.45 pO 2 11.9 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa pCO 2 6.1 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa ECG Widespread anterior T wave inversion Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cardiac tamponade
The clinical scenario is of a 67 years old man who had a road traffic accident with steering wheel injury and became hypotensive (B.P = 90/50 mmHg), tachycardic (P = 95 bpm, regular) and peripherally shut down (poor peripheral perfusion). He has a past history of inferior wall MI 7 years ago. On examination, there are muffled

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with crushing pain in the centre of the chest radiating to the left arm. He has a history of type-II diabetes mellitus (for which he takes metformin) and angina (for which he takes bisoprolol) for symptom control. From his physical examination and electrocardiogram (ECG) findings you suspect a right ventricular myocardial infarction. Right ventricular myocardial infarction is characterised by which one of the following?
options: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF
Occlusion of the left coronary artery
A rise in systolic blood pressure
explanation:
ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF
Usually right ventricular myocardial infarction occurs in association with an inferior-wall, left ventricular infarction, as revealed by an ECG.

Marked pulmonary vascular congestion
Marked pulmonary vascular congestion is incorrect. Characteristic clinical features include low cardiac-output syndrome with jugular venous distension, but no pulmonary vascular congestion. Therefore, marked pulmonary vascular congestion is incorrect.

stem: Which one of the following conditions is most likely to produce a wide, relatively fixed split of S2?
options: Right bundle-branch block with heart failure
explanation:
Right bundle-branch block with heart failure
In a normal adult, S2 is split during inspiration, and synchronous during expiration. This is because during inspiration there is increased venous return to the right heart, which delays the closure of the pulmonary valve (P2) relative to the aortic valve (A2). A wide, fixed split of S2 is typically associated with an atrial septal defect, but this is not one of the options here. You are therefore required understand the underlying physiology and consider if these other causes or combinations can cause this phenomenon. In this case, right bundle-branch block widens the split, and heart failure makes the split fixed. Heart failure can reduce the phasic changes in ventricular volume with ventilation due to shallow breathing with congested lungs and hence ‘fixes’ the split.

Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome
Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome is incorrect. In Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome and other causes of electrical delay of left ventricular conduction, including left bundle-branch block, there is a narrowly split S2 (ie A2 and P2 become closer together).

stem: A 45-year-old man with previously diagnosed type II diabetes presents to the Emergency Department with severe central chest pain, nausea and sweating. He was riding his bike in an attempt to lose weight when the chest pain began 25 minutes ago. He also smokes 15 cigarettes per day and is hypertensive, managed with ramipril and amlodipine. On examination, his BP is 155/95 mmHg, he is pale, sweaty and anxious. He has been given 300 mg of aspirin by a passer-by. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 132 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 209 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 17.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* ECG Inferior ST elevation Which one of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Percutaneous coronary intervention
Studies have shown that in patients with acute STEMI, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is superior to thrombolysis. Therefore, PCI is recommended here above both streptokinase and alteplase. Percutaneous coronary intervention should be offered as the preferred coronary reperfusion strategy for people with acute STEMI if presentation is within 12 hours of onset of symptoms and primary PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time when fibrinolysis could have been given.

Low molecular-weight heparin
Low molecular-weight heparin is incorrect. Unfractionated or low molecular weight heparin is offered to people with acute STEMI who are undergoing percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty and have been treated with prasugrel or ticagrelor. However, in this question the most appropriate and definitive treatment is early percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty.

Alteplase
Alteplase is incorrect. First line treatment for patients presenting with evidence of acute STEMI should be managed percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA), with patients presenting with a history cocaine abuse treated in the same way. Recombinant tissue plaminogen activators (rtPA) for example Alteplase is offered to patients with acute STEMI presenting within 12 hours of symptoms if primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of the time when fibrinolysis could have been given.

Streptokinase
Streptokinase is incorrect. Streptokinase is a fibrinolytic used for the treatment of acute STEMI if percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of the time when fibrinolysis could have been given. Therefore, percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty is the most appropriate way of managing this patient in this scenario.

Abciximab
Abciximab is incorrect. Abciximab is a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor and guidelines indicated it should not be offered before arrival to the catheter laboratory to people with acute STEMI for whom percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty is planned. The American Heart Association guidelines endorse their use in a clinically appropriate situation despite the fact that no randomised controlled trial evidence exists (circ.ahajournals.org (

stem: Which one of the following statements is true regarding pulsus alternans?
options: It is found in beriberi heart disease
It can be found in association with a third heart sound
It is found in patients with a small pericardial effusion
explanation:
It can be found in association with a third heart sound
Pulsus alternans is found in patients with acute left ventricular failure, and therefore may be found in association with a third heart sound. It occurs only in low output states. Pulsus alternans: Pulsus alternans is found in patients with acute left ventricular failure Alternate weak and strong pulses occur, which are regularly placed A pathological third heart sound is usually associated The condition may be associated with heart failure or pericarditis, for example, but is not usually seen in association with pericardial effusion Beriberi heart disease is a high cardiac output state. It is associated with long QT, T-wave inversion and low voltage complexes. Electrical alternans: Electrical alternans is diagnosed electrocardiographically The amplitude of QRS complexes varies alternately

stem: A 32 year old man presents with a two day history of severe breathlessness, fever and malaise. He also describes extreme fatigue, and a cough productive of frothy sputum. He is an intravenous drug user. On examination, his temperature is 38.9ºC, blood pressure is 126/54 mmHg, and heart rate is 98bpm. He has multiple splinter haemorrhages, and a loud diastolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. Auscultation of his chest reveals crepitations to the midzones bilaterally. There is 2cm splenomegaly. Urine dipstick demonstrates haematuria. Investigations: Blood culture Gram positive cocci What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of endocarditis, and is the most common cause of acute endocarditis and endocarditis associated with intravenous drug abuse. This patient is an intravenous drug user and presents with acute endocarditis; a blood culture has isolated Gram positive cocci: all of which are consistent with Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis. Therefore the most likely causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus.

stem: A 56-year-old man is referred to the outpatient clinic for review. He has a history of hypercholesterolaemia and a myocardial infarction 2 years previously. His blood pressure is 144/82mmHg and the remainder of the examination is unremarkable. Investigations: Fasting lipid profile: Result Normal Value Cholesterol 6.4 mmol/l <5.2 mmol/l Non-HDL cholesterol 4.1 mmol/l <3.36 mmol/l HDL cholesterol 1.4 mmol/l >1.0 mmol/l Triglycerides 3.9 mmol/l 0–1.5 mmol/l Which of the following increase HDL cholesterol levels?
explanation:
Alcohol
Alcohol, through an unknown mechanism, does increase levels of HDL cholesterol and this is probably at least partly why moderate alcohol intake is protective against cardiovascular disease. Of course, increased alcohol intake comes with other risks that may outweigh its benefits in the prevention of cardiovascular disease.

stem: A 63-year-old man with known chronic heart failure is admitted with symptoms at rest. Examination reveals pitting oedema to his knees, elevated jugular venous pressure, and basal crepitations. He is in sinus rhythm at 80 bpm and his blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg. Current medication is bisoprolol (10 mg, once daily), frusemide (80 mg, once daily) and ramipril (2.5 mg, twice daily). Blood tests reveal a sodium concentration of 133 mmol/l, potassium 4.4 mmol/l and creatinine of 169 μmol/l. The admitting doctor commences him on frusemide (80 mg, twice daily, iv) and increases his ramipril to 5 mg (twice daily). When you review him the following day, which other drug would be most appropriate to include?
explanation:
Spironolactone (25 mg, once daily)
This man has decompensated congestive heart failure (CHF) with symptoms at rest (New York Heart Association class IV). Examination has revealed significant fluid retention. The initial management plan of changing to frusemide (iv) is sensible because coexistent gut-wall oedema is likely to impinge oral absorption, and increasing the dose of ramipril (a vasodilator) is also sensible. The aldosterone antagonist spironolactone has been shown to improve the prevalence of mortality, symptoms, and hospitalisation in patients with severe CHF already on conventional treatment. Benefits are in addition to its diuretic effect because aldosterone itself has adverse effects on the structure and function of the myocardium. Careful monitoring of renal function and biochemistry is important in these patients.

stem: A 61-year-old man is admitted to the clinic with central crushing chest pain which radiates to his left arm. He says this began approximately 30 min ago, and was accompanied by very rapid palpitations and a feeling of light headedness. He has a history of smoking 40 cigarettes per day, and has known peripheral arterial disease. On examination his BP is 90/60 mmHg, his pulse appears to be > 150 bpm measured by carotid palpation. He has bilateral crackles on auscultation of the chest consistent with heart failure. You arrange an ECG. Which one of the following findings would be most consistent with a diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia?
options: RS duration > 80 milliseconds in any precordial lead
Ventriculoatrial dissociation in any of the 12 leads
explanation:
Ventriculoatrial dissociation in any of the 12 leads
The clinical scenario is of an elderly gentleman (61 years old) with central crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm for the past 30 minutes. This history is typical for a cardiac event and the most likely diagnosis is myocardial infarction. The chest pain is associated with very rapid palpitations and a feeling of light- headedness. On examination the B.P is low = 90/60 mmHg and pulse is rapid (>150 bpm). This indicates likely VT secondary to the myocardial infarction (arrhythmias are a common complication of MI and can be the presenting feature in some patients). The finding on ECG that would be most consistent with a diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia (VT) would be ventriculoatrial dissociation in any of the 12 leads.

Left bundle-branch block
Left bundle-branch block is incorrect. This may be long standing, and not necessarily indicative of ventricular tachycardia (there is still potential for it to be PSVT with aberrant conduction).

stem: You are working in the chemical pathology laboratory and receive a sample request for analysis of BNP. You do not have any clinical details on the form apart from ‘chest pain’. You plan to ring the SHO who requested the test for further details. In which one of the following situations is BNP most likely to be normal?
explanation:
Unstable angina
B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is secreted in response to raised intra-cardiac pressures, primarily owing to volume distension, and leads to increased sodium excretion and decreased systemic vascular resistance.

Acute mitral valve rupture
Acute mitral valve rupture is incorrect. Acute mitral valve rupture may result in volume distension, leading to elevated levels of BNP.

Pulmonary embolus
Pulmonary embolus is incorrect. Large pulmonary embolus produces raised right-sided cardiac pressures and thus may lead to elevated BNP.

stem: A 67-year-old man attends the Cardiology Clinic. He has been suffering some angina-type chest pain on going out in the cold air and is worried that he might have coronary artery disease. There is a past medical history of smoking 20 cigarettes per day and hypertension, which is managed with ramipril 10 mg daily. His GP has sent an ECG, which appears to show that he is in left bundle-branch block. Which one of the following would you expect to hear on auscultation?
options: Loud first heart sound, normal second heart sound
Loud first heart sound, reversed splitting of the second heart sound
Soft first heart sound, fixed splitting of the second heart sound
Soft first heart sound, normal second heart sound
Soft first heart sound, reversed splitting of the second heart sound
explanation:
Soft first heart sound, reversed splitting of the second heart sound
Left bundle-branch block (LBBB) results in the left ventricle depolarising from cell-to-cell conduction via the right ventricle, rather than via the normal pathway. This results in reversed splitting of the second heart sound, in other words split in expiration and single in inspiration due to delayed closure of the aortic valve due to the delayed depolarisation. Additionally the first heart sound tends to be softer than usual. Left bundle-branch block in this age group is most likely to be ischaemic in origin, hence his chest pain almost certainly warrants further investigation, especially given his history of smoking and hypertension.

stem: A 26-year-old woman attends her GP for an insurance medical. Her previous medical history is unremarkable. On examination, her BMI is 21, blood pressure is 105/62 mmHg, and auscultation of the heart reveals a mid systolic click and a late systolic murmur at the apex, which is accentuated in the standing position. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Mitral valve prolapse
The picture best fits with mitral valve prolapse. The other conditions have other features not present here. Mitral valve prolapse Mitral valve prolapse is the posterior bulging of leaflets of the mitral valve in systole. Mitral valve prolapse is thought to be present in around 4% of the population. Clinically, patients with mitral valve prolapse are often young females with a narrow anteroposterior (AP) chest diameter, low body weight and low/normal blood pressure (all of which are present in this case). Epidemiology Increased incidence is associated with: autoimmune thyroid disease Ehlers–Danlos syndrome Marfan syndrome pseudoxanthoma elasticum

stem: A 52-year-old woman who has been treated for many years with lithium for bipolar disorder presents to the clinic with hypertension. Her psychiatric disease has been stable for many years and she is reluctant to alter/discontinue her therapy. Her BP is 158/95 mmHg, pulse is 80/min and regular and her BMI is 35. A recent creatinine is 122 micromol/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice of anti-hypertensive?
explanation:
Amlodipine
Amlodipine is the most appropriate choice of anti-hypertensive from the list available, although calcium antagonists may be associated with symptoms of neurotoxicity and patients should be monitored after therapy is initiated.

Atenolol
Atenolol is incorrect. Atenolol is not a first or second-line anti-hypertensive, and in obese patients AI be may Tutor associated with a worsening in insulin resistance.

Bendroflumethiazide
Bendroflumethiazide is incorrect. Bendroflumethiazide can result in water retention and lithium intoxication when used in conjunction with lithium.

stem: A 61-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with central crushing chest pain radiating down his left arm. He is sweating and tachycardic and has vomited twice during the ambulance journey. There is a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension, for which he takes multiple medications. On examination his BP is 115/80 mmHg, with pulse 95/min and regular. There are bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest. Electrocardiogram (ECG) shows ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6.. Which of the following is the most likely site of the underlying lesion?
explanation:
Left circumflex artery (LCX)
The pattern of ECG changes seen in LCX occlusion fits with a lateral MI. The presence of ST-segment elevation in lead II, which is equal to that of lead III, especially when combined with ST-depression in leads V1 to V3 or ST-elevation in leads I and aVL, is a useful but not absolute predictor of a left circumflex coronary artery occlusion; these findings may also be seen in distal occlusion of a dominant right coronary artery. Localisation ST elevation Reciprocal ST depression Coronary artery Anterior MI V1–V6 None LAD V1–V4, disappearance of LAD-septal Septal MI None septum Q in leads V5,V6 branches

stem: A 62-year-old man with two previous myocardial infarctions and a history of left ventricular failure, controlled with ramipril and furosemide, presents to his General Practitioner with palpitations. He also has a history of myasthenia gravis, which is stable on long-term mycophenolate. On examination, his blood pressure is 100/72 mmHg, and his pulse is 95 bpm in atrial fibrillation. He also has bibasal crackles, consistent with heart failure. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.4 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 234 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Echocardiogram shows dilated left atrium and left ventricle. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate agent to control his atrial fibrillation?
explanation:
Digoxin
This patient presents with atrial fibrillation (AF), a rapid ventricular response and left ventricular failure. The history of previous myocardial infarction and a dilated left atrium fits with chronic AF. Successful cardioversion is therefore unlikely and rate control with digoxin is a more reasonable aim. Monotherapy with a beta blocker or a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker, such as diltiazem, should be prescribed in the first instance; as such, a combination of any two of digoxin, diltiazem or bisoprolol should be used. In this case, both diltiazem (due to heart failure) and bisoprolol (due to myasthenia gravis) make digoxin the best option.

Bisoprolol
Although beta blockers are used in rate control of atrial fibrillation, they can exacerbate myasthenia gravis and should not be used.

Diltiazem
Diltiazem is a cardioselective calcium channel antagonist and is significantly negatively inotropic. Therefore, it is likely to worsen cardiac failure.

Ivabradine
Ivabradine is an option to control heart rate in heart failure and angina. It can however, worsen or precipitate atrial fibrillation.

Verapamil
Like diltiazem, verapamil is a cardioselective calcium channel antagonist. It runs the risk of significantly worsening cardiac failure in this situation.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is admitted with chest pain and breathlessness of 12 hours duration. She has a past history of hypertension controlled with ramipril and brittle asthma, for which she has previously been admitted to ITU. She has suffered an inferior myocardial infarction some two years earlier and has been diagnosed with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) on echocardiography since then. On examination, her heart rate is 170 bpm and her blood pressure is 125/72 mmHg. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. There is mild wheeze throughout her chest, with crackles at both lung bases. Low molecular weight heparin is administered. What is the next step in stabilising her?
explanation:
Administration of digoxin
In a patient experiencing atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response who also has a reduced ejection fraction, digoxin would be the preferred choice in the context of a brittle asthmatic. Digoxin is positively inotropic and would thus help the ejection fraction with both rate control (allowing greater diastolic filling) and a positive inotropic effect.

Asynchronous cardioversion
Asynchronous cardioversion is incorrect. DC cardioversion should always be considered for haemodynamically unstable patients. However, not only is this patient stable, but the option states ‘asynchronous’,which would risk giving the shock during a T-wave; ‘R on T’ phenomena will trigger polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Only shocks in cardiac arrest for ventricular fibrillation should be asynchronous; all other shocks should be synchronous.

stem: A 42-year-old Afro-Caribbean man sustains a myocardial infarction (MI); he is discharged from hospital 4 days later. His medications consist of aspirin, clopidogrel, simvastatin, ramipril and a β-blocker. A month later, he has transient mild proximal muscle tenderness and blood tests by his General Practitioner show a CK level of 400 U/l. His simvastatin is stopped immediately, his symptoms resolve by the following day but 6 months later his CK is 415 U/l. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the high CK when he was reviewed in outpatients?
explanation:
Racial variant
Serum creatinine kinase (CK) activity in Afro-Caribbean people is often up to three times the upper limit of normal for White populations. The underlying genetic basis for raised baseline CK is being slowly elucidated, with polymorphisms in the CKM and LILRB5 genes associated with higher baseline levels.It would seem this patients baseline CK is around 400 U/l.

Heavy exercise
Heavy exercise is incorrect. Although this may increase CK, again the value here at 1 month is within this patient’s baseline range.

stem: A 47-year-old man presents with a history of numerous myocardial infarctions (MIs) resulting in heart failure and is on aspirin after an acute MI. Which one of the following is most likely to prolong his survival?
explanation:
Ramipril
In practice, a number of these interventions would be commenced together, but as the question asks specifically for one intervention, the correct answer is as stated ramipril. After a patient has had a myocardial infarction (MI), it is imperative to consider all modifiable risk factors to lower the risk of further vascular events. Non-pharmacological interventions The most important intervention is to stop smoking; after just 1 year there is a significant drop in the risk of MI. Weight loss in an obese individual will reduce co-morbidity but has not been shown to prolong survival. It would be ethically impossible to arrange randomised trials of smoking cessation or weight loss, so such interventions have to rely on epidemiological evidence to judge the outcome. Pharmacological interventions

stem: A 30-year-old woman is routinely seen by her GP 24 weeks into her first pregnancy. She is well, without adverse symptoms. Her blood pressure is 150/96 mmHg. Her baseline blood pressure at booking was 136/84 mmHg. No other abnormalities are found. What drug therapy would you prescribe?
explanation:
Labetalol
Hypertension in pregnancy Hypertension in pregnancy is defined as a blood pressure > 140/90 mmHg or a rise of 25 mmHg of systolic and/or 15 mmHg of diastolic pressure above baseline. It is seen in around 10% of all pregnancies. Gestational hypertension is more common than pre-eclampsia, which is associated with maternal organ dysfunction; to make the diagnosis of pre-eclampsia there must also be proteinuria (> 300 mg on a 24-hour collection). This can only be treated by delivery of the baby if the timing allows. Treatment First-line agents, proven to be safe in pregnancy, include: labetalol – this is because it has a long track record of safety methyldopa.

stem: A 50-year-old professor of economics presents with a 6-week history of progressive breathlessness and bilateral ankle swelling. The ECG shows inverted p in V1 and partial LBBB. Echocardiography confirms dilated cardiomyopathy. Which one of the following statements is true?
options: There is no relevance of history of alcohol abuse
A family history of a similar problem is unrelated
Past cytotoxic drug therapy is relevant
Viral illness in the past is unrelated
History of pulmonary tuberculosis in the past is relevant
explanation:
Past cytotoxic drug therapy is relevant
Chemotherapy agents from the anthracycline class (such as doxorubicin), and trastuzumab (Herceptin) are cardiotoxic and impair or cause myocardial dysfunction by interfering with cardiomyocyte function. ECG changes – with a broadening of the QRS complex, arrhythmias and overt heart failure – can occur. In the majority of cases of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), no definitive cause can be found (idiopathic). DCM is characterised by dilatation and impaired systolic function of the left and/or right ventricle. Aetiology The aetiology is idiopathic in the majority of cases DCM is familial (autosomal dominant) in at least 20% of cases and a role of autoimmunity is proposed in the pathogenesis of this disease About 30–40% of patients with DCM have organ-specific antibodies and these may become negative with disease progression There is an association with viral (coxsackievirus or HIV) infection, which may be immune-related.

stem: A 32-year-old man is admitted with a syncopal episode. He collapsed with palpitations whilst at the local pub with friends, having celebrated completing a marathon. He is usually fit and well, and completed the marathon in under 4 h. On examination, his BP is 122/72 mmHg, pulse is 160/bpm and regular. His chest is clear. Arterial blood gas reveals normal U&Es. Carotid sinus massage and the Valsalva manoeuvre fail in converting to sinus rhythm. ECG reveals paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
IV adenosine
IV adenosine has a rapid onset, is short acting and blocks conduction through the AV node. In this situation, it is preferred to verapamil as a first line option because of its short half-life; therefore, there is no risk of prolonged depression of left ventricle (LV) function.

DC cardioversion
DC cardioversion is incorrect. DC cardioversion would be considered where the patient is unstable.

IV amiodarone
IV amiodarone is incorrect. Amiodarone is indicated for atrial fibrillation (AF) where there is a history of previous heart disease.

stem: A 30-year-old man is being investigated for hypertension. A combination of BPs estimated by colour flow Doppler and measured values are listed in the table below: LV 200/10 mmHg Ascending aorta 200/70 mmHg Right arm 190/70 mmHg Right femoral artery 110/70 mmHg Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Coarctation of aorta
The clinical scenario is of a young man (30 years old) with hypertension. He has differential blood pressure in the right arm and leg (lower blood pressure in the leg). Normally the blood pressure in the lower limbs is 10-20 mmHg greater than that in the upper limbs. The findings of reduced systolic blood pressure in the lower extremities compared with upper extremities would be typical for a diagnosis of coarctation of the aorta. It also leads to a delay between the radial and femoral pulses (radio-femoral delay). In this clinical scenario, cardiac catheterisation ± MRI scanning is the next most appropriate next step in further characterising the pressure gradient across the coarctation.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the clinic with increasing shortness of breath. He has a history of smoking 10 cigarettes per day and hypertension for which he takes ramipril 10 mg daily. On examination his BP is 152/87 mmHg, his pulse is 75 bpm and there is reversed splitting of the second heart sound. There are no signs of cardiac failure. Which one of the following is the most likely finding?
explanation:
Left bundle-branch block
Reversed splitting of the second heart sound occurs when the sound from the closure of the pulmonary valve occurs prior to that from the closure of the aortic valve. Causes include: aortic stenosis, left bundle-branch block and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. Of these options, left bundle-branch block is the correct choice.

Ventricular septal defect
Ventricular septal defect is incorrect. A ventricular septal defect can result in the aortic valve closure occurs before the pulmonary, therefore causing fixed splitting of the second heart sound which doesn’t vary with inspiration.

stem: A 26-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department after a road traffic collision. His ECG shows ST segment elevation in leads V2–V5. Which one of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Myocardial infarction secondary to thrombosis of RCA
explanation:
Myocardial contusion
Road traffic injuries are a common cause of blunt chest trauma. This most commonly causes myocardial contusion. Chest trauma can also cause: myocardial rupture aortic rupture valve injury lacerations or thrombosis of the coronary arteries – these are fairly rare All of these are rapidly fatal unless immediate treatment is given. Myocardial contusion will cause chest pain and cardiac failure due to acute impairment. Patients may have a pericardial rub, a gallop (S3) and have ST changes anteriorly. Heart block and RBBB may also be present. Urgent echocardiography should be performed. A localised pericariditis is unlikely. Localised injury to the sino-atrial or atrio-ventricular nodes may cause arrhythmias.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of chest pain. She has been unwell with an influenza-like illness for the last week. The ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation in the inferior, anterior and lateral leads. Which one of these ECG changes would you expect to see in the next week or two?
options: Development of deep Q waves in all leads
ST depression in inferior and lateral leads
Tall and peaked T waves in all leads
Loss of R waves in all leads
explanation:
T-wave inversion in all leads
To answer this question correctly requires you to recognise that the patient has pericarditis. The patient is young and unlikely to have ischaemic heart disease. The history of recent influenza is a predisposing factor for pericarditis. The presence of concave ST-segment change in multiple coronary territories is also strongly suggestive of pericarditis. Interpreting an ECG: The ECG changes in acute pericarditis consist of ST elevation with concavity upward in all leads facing the epicardial surface, ie anterior, inferior and lateral is the correct answer Only ‘cavity’ leads aVR, V1 and, rarely, V2 show ST depression This is followed by the return of ST segments to baseline and flat or inverted T waves Without the loss of R waves or development of Q waves

stem: A 74-year-old man comes to the Cardiology Clinic for assessment of his aortic stenosis. He had echocardiogram some 3 years earlier, and the decision at that stage was not to move to surgery. Which of the following is the best clinical marker of aortic stenosis severity?
options: Increasing loudness of the second heart sound
Quietening of the second heart sound
explanation:
Quietening of the second heart sound
Severe aortic stenosis is associated with a quiet or even absent second sound.

Third heart sound
Third heart sound is incorrect. A third heart sound is not specifically associated with aortic stenosis, but is found in left ventricular failure.

Increasing loudness of the second heart sound
Increasing loudness of the second heart sound is incorrect. A loud second heart sound is more usually seen in aortic sclerosis rather than aortic stenosis.

stem: A 57-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease, and a recent transient ischaemic attack, is prescribed clopidogrel. How would the mechanism of action of this drug be best described?
explanation:
Blocks ADP receptors
Clopidogrel blocks platelet adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptors, while aspirin blocks thromboxane production. Aspirin and ADP-receptor antagonists such as clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor have complementary actions on platelets, leading to effective inhibition. This is important in ACS and when performing angioplasty. The figure shows the sites of action of different antiplatelet drugs.

stem: A 40-year-old woman has a moderate VSD. Before undergoing which of the following procedures will she need antibiotic prophylaxis?
explanation:
Permanent pacemaker insertion
NICE guidance for the use of antibiotic prophylaxis changed in 2008. Prior to this, patients at risk of endocarditis were given antibiotics prior to a wide variety of procedures, including dental work and bronchoscopy. In the 2008 guidance, people with the following conditions were identified as being at high risk of endocarditis: acquired valvular heart disease with stenosis or regurgitation valve replacement structural congenital heart disease, including surgically corrected or palliated structural conditions, but excluding isolated atrial septal defect, fully repaired ventricular septal defect or fully repaired patent ductus arteriosus, and closure devices that are judged to be endothelialised previous infective endocarditis hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis was no longer recommended for: dental procedures

stem: A 25-year-old woman is seen in the outpatients department and found to have a loud first heart sound, an early diastole sound, followed by a mid-diastolic murmur. She tells you that when she was a child, she had a non- specific illness which her doctor at the time thought may be rheumatic fever, but which was never proven by biochemical testing. What is the likely diagnosis?
options: Mitral stenosis with a fourth heart sound
explanation:
Mitral stenosis with mobile leaflets
There is a loud first heart sound and, if an opening ‘snap’ is heard, this indicates that the mitral valve is mobile (‘mobile leaflets’). The snap occurs if the superior systolic bowing of the anterior mitral valve leaflet is reversed rapidly towards the left ventricle in early diastole, owing to the high left atrial pressure.

Mitral stenosis with a fourth heart sound
Mitral stenosis with a fourth heart sound is incorrect. There is no mention of a fourth heart sound. The latter is often associated with filling of a stiff left ventricle (this can be seen in left ventricular hypertrophy, amyloid, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or scarred/fibrosed left ventricle due to ischaemia). The fourth heart sound is classically late diastolic or presystolic. It occurs if augmented atrial contraction causes presystolic ventricular distension so that the ventricle contracts with greater force.

stem: A 21-year-old woman presents to the clinic with symptoms of increased shortness of breath and decreased exercise tolerance. She used to be a keen hockey player when at school but is now virtually unable to even walk to the bus stop without becoming short of breath. On examination she looks tired and slightly short of breath at rest. Her BP is elevated at 145/92 mmHg. Echocardiogram showed increased right atrial size and elevated right atrial pressure by Doppler. Cardiac catheterization results were as follows: O 2 saturation SVC = 74% O 2 saturation RA = 82% O 2 saturation RV = 82% O 2 saturation LA = 95% O 2 saturation LV = 95%. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Secundum atrial septal defect
Cardiac catheterization is an invasive procedure in which catheters are inserted into the various chambers and vessels of the heart for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes. They can measure pressure and oxygen concentrations in the various chambers and vessels and help us to diagnose complex cardiac conditions.

stem: A 30-year-old pilot, who is otherwise fit and well, is found to have a WPW (Wolff–Parkinson–White) pre- excitation pattern on a routine ECG. The pilot does not report any symptoms. Which one of the following is the most suitable management?
options: Leave alone and repeat ECG after 6 months
Radiofrequency catheter ablation of accessory pathway
explanation:
Radiofrequency catheter ablation of accessory pathway
Patients with symptoms attributable to the accessory pathway, with a family history of sudden cardiac death, or asymptomatic patients in whom unpredictable tachyarrhythmias could affect their own or others’ well-being should proceed directly to a radiofrequency catheter ablation.

Amiodarone
Amiodarone is an alternative to ablation, but not in high risk professions or those who are symptomatic.

Class Iaantiarrhythmics
Class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics are an alternative to ablation, but not in high-risk professions or those who are symptomatic.

stem: A 40-year-old salesman presents with frequent flushing of his face and neck, abdominal pain, watery diarrhoea, fatigue, breathlessness, anorexia and nausea. On examination, there is jugular venous distension with prominent v waves, hepatomegaly and dependent oedema. On auscultation, a blowing pan-systolic murmur is heard on inspiration at the lower left sternal edge. What is the most likely cardiac abnormality in this case?
explanation:
Tricuspid incompetence
The auscultatory findings are suggestive of tricuspid incompetence. This patient most probably has carcinoid syndrome, which can occur in 5% of patients with carcinoid tumours if there are liver metastases. Cardiac abnormalities are found in 50% of patients, and consist of pulmonary stenosis or tricuspid incompetence.

Tricuspid stenosis
Tricuspid stenosis is incorrect. A rumbling mid-diastolic murmur is characteristic of tricuspid stenosis along with a prominent jugular venous a wave.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with a history of heavy smoking presents for review. She has woken during the early hours of the morning for the second time with shortness of breath so bad that she had to fling open the windows. On examination there are crackles in the lung bases, her chest X-ray (CXR) shows bilateral fluffy perihilar shadowing. ECG reveals small anterior Q waves and a sinus tachycardia of 105 bpm. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Pulmonary oedema
The clinical presentation is classic for pulmonary oedema. The description of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea is classical and fits best with an answer of Pulmonary oedema. The presence of fluffy CXR changes and the evidence of previous myocardial infarction all point to pulmonary oedema. Left ventricular failure The history of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, chest X-ray suggestive of pulmonary oedema and ECG with changes of a previous anterior myocardial infarction suggests that this woman is suffering from left ventricular failure. A history of pink frothy sputum and distended neck veins on examination would also contribute to the diagnosis. Causes of pulmonary oedema

stem: A 59-year-old man presents to the clinic for review. He suffered an inferior myocardial infarction some 3 years earlier, treated with coronary stenting. More recently he has begun to have difficulty maintaining his erection and wishes to start sildenafil. On examination his BP is 132/80 mmHg, pulse is 72/min and regular. He is not in cardiac failure. Which of the following medications should be discontinued prior to starting sildenafil?
explanation:
Nicorandil
Sildenafil (Viagra) is a drug that acts by inhibiting cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE 5), an enzyme that promotes degradation of cGMP that regulates blood flow to the penis. This causes activation of the nitric oxide (NO)/cGMP pathway and leads to vasodilation. It is used to treat erectile dysfunction in males and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Common side effects include headaches, heartburn and flushed skin. Caution is advised in those who have cardiovascular disease. Rare but serious side effects include prolonged erections (which can lead to damage to the penis) and sudden-onset hearing loss. Sildenafil should not be taken along with nitrates or nitrate donors such as nitroglycerin (GTN), as this may result in a severe and potentially fatal drop in blood pressure. Nicorandil is an anti-anginal medication that has dual properties of a nitrate and a potassium channel activator. It is an arterial and venous dilator and improves coronary blood flow due to potassium channel opening and nitrate effect. Nicorandil stimulates guanylate cyclase to increase formation of cyclic GMP at (cGMP) eventually causes vasodilation. It also acts as a potassium channel activator to promote K+ efflux and the

stem: A 50-year-old man presents to the Cardiac Ward with known poor left ventricular function. He has a regular broad complex tachycardia with capture and fusion beats at a rate of 150 bpm. His blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg. What is the most appropriate treatment of this patient?
explanation:
Amiodarone
Overall, by a process of elimination and by following the ALS guidelines, amiodarone is the most appropriate choice. Treating ventricular tachycardia: in the presence of poor left ventricular function, a regular broad complex tachycardia is highly likely to be ventricular tachycardia (VT). The capture and fusion beats are suggestive of VT VT, if haemodynamically compromised, must be treated with immediate DC cardioversion if the blood pressure is maintained, medical therapy can be tried amiodarone is typically first line and therefore is the correct answer. It should be given intravenously and should be given via a central line due to the risk of extravasation and consequent tissue damage.

stem: A 72-year-old man was admitted with an acute anterior myocardial infarction. He has chronic renal impairment, with a recent creatinine recorded at 148 μmol/litre. Medication included ramipril, atorvastatin and indapamide for the treatment of hypertension. He was taken straight to the angiography suite where he received stenting of a left main-stem stenosis. You are asked to see him after about 30 hours as the nurses feel he is deteriorating. On examination his BP is 149/84 mmHg, his pulse is 75 bpm and regular. His legs look dusky in colour, particularly his right big toe which looks blue in colour. He has splinter haemorrhages affecting toenails on both feet. There is a loud left femoral bruit. The table below contains the investigation results. Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 132 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.0 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 190 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 630 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine blood ++, protein + Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cholesterol embolism
The clinical scenario is of a 72-year-old man admitted with myocardial infarction. He has a past history of chronic renal impairement (baseline creatinine is 148 μmol/litre) and hypertension (on ramipril and indapamide). He has various skin changes including: Dusky colour of his legs – this indicates that the patient either has cyanosis (reduced blood flow) or livedo reticularis (reticulated mottled, bluish or erythematous skin due to blood flow compromise and oxygen desaturation through an affected area) His right big toe is blue in colour – this indicates cyanosis due to compromised blood flow. Acrocyanosis is a recognised sign of cholesterol embolism. Splinter haemorrhages affecting the toenails of both the feet – splinter haemorrhages are tiny blood clots that tend to run vertically under the nails. They are not specific to any particular condition and are associated with subacute infective endocarditis, SLE, scleroderma, psoriatic arthritis. Out of the given options, they are a cutaneous manifestation of cholesterol embolism. The patient also has a loud left femoral bruit – this indicates possible occlusion at the level of the femoral artery. Investigations show normal complete blood count with a high serum creatinine, hyperkalemia as well as blood and protein in urine indicative of acute kidney injury. Taking all these features into account suggests that cholesterol embolism is the most likely cause of the clinical picture seen here.

Renal vein thrombosis
Renal vein thrombosis is incorrect. Renal vein thrombosis is most often seen in patients with a hypercoagulable state (most commonly nephrotic syndrome, malignancy, renal cancer, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome etc). Patients usually present with other clinical features pointing towards the underlying cause (e.g. weight loss in malignancy, edema in nephrotic syndrome). Patients can also present with acute onset of flank pain and visible haematuria. Atherosclerosis and skin changes usually do not occur and there is no relation with cardiac vascular surgery. The clinical features given in the picture do not support a diagnosis of renal vein thrombosis.

Acute tubular necrosis
Acute tubular necrosis is incorrect. Acute tubular necrosis is the most common cause of acute kidney injury. It is usually related to ischaemic or toxic insult to the renal tubules (e.g. from hypovolemia, sepsis, drugs, contrast etc.). Patients usually present with clinical features of the underlying cause (e.g. fever from sepsis or drug history) and acute kidney injury. It does not cause embolic occlusion of blood vessels or atherosclerosis; hence the clinical scenario given does not fit with a diagnosis of acute tubular necrosis.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents to the cardiology clinic for review. His brother died suddenly of a cardiac arrest while playing Sunday league football, and was found on post-mortem to have an underlying diagnosis of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM). Which one of the following is the most appropriate way to rule out HOCM?
explanation:
Transthoracic ECHO
Patients with HOCM are at an increased risk of sudden cardiac death. The most common cause is ventricular arrhythmia. It usually occurs in young and asymptomatic patients and has been linked with physical exertion. HOCM is an autosomal dominant condition and most mutations have a high degree of penetrance, hence first- degree family members of an affected individual should be screened for the disease. Family screening should include history, physical examination, ECG and ECHO. Routine genetic testing is not recommended for screening of first-degree relatives unless a definite HOCM-causing mutation has been identified in the index case. The clinical diagnosis of HOCM is made with cardiac imaging – most commonly 2D ECHO or with cardiac MR. Transthoracic ECHO (TTE) is the investigation of choice for diagnosis and screening of HOCM. Transoesophageal ECHO (TEE) can also be used and provides better images but because it is invasive it is avoided unless the diagnosis is suspected, views are poor, and enhanced assessment is needed. The diagnosis is based on the presence a hypertrophied and nondilated left ventricle in the absence of any other cardiac or systemic disease capable of producing the degree of hypertrophy (usually >=15mm in Tutor adults).

stem: A 21-year-old man with Down syndrome presents to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath. He tells you this has increased significantly over the last few months and he is now unable to go out with his friends. On examination, he is clubbed and cyanosed at rest, his BP is 145/82 mmHg and pulse is 85/min. The patient has previously been noted to have a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal edge which is now less audible. Routine chest X-ray carried out by his GP a few weeks earlier shows prominent pulmonary vasculature, but nil else of note. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ventricular septal defect (VSD)
Atrioventricular septal defects (AVSDs) are the commonest cardiovascular abnormality seen in Down syndrome; the next most commonly seen are VSDs and ASDs. In this case the murmur is typical of that seen in VSD, and the clinical picture raises the possibility of a significant right to left shunt. Two-dimensional echocardiography coupled with Doppler flow analysis can be used to quantify the location of the lesion and estimate the size of any shunt. This patient should have a surgical consultation to determine surgical repair is indicated, although late presentation with evidence of shunt is associated with a poor outlook. Smaller VSDs may spontaneously close during childhood.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of increasing dyspnoea with strenuous exertion. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HOCM) is diagnosed. Which is the most appropriate screening method for his brother?
explanation:
Echocardiography
The diagnosis of HOCM requires unexplained myocardial hypertrophy, which is best visualised using two- dimensional echocardiography. Diagnostic = wall thickness exceeding 2 standard deviations for sex-, age- and size-matched populations. In practice, in an adult of normal size, a left ventricular myocardial segment of 1.5 cm or greater in thickness, in the absence of a recognised cause, is usually considered to be diagnostic. Less stringent criteria should be applied to first-degree relatives of an affected individual, where the probability of carrying the disease gene increases from 1:500 to 1:2. (HOCM is usually familial, with autosomal dominant transmission.)

Genetic screening
Genetic screening is incorrect. Genetic testing is useful for families with HOCM. However, it would be indicated for the brother only if a clinical diagnosis was made on echo, as genetic abnormalities are found in only approximately 50% of families.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with severe heart failure presents with increasing shortness of breath. Her current pharmacological treatment consists of an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, loop diuretic and ß- blocker. There is only mild ankle swelling and bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest. Her BP is 142/82 mmHg. Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Add spironolactone
Low-dose spironolactone has been shown to have positive effects on cardiovascular mortality in patients with end-stage heart failure.

Add digoxin
Add digoxin is incorrect. The positive inotropic effects of cardiac glycosides can be useful in reducing symptoms (mainly breathlessness) in patients already taking diuretics and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors; however, they have no effect on mortality and must be used with caution in patients such as this who are prone to disturbances of potassium.

stem: A 40-year-old man is referred by his GP for advice with regard to primary prevention of cardiovascular disease. He is a smoker with a strong family history of premature death from ischaemic heart disease. Following a period of lifestyle modification, his fasting cholesterol concentration is 7.2 mmol/litre. On consultation of the local guidelines you find that his estimated 10-year risk of a coronary heart disease event is > 30%. What would you advise?
explanation:
Statin
Prevention of cardiovascular disease The Joint British Societies (JBS) for the Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease have recently updated their guidelines for managing lipids. Non-fasting blood samples should be taken to measure total cholesterol (TC) and HDL-cholesterol. In the past, fast LDLc was used, but a more pragmatic approach of measuring non-HDL-c is now being proposed (determined by TC minus HDL-c = non-HDL-c). All high-risk people should receive professional lifestyle support to reduce total and LDL-c, raise HDL-c and lower triglycerides to reduce their CVD risk. Individuals should be offered interventions to address all modifiable risk factors, including: dietary advice smoking cessation advice and support

stem: A 62-year-old man with a blood pressure of 160/98 mmHg, total serum cholesterol of 6.5 mmol/l and HDL of 1.3 mmol/l is seen by his GP. On reviewing his records it appears the nurse has also documented hypertensive blood pressure readings at his last two well man checks. He is not diabetic and has never smoked. His family history is unknown as he was adopted. There is a history of exertional angina, which is worse on hill climbing and when walking his dog in cold weather. Apart from advice on lifestyle modification, which one of the following combination of drugs should he receive under current guidelines?
explanation:
Antihypertensive treatment, aspirin, statin
Based on a classical history of angina in a man aged > 55 with a total cholesterol > 6.47 mmol/l you can make a clinical diagnosis of coronary artery disease with a probability > 90% (NICE guidance 95). Therefore, aspirin should be recommended as the first-line anti-platelet agent. A statin should also be recommended. The selection of antihypertensive agents should be tailored to those that provide symptomatic benefit such as β-blockers or calcium-channel inhibitors, and prognostic benefit such as ACE inhibitors (NICE guidance 126).

Statin, aspirin
Statin, aspirin is incorrect. Current NICE guidance encourages the use of ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (NICE guidance 127) before treatment. However, with two previous readings and evidence of end-organ disease antihypertensive therapy should be initiated at this appointment.

stem: A cardiac catheter study was undertaken to establish the aetiology of pulmonary hypertension in a 49-year-old patient presenting with syncope and progressive shortness of breath. The wedge pressure was normal and the mean mitral valve diastolic pressure gradient was > 30 mmHg at rest, both of which increased with exercise. From these data, what is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Mitral stenosis
This is a relatively difficult question and requires familiarity with cardiac catherisation or understanding the relevance of abnormal values. The diastolic pressure in the left atrium is increased at rest and upon exercise, suggesting reduced flow through the mitral valve (as you might expect in mitral stenosis). The haemodynamic pattern is typical of mitral stenosis and may also be seen in cor triatriatum, in which there is a left atrial membrane.

Major occlusion of pulmonary arteries
Major occlusion of pulmonary arteries is incorrect. Major occlusion of pulmonary arteries by a clot or tumour is associated with a focal pressure gradient in a lobar or larger pulmonary artery, intravascular filling defect, or narrowing.

stem: In a 36-year-old patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy who has had a ventricular fibrillation arrest, which one of the following is likely to improve prognosis?
explanation:
Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator (ICD)
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) are at high risk of arrhythmogenic events. Patients with a confirmed episode of life-threatening arrhythmia (VF or sustained VT), should have an implanted defibrillator. This will monitor for other episodes of tachycardia and, if within defined treatment zones, will either attempt to perform anti-tachycardia pacing (to gain control over the arrhythmia and gradually slow it down) or it will perform DC defibrillation. The other options are all established therapies for HCM but are for symptomatic improvement and do not improve prognosis in a patient with confirmed VF. HCM Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is diagnosed by echocardiography. Asymmetrical septal hypertrophy, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and mitral regurgitation are all features. Angina, palpitations, dyspnoea and sudden death occur. Improvement of ventricular function with a β blocker, verapamil or amiodarone may help symptoms. Amiodarone may help prevent arrhythmias and sudden death. Dual-chamber pacing may help drug-resistant symptoms by causing depolarisation from Chatthe right with ventricular apex, resulting in altered motion of the intraventricular septum and a diminished subaortic

stem: A patient who has been inadvertently given an intravenous injection of potassium chloride develops ventricular tachycardia. His pulse is 150 bpm and blood pressure 60/40 mmHg. What would be the best first line of treatment in this case?
options: Insulin 10 units and 50 ml of 50% glucose
explanation:
DC cardioversion
Management of VT secondary to hyperkalaemia Since the patient is haemodynamically compromised, the first emergency step is immediately to perform DC cardioversion (DCCV) – otherwise VT will become VF leading to death.

10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate
10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate is incorrect. Injection of 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate would help to protect the myocardium against hyperkalaemia and the initiation of VT. It is typically used in a monitored environment. Calcium ions protect the cell membranes from the effects of hyperkalaemia but do not alter the potassium

Amiodarone
Amiodarone is incorrect. Amiodarone is only useful in haemodynamically stable cases of VT. Amiodarone is not therefore the first line option here.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Department with a collapse and palpitations after attending her end-of-term prom. The only medication history of note includes a recent antibiotic prescription for an infected toe. Past medical history includes allergy to penicillin. Family history reveals that her mother died suddenly at the age of 34 when the daughter was 3 years old. One aunt and one uncle have also passed away suddenly. Electrocardiogram (ECG) reveals sinus rhythm in the Emergency Department, but the QT interval is prolonged at 550 ms (corrected). Which one of the following conditions is most likely to be related to the patient’s collapse?
explanation:
Congenital long QT syndrome
The QT prolongation and history of sudden death in the family suggests the possibility of congenital long QT syndrome. QT interval can be prolonged in association with a number of medications, including: Erythromycin (prescribed for the patient’s foot) Ketoconazole Antihistamines Antiarrythmics. The condition is associated with torsades de pointes ventricular tachycardia.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with persistent indigestion-like pain, retrosternal in nature and radiating to his jaw. He is a heavy smoker of some 40 cigarettes per day and has been previously treated for Barrett’s oesophagus. On examination he is bradycardic at 55 bpm, has a blood pressure of 100/50 mmHg and looks unwell. ECG reveals ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Inferior myocardial infarction
Acute myocardial infarction Inferior myocardial infarction (MI) is the correct answer. This man has symptoms and signs of an acute MI; changes in the inferior leads on ECG testing confirm the diagnosis of inferior MI. Anterior MI: LAD occlusion – ST elevation in V1–V4. Lateral MI: LAD occlusion – ST elevation in V5, V6, aVL. Inferior MI: RCA occlusion – ST elevation in II, III, AVF, reciprocal depression in aVL Inferior MI with RV infarction: RCA occlusion – ST elevation in II, III, aVF, V1 and right-sided V4 lead (V4R). Posterior MI: RCA or LCx occlusion: ST depression in V1–V2, ST elevation in posterior leads if placed (V7–V9).

stem: For a 20-year-old man who has survived an out of hospital (VF) cardiac arrest, which one of the following is likely to be the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Implanted cardioverter defibrillator
Patients who have an out of hospital ventricular fibrillation (VF) arrest should undergo investigation to discover if the arrest was caused by infarction/ischaemia or by a chronic electrophysiological instability. 30% of patients will have a recurrence within 1 year, rising to 60% at 2 years. Treatment, in this case, at such a young age, a proarrhythmic state (such as due to cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, etc) is more likely than ischaemia and an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) is the most appropriate treatment. It is essential to exclude clear precipitants such as drug overdose or cocaine ingestion before ICD implantation. VT ablation may be appropriate in patients with definite VT.

Beta blocker
Beta blocker is incorrect. A β blocker is of use if ischaemia is the cause.

stem: You are crash-called to a 67-year-old man who is recovering on the Surgical Ward after a cholecystectomy. He has a history of ischaemic heart disease (IHD) and type II diabetes mellitus. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 70/50 mmHg. His pulse is 240 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. He is attached to the deﬁbrillator, his rhythm strip is shown below. Which of the following is the most important intervention?
explanation:
C DC cardioversion This man has unstable VT and is at imminent risk of developing pulseless VT or ventricular ﬁbrillation (VF). Following the Resuscitation Council adult tachyarrhythmia guidelines, the immediate treatment is DC cardioversion and therefore option C is correct. Anaesthetics should be involved so that sedation can be used. A IV amiodarone IV amiodarone, is used second line after DC cardioversion or for stable VT.

B IV lignocaine IV lignocaine, can also be used for VT, but is not part of the guidelines and should be used only with specialist involvement – ITU or Cardiology. D IV adrenaline IV adrenaline, is part of the adult advanced life support (ALS) algorithm, but is not indicated in this situation where the patient has not yet descended to cardiac arrest. E IV magnesium IV magnesium, is used for broad-complex tachycardias including polymorphic VT (torsades de pointes), again with expert advice. It will also be worth considering why the patient has developed this arrhythmia and become so unwell. Given that the patient has undergone abdominal surgery, he may be potassium and magnesium depleted, but these can be replaced soon after the cardioversion if required.

stem: A 48-year-old woman of West African origin comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review. She attended the Emergency Department after the General Practitioner was surprised to find a fast irregularly irregular pulse at routine review some one month ago. She was found to be in atrial fibrillation and now takes bisoprolol 5 mg daily. She comments that she has noticed progressive breathlessness over the past few months. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 118/77 mmHg; her pulse is 71 bpm (AF). There are minor bibasal crackles on auscultation of the chest. She has a red discoloration of both cheeks. There is a mid-late diastolic murmur, best heard with the patient in the left-lateral position. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 117 g/l 115–155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.4 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 271 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 119 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l You order an echocardiogram and suspect mitral stenosis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her mitral stenosis?
explanation:
Rheumatic fever
Rheumatic fever is the most likely cause of mitral stenosis in a patient of this age, although it is becoming considerably less common in the United States of America and Western Europe. It has now fallen to less than 1 in 100 000 per year. The fact that this patient originates from West Africa makes exposure to rheumatic fever more likely.

Carcinoid syndrome
Carcinoid syndrome is related to metastases from an underlying carcinoid tumour and is associated with diarrhoea, paroxysms of flushing, weight loss and tachycardia (including episodes of atrial fibrillation). Left- sided cardiac lesions, including mitral stenosis, are seen more rarely than right-sided lesions in carcinoid syndrome and are associated with pulmonary metastases.

Degenerative valve calcification
Degenerative valve calcification is the next most common cause of mitral stenosis outside of rheumatic fever; however, given that this patient is 48 years old, it is unlikely here. Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy is the intervention of choice for symptomatic mitral stenosis – especially where there is evidence of pulmonary hypertension.

stem: A 55-year-old man who has sustained an acute myocardial infarction (MI) subsequently presents with heart failure. As well as other treatments the cardiologist has recommended that a β-blocker be commenced. According to currently available evidence, which of the following β-blockers would be most appropriate?
explanation:
Bisoprolol
Beta-blockers may produce benefit in heart failure by blocking sympathetic activity. The β-blockers currently licensed for heart failure in the UK are bisoprolol, carvedilol and nebivolol – they reduce mortality in any grade of stable heart failure.

Celiprolol
Celiprolol is incorrect. Celiprolol is a β-blocker whose pharmacology makes it useful for hypertension and control of effort-induced angina.

Propranolol
Propranolol is incorrect. Propranolol is a β-blocker used for a variety of indications including hypertension, palpitations, thyrotoxicosis, performance anxiety and essential tremor. It is not licensed for heart failure.

stem: A 58-year-old male patient has suffered from a recent acute inferior myocardial infarction 3 days ago. He initially recovered well, but has become acutely unwell with a hypotensive episode. There is a pansystolic murmur, which is accentuated by inspiration, along the lower left sternal border. A Swan–Ganz catheter is inserted and the following noted: right atrial pressure is 12 (very high); calculated left atrial pressure is 2 (low normal). Which one of the following is the likely cause?
explanation:
Tricuspid regurgitation
The right atrial pressure is significantly elevated while the left atrial pressure is low. Therefore, the condition must affect the right side of the heart and not the left. Tricuspid regurgitation is the correct answer as it also explains the murmur – which right-sided heart failure does not alone. Tricuspid regurgitation Tricuspid regurgitation may occur in post-myocardial infarction, in association with: cor pulmonale rheumatic heart disease infective endocarditis carcinoid syndrome Ebstein anomaly

stem: An 18-year-old man with Marfan syndrome attends for review in the cardiology clinic, after an abnormal screening electrocardiogram that showed left axis deviation and prominent Q waves in II, III, aVF and V3–V6. His blood pressure is 140/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 70 bpm. Which cardiac abnormality is most likely?
explanation:
Aortic regurgitation
Marfan syndrome is characteristically associated with progressive aortic root dilatation, leading to aortic regurgitation and an increased risk of dissection. Other skeletal manifestations include: tall stature scoliosis chest wall malformations high arched palate lens dislocation. Mitral valve prolapse is also common but there is no association with other congenital malformations or cardiomyopathy. ECG showing left axis deviation and prominent Q waves are mainly due to left ventricular hypertrophy. The left ventricular hypertrophy is due to the aortic regurgitation as obvious due to repeated regurgitation of blood in the ventricles. Moreover, left axis deviation in ECG may also be significant for inferior wall myocardial infarction.

stem: An 18-year-old student is admitted from a night club in a state of collapse. On admission to the Emergency Department his blood pressure is 90/45 mmHg, and he has a pulse of 190 bpm. ECG reveals a narrow complex tachycardia, which is terminated with adenosine. ECG after termination of the tachycardia reveals a PR interval of approximately 100 ms, and a slurred QRS complex with delta wave. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome
The ECG description is classical for Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome. Features of the other conditions are not present and therefore these conditions are not the right answer. Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome Wolff–Parkinson–White (WPW) syndrome is due to a congenital accessory cardiac conduction pathway, called the bundle of Kent, that connects the atria to the ventricles, enabling electrical activity to bypass the atrioventricular node. There can be more than one pathway and these may conduct antegrade (towards the ventricle), retrograde (towards the atria), or in both directions. ECG abnormalities are characterised by the presence of a PR interval < 120 ms and a QRS complex > 120 ms with slurred, slowly rising onset (delta wave). They present with paroxysmal tachycardias in 10% of patients aged 20–40 years, and 35% of sufferers aged over 60 years. Common types of arrhythmia at presentation include reciprocating tachycardia at 150–250 bpm (80%), atrial fibrillation (15%) and atrial flutter (5%).

stem: The use of prostaglandin to keep the ductus arteriosus open is necessary in which of the following?
options: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return with obstruction
explanation:
Tricuspid atresia
Keeping the ductus arteriosus patent is beneficial in any cyanotic heart disease. That is, any condition in which blood flow to the lungs for oxygenation is compromised. The cyanotic heart diseases include: tetralogy of Fallot (ToF) total anomalous pulmonary venous connection hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) transposition of the great arteries (d-TGA) truncus arteriosus (persistent) tricuspid atresia interrupted aortic arch pulmonary atresia (PA) pulmonary stenosis (critical). In each of these conditions, prostaglandin E may be administered to keep the ductus open.

stem: A 52-year-old man is referred by his General Practitioner (GP) due to a systolic murmur. The GP suspects aortic stenosis (AS). Which of the following factors in this patient's history would cause a decrease in the intensity of his AS murmur?
explanation:
Atrial fibrillation
The classical murmur of aortic stenosis is a crescendo-decrescendo murmur, which begins shortly after the first heart sound (ejection systolic murmur) heard best with the diaphragm of the stethoscope in the 2nd intercostal space in a patient who is sitting upright leaning forward. The intensity increases toward midsystole, then decreases, and the murmur ends just before the second heart sound (S2). It is generally a harsh, low-pitched murmur with a grating quality. The murmur typically radiates to the right clavicle and both carotid arteries (left often louder than right). The intensity of the systolic murmur does not correspond to the severity of aortic stenosis; rather, the timing of the peak and the duration of the murmur correspond to the severity of aortic stenosis. The more severe the stenosis, the longer the duration of the murmur and the more likely it peaks at late systole. As LV contractility decreases in critical AS, the murmur becomes softer and shorter. The intensity of the murmur may therefore be misleading in these circumstances. When the left ventricle fails and cardiac output falls, the aortic stenosis murmur becomes softer and may be barely audible. Atrial fibrillation with short R-R intervals can also decrease the murmur intensity or make it inaudible.

stem: A patient has tuboeruptive xanthomas as characterised by red papules and nodules that appear inflamed and tend to coalesce, distributed subcutaneously and mainly on the extensor surface of the extremities. Lipid-profile testing showed increased levels of total cholesterol and triglyceride, and decreased levels of high-density lipoprotein. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Type III hyperlipoproteinaemia
Tuboeruptive xanthomas occur in type-III hyperlipoproteinaemia, which is due to high numbers of chylomicrons and high levels of intermediate-density lipoprotein. The most common cause for this form is the apolipoprotein E2/E2 genotype. Type-III hyperlipoproteinaemia is due to cholesterol-rich, very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL).
